stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the pedigree, determine the most likely mode of inheritance of Syndrome X (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, or X-linked recessive). Provide evidence from the pedigree to justify your answer. Then determine the genotypes of individuals I-1, I-2, II-3, and II-4.

Part B: Individual II-3 and individual II-4 (who is phenotypically unaffected but a known carrier) plan to have children.
Using a Punnett square or probability notation, determine the probability that their first child will be affected by Syndrome X.
Individual II-3 and II-4 have four children. Three are unaffected and one is affected. Perform a chi-square (χ²) analysis to determine whether these data are consistent with the expected ratio. Use a significance level of p = 0.05 and 1 degree of freedom (χ²_crit = 3.84).

Part C: A new genetic test reveals that the gene responsible for Syndrome X is located on chromosome 7, approximately 8 cM from a molecular marker called M1. In a test cross of an individual heterozygous at both loci (in coupling) with a doubly homozygous recessive individual, 200 offspring are produced.
Predict the number of offspring expected in each of the four phenotypic classes.
Explain why the linked loci produce offspring frequencies that differ from the 1:1:1:1 ratio expected if the loci were unlinked.

Part D: Explain how nondisjunction of chromosome 7 during meiosis II changes the chromosome number of the resulting gametes. Predict the chromosome number of a zygote formed when an abnormal gamete containing two copies of chromosome 7 is fertilized by a normal gamete.
stimulus:
Pedigree for Syndrome X (three generations):

Generation I:  I-1 (affected female) × I-2 (unaffected male)
Generation II: II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected female), II-3 (affected female), II-4 (unaffected male), II-5 (unaffected male), II-6 (unaffected female)
Generation III: III-1 (unaffected), III-2 (affected), III-3 (unaffected), III-4 (unaffected)

Note: II-3 and II-4 are mated (III-1 through III-4 are their children). II-4 is a known carrier.

criteria.learner_facing_text: Determine autosomal-recessive inheritance from pedigree evidence and assign the four requested genotypes.
Determine the affected-child probability and complete the chi-square analysis against the 1:1 expectation.
Predict the four linked testcross classes and explain their departure from the unlinked 1:1:1:1 expectation.
Explain meiosis-II nondisjunction and predict the resulting abnormal gamete and zygote chromosome numbers.

canonical_answer_1:
(a) Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive. Evidence: the affected mother I-1 and unaffected father I-2 have both affected and unaffected children, consistent with aa × Aa; affected II-3 and unaffected known-carrier II-4 likewise produce both phenotypes. X-linked recessive inheritance is ruled out because I-1 is an affected female; if the trait were X-linked recessive, I-1 would be homozygous (XaXa) and would necessarily pass one Xa chromosome to EVERY son, making all of her sons affected — but sons II-4 and II-5 are unaffected, which is inconsistent with X-linked recessive inheritance. Dominant inheritance (autosomal or X-linked) is inconsistent with two unaffected parents (I-2, and II-4 "known carrier") producing affected children. Therefore the trait is autosomal recessive.
Genotypes (A = normal/dominant allele, a = disease/recessive allele): I-1 (affected) = aa; I-2 (unaffected father, must be a carrier because he and affected I-1 produced affected children) = Aa; II-3 (affected) = aa; II-4 (unaffected, given as a known carrier) = Aa.

(b)(i) Cross II-3 (aa) × II-4 (Aa) is a testcross. Punnett square: gametes from Aa parent = 1/2 A, 1/2 a; combined with aa parent's a gamete → offspring genotypes: 1/2 Aa (unaffected), 1/2 aa (affected). Probability the first child is affected = 1/2 (50%).

(b)(ii) Expected ratio for this Aa × aa cross is 1:1 (unaffected:affected). With 4 children, expected = 2 unaffected, 2 affected. Observed = 3 unaffected, 1 affected.
χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E = (3−2)²/2 + (1−2)²/2 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0.
With df = 1, χ²_crit = 3.84. Since the calculated χ² (1.0) is less than χ²_crit (3.84), we fail to reject the null hypothesis — the observed data are NOT significantly different from the expected 1:1 ratio; the small deviation is consistent with chance sampling variation given the small sample size (n=4).

(c)(i) The disease locus and marker M1 are 8 cM apart, so recombination frequency = 8%. In a coupling heterozygote (disease allele and M1 on one homolog; normal allele and m1 on the other) testcrossed to a doubly homozygous recessive individual, gametes from the heterozygous parent are: parental types (92% total, split 46%/46%) and recombinant types (8% total, split 4%/4%). Of 200 offspring:
• Parental class 1 (disease-allele phenotype with M1 marker present): 46% × 200 = 92
• Parental class 2 (normal phenotype, marker M1 absent): 46% × 200 = 92
• Recombinant class 1 (disease-allele phenotype, marker M1 absent): 4% × 200 = 8
• Recombinant class 2 (normal phenotype, marker M1 present): 4% × 200 = 8
(Total = 200.)

(c)(ii) If the two genes were unlinked (on different chromosomes or far enough apart to assort independently), independent assortment during meiosis I would randomize allele combinations equally, producing an expected 1:1:1:1 ratio (50 offspring per class) regardless of parental combinations. Because these genes ARE linked (only 8 cM apart), the two alleles that started out together on the same parental homolog (coupling) are transmitted together far more often than not, since separating them requires a crossover event between the loci, which happens in only ~8% of meioses. This produces a large excess of parental-type offspring (92 each) relative to recombinant types (8 each), sharply deviating from the 1:1:1:1 ratio expected under independent assortment.

(d) Normally, meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (one maternal, one paternal homolog) into different secondary cells, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids (genetically identical copies produced by DNA replication of a single homolog) into different gametes. If nondisjunction occurs during meiosis II -- sister chromatids of chromosome 7 fail to separate at anaphase II -- one resulting gamete receives both (identical) sister-chromatid copies of chromosome 7, making it disomic (n+1) for chromosome 7, while the other resulting gamete receives no copy of chromosome 7 (n-1). When the n+1 gamete (carrying two copies of chromosome 7) is fertilized by a normal gamete (carrying one copy of chromosome 7), the resulting zygote has three total copies of chromosome 7 -- it is trisomic for chromosome 7 (2n+1), one chromosome more than the normal diploid number.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The Meselson-Stahl experiment demonstrated that DNA replication is semiconservative. Describe the experimental design and results of the Meselson-Stahl experiment. Explain how the results support the semiconservative model rather than the conservative or dispersive models.

Part B: Describe the roles of the following enzymes during DNA replication in eukaryotes, and explain why each is necessary:
Helicase
DNA primase
DNA polymerase III (or the equivalent leading-strand polymerase)
DNA ligase

Part C: The template DNA strand for a gene has the following sequence:
5'-ATCGGATCCAAGTCG-3'
Write the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this template strand.
Using the genetic code table, determine the amino acid sequence encoded by the mRNA, beginning from the first codon. Identify which codon, if any, is a start codon or stop codon.
A point mutation changes the 8th base of the template strand from C to T. Determine whether this mutation is synonymous or nonsynonymous, and explain the consequence for the protein.

Part D: A researcher treats cells with a drug that specifically blocks the activity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Predict and explain the cellular consequences of this drug treatment for protein synthesis.
stimulus:
DNA replication and gene expression are fundamental processes of the central dogma. Key facts:

• DNA replication is semiconservative: each daughter molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand
• Replication occurs 5'→3' on the new strand; the template is read 3'→5'
• RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA using the template (antisense) strand
• The genetic code is read in triplet codons (non-overlapping)
• AUG = start codon (Met); UAA, UAG, UGA = stop codons

Partial codon table (relevant to part c):
AUC = Ile | GGA = Gly | UCC = Ser | AAG = Lys | UCG = Ser
AUG = Met | CCA = Pro | AGU = Ser | CUU = Leu
UAG = stop | UCA = Ser | GAC = Asp | GUC = Val
canonical_answer_1:
(a) In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, E. coli were grown for many generations in medium containing heavy nitrogen (15N) as the sole nitrogen source, so that all newly synthesized DNA incorporated 15N into its nitrogenous bases, producing uniformly "heavy" DNA. Cells were then transferred to medium containing only light nitrogen (14N), and DNA was extracted after each round of replication (generation). DNA samples were separated by cesium chloride (CsCl) density-gradient centrifugation, which separates DNA molecules by density. Results: after one generation, all DNA banded at a single, intermediate density — halfway between pure heavy (15N/15N) and pure light (14N/14N) DNA. After two generations, DNA showed two bands: one at the intermediate density and one at the fully light density, present in equal amounts. This pattern supports the semiconservative model: the intermediate band after generation 1 shows each new DNA duplex contains one old (heavy) strand paired with one new (light) strand — ruling out the conservative model, which predicts that after one generation there would be one fully heavy band (the original parental duplex, intact) and one fully light band (an entirely new duplex), never an intermediate band. The appearance of a fully light band after the second generation (from a duplex whose original heavy strand was paired with light in generation 1, then that light strand served as template for another light strand) together with a persisting intermediate band rules out the dispersive model, which predicts that DNA would remain as a single band of progressively decreasing (but never purely light) density each generation, since old and new DNA would be randomly interspersed throughout every molecule.

(b)(i) Helicase: unwinds the parental DNA double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs at the replication fork, generating the single-stranded template DNA needed for replication; necessary because DNA polymerase can only synthesize using single-stranded template.
(ii) DNA primase: synthesizes a short RNA primer complementary to the template strand, providing a free 3'-OH group to which new nucleotides can be added; necessary because DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo — they can only extend an existing strand from a free 3'-OH.
(iii) DNA polymerase III (the main replicative/leading-strand polymerase): synthesizes new DNA by adding nucleotides complementary to the template strand in the 5'→3' direction (continuously on the leading strand, in short Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand); necessary because it is the enzyme that actually catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation to extend the growing DNA strand, with proofreading (3'→5' exonuclease) activity that maintains replication fidelity.
(iv) DNA ligase: seals the remaining nicks between adjacent DNA fragments (e.g., between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand after RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA) by catalyzing formation of a phosphodiester bond between a 3'-OH end and an adjacent 5'-phosphate end; necessary to produce one continuous, unbroken DNA strand rather than a series of disconnected fragments.

(c)(i) Template strand: 5'-ATCGGATCCAAGTCG-3'. mRNA is synthesized complementary and antiparallel to the template (mRNA polymerized 5'→3' as the template is read 3'→5'), so the mRNA sequence equals the reverse complement of the template:
mRNA: 5'-CGACUUGGAUCCGAU-3'

(c)(ii) Reading the mRNA in codons from the first base: CGA-CUU-GGA-UCC-GAU. Using the standard genetic code: CGA = Arginine (Arg), CUU = Leucine (Leu) [confirmed in the provided partial codon table], GGA = Glycine (Gly) [confirmed in table], UCC = Serine (Ser) [confirmed in table], GAU = Aspartate (Asp). Amino acid sequence: Arg-Leu-Gly-Ser-Asp. None of these five codons is AUG (start) or a stop codon (UAA/UAG/UGA) — comparing against the table's AUG and UAG entries confirms neither appears in this sequence — so this reading frame contains no start codon and no stop codon; translation of this specific mRNA segment (as an isolated open reading frame) would not initiate or terminate within the given sequence.

(c)(iii) The mutation changes the 8th base of the template strand from C to T. Template position 8 is the middle base of the third template triplet (positions 7-9, template sequence TCC), which corresponds to mRNA codon 3 (mRNA positions 7-9 = GGA = Glycine, Gly). Template position 8 (C) pairs with mRNA position 8 (G); after the template C->T mutation, the complementary mRNA base becomes A (T pairs with A), so mRNA codon 3 changes from GGA (Gly) to GAA (Glutamate, Glu). Because the resulting codon specifies a different amino acid (Gly->Glu) rather than the same one, this is a NONSYNONYMOUS (missense) point mutation. Consequence: the protein product now has glutamate instead of glycine at this position; this is a single amino acid substitution (not a frameshift, since it is a substitution not an insertion/deletion, and not a nonsense mutation, since it doesn't create a premature stop codon) — glycine's small size and flexibility are often structurally important (e.g., in tight turns), so depending on how critical this residue is to protein folding or function, this substitution could range from minimal effect to significantly altering or abolishing protein function.

(d) Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases catalyze the covalent attachment ("charging") of each amino acid to the 3' CCA end of its correct, cognate tRNA, using ATP. If a drug blocks this enzyme activity, tRNAs can no longer be charged with their amino acids. Without charged (aminoacyl-) tRNAs available, ribosomes have no amino acids to deliver to the A site during translation, so the addition of new amino acids to a growing polypeptide chain cannot occur — protein synthesis (translation) would be halted globally across the cell. Existing proteins already made would remain functional in the short term, but the cell would be unable to synthesize any new proteins (needed to replace degraded/short-lived proteins, respond to signals, replicate, or carry out normal cellular functions), which would ultimately be lethal to the cell.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe the Meselson-Stahl experiment and explain how results support semiconservative replication.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must include: (1) Design — bacteria grown in heavy ¹⁵N medium → DNA becomes all-heavy; then switched to ¹⁴N medium → allow one or two rounds of replication; DNA isolated and centrifuged in CsCl gradient to separate by density; (2) Results — after 1st replication: ONE BAND at intermediate density (hybrid ¹⁵N/¹⁴N); after 2nd replication: TWO BANDS — one intermediate, one light; (3) Interpretation — semiconservative predicts hybrid at generation 1 (one old ¹⁵N strand + one new ¹⁴N strand per molecule); dispersive predicts one intermediate band at generation 1 too, but generation 2 dispersive predicts ONE band (still intermediate) vs. semiconservative (two bands). Conservative predicts one heavy + one light band after generation 1 (not seen). The two-band result at generation 2 eliminates dispersive and confirms semiconservative. 1 pt for design/results, 1 pt for eliminating at least one alternative model with explanation.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Bacteria grown in ¹⁵N → switched to ¹⁴N → DNA banded in CsCl gradient; after generation 1: one hybrid band; after generation 2: hybrid + light bands. This eliminates conservative (would give heavy + light at gen 1) and dispersive (would give one gradually lightening band at gen 2) models.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe the roles of helicase, DNA primase, DNA polymerase III, and DNA ligase in replication.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must correctly describe each role: (1) Helicase — unwinds/unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs; creates the replication fork; (2) DNA primase — synthesizes short RNA primers complementary to the template strand; provides the 3'-OH that DNA polymerase requires to begin synthesis (DNA polymerase cannot initiate de novo); (3) DNA polymerase III — synthesizes the new DNA strand by adding deoxyribonucleotides to the 3'-OH of the primer, reading the template 3'→5' and synthesizing 5'→3'; proofreads via 3'→5' exonuclease; (4) DNA ligase — joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent DNA fragments after RNA primers are removed and replaced. Award 1 pt per 2 correct enzyme descriptions (minimum: role must be mechanistically correct).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Helicase unwinds DNA; primase makes RNA primers so polymerase can start; DNA pol III synthesizes new strand 5'→3' using template; ligase joins Okazaki fragments on lagging strand.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Write the mRNA sequence; determine the amino acid sequence; analyze the point mutation.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (c)(i) mRNA (5'->3') = CGACUUGGAUCCGAU, obtained by complementing the template (read 3'->5') and substituting U for T. (c)(ii) Codons read from the first base: CGA-CUU-GGA-UCC-GAU = Arg-Leu-Gly-Ser-Asp (using the standard genetic code for CGA/GAU, confirmed by the provided table for CUU/GGA/UCC); no AUG start or UAA/UAG/UGA stop codon appears in this segment. (c)(iii) The template's 8th base (C) is the middle base of codon 3 (mRNA positions 7-9 = GGA = Gly). Changing template position 8 from C to T changes the complementary mRNA base from G to A, so codon 3 becomes GAA = Glu. This is a NONSYNONYMOUS (missense) mutation (Gly->Glu), a single amino-acid substitution, not a frameshift or nonsense mutation.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: mRNA = 5'-CGACUUGGAUCCGAU-3'; codons CGA-CUU-GGA-UCC-GAU = Arg-Leu-Gly-Ser-Asp; template position 8 (C->T) falls in codon 3, changing GGA (Gly) to GAA (Glu) -- a nonsynonymous substitution.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain the consequences of blocking aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must explain mechanism first: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are the enzymes that attach the correct amino acid to the correct tRNA (charging the tRNA). Each synthetase is specific for one amino acid and recognizes the corresponding tRNA anticodon. Blocking them → tRNAs cannot be charged with amino acids → uncharged tRNAs accumulate; tRNA cannot deliver amino acids to the ribosome → translation halts (ribosomes stall at the A site, waiting for aminoacyl-tRNA) → no new proteins are synthesized → cell loses ability to make all proteins → cell dies. Additional consequences: accumulation of uncharged tRNAs; ribosome stalling; activation of amino acid starvation response (stringent response in bacteria); in eukaryotes, activation of integrated stress response (ISR), eIF2α phosphorylation. 1 pt for mechanism (tRNA not charged, translation halted), 1 pt for cellular consequence (all protein synthesis stops → cell death / stress response).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs with their correct amino acids. Blocking them → tRNAs remain uncharged → cannot deliver amino acids to ribosomes → translation halts globally → all protein synthesis stops → cell cannot maintain homeostasis → cell death.

mRNA: 5'-CGACUUGGAUCCGAU-3'

(c)(ii) Reading the mRNA in codons from the first base: CGA-CUU-GGA-UCC-GAU. Using the standard genetic code: CGA = Arginine (Arg), CUU = Leucine (Leu) [confirmed in the provided partial codon table], GGA = Glycine (Gly) [confirmed in table], UCC = Serine (Ser) [confirmed in table], GAU = Aspartate (Asp). Amino acid sequence: Arg-Leu-Gly-Ser-Asp. None of these five codons is AUG (start) or a stop codon (UAA/UAG/UGA) — comparing against the table's AUG and UAG entries confirms neither appears in this sequence — so this reading frame contains no start codon and no stop codon; translation of this specific mRNA segment (as an isolated open reading frame) would not initiate or terminate within the given sequence.

(c)(iii) The mutation changes the 8th base of the template strand from C to T. Template position 8 (the middle base of the template triplet spanning positions 7–9, "TCC") pairs with mRNA position 8 (since mRNA is the antiparallel complement, template position p corresponds to mRNA position 16−p for this 15-base sequence). mRNA position 8 falls in mRNA codon 3 (positions 7–9 = UCC = Ser). Complementary to template C, mRNA position 8 was G; after the template C→T mutation, the complementary mRNA base becomes A (T pairs with A), so mRNA codon 3 changes from UCC (Ser) to UAC (Tyrosine, Tyr). Because the resulting codon specifies a different amino acid (Ser→Tyr) rather than the same one, this is a NONSYNONYMOUS (missense) point mutation. Consequence: the protein product now has tyrosine instead of serine at this position; this is a single amino acid substitution (not a frameshift, since it is a substitution not an insertion/deletion, and not a nonsense mutation, since it doesn't create a premature stop codon) — depending on how critical this residue is to protein folding or function (e.g., if serine's polar/phosphorylatable side chain was functionally important), this substitution could range from having minimal effect to significantly altering or abolishing protein function.

(d) Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases catalyze the covalent attachment ("charging") of each amino acid to the 3' CCA end of its correct, cognate tRNA, using ATP. If a drug blocks this enzyme activity, tRNAs can no longer be charged with their amino acids. Without charged (aminoacyl-) tRNAs available, ribosomes have no amino acids to deliver to the A site during translation, so the addition of new amino acids to a growing polypeptide chain cannot occur — protein synthesis (translation) would be halted globally across the cell. Existing proteins already made would remain functional in the short term, but the cell would be unable to synthesize any new proteins (needed to replace degraded/short-lived proteins, respond to signals, replicate, or carry out normal cellular functions), which would ultimately be lethal to the cell.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe the Meselson-Stahl experiment and explain how results support semiconservative replication.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must include: (1) Design — bacteria grown in heavy ¹⁵N medium → DNA becomes all-heavy; then switched to ¹⁴N medium → allow one or two rounds of replication; DNA isolated and centrifuged in CsCl gradient to separate by density; (2) Results — after 1st replication: ONE BAND at intermediate density (hybrid ¹⁵N/¹⁴N); after 2nd replication: TWO BANDS — one intermediate, one light; (3) Interpretation — semiconservative predicts hybrid at generation 1 (one old ¹⁵N strand + one new ¹⁴N strand per molecule); dispersive predicts one intermediate band at generation 1 too, but generation 2 dispersive predicts ONE band (still intermediate) vs. semiconservative (two bands). Conservative predicts one heavy + one light band after generation 1 (not seen). The two-band result at generation 2 eliminates dispersive and confirms semiconservative. 1 pt for design/results, 1 pt for eliminating at least one alternative model with explanation.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Bacteria grown in ¹⁵N → switched to ¹⁴N → DNA banded in CsCl gradient; after generation 1: one hybrid band; after generation 2: hybrid + light bands. This eliminates conservative (would give heavy + light at gen 1) and dispersive (would give one gradually lightening band at gen 2) models.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe the roles of helicase, DNA primase, DNA polymerase III, and DNA ligase in replication.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must correctly describe each role: (1) Helicase — unwinds/unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs; creates the replication fork; (2) DNA primase — synthesizes short RNA primers complementary to the template strand; provides the 3'-OH that DNA polymerase requires to begin synthesis (DNA polymerase cannot initiate de novo); (3) DNA polymerase III — synthesizes the new DNA strand by adding deoxyribonucleotides to the 3'-OH of the primer, reading the template 3'→5' and synthesizing 5'→3'; proofreads via 3'→5' exonuclease; (4) DNA ligase — joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent DNA fragments after RNA primers are removed and replaced. Award 1 pt per 2 correct enzyme descriptions (minimum: role must be mechanistically correct).
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Helicase unwinds DNA; primase makes RNA primers so polymerase can start; DNA pol III synthesizes new strand 5'→3' using template; ligase joins Okazaki fragments on lagging strand.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain the consequences of blocking aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Analyze the beak depth data from Table 1. Using evidence from the data, describe the change in the finch population's beak depth between 1976 and 1978, and explain the mechanism of natural selection responsible for this change. Address: the source of variation, the selective agent, differential survival, and heritability.

Part B: Using the allele frequencies provided in Table 2, determine whether the medium ground finch population in 1976 was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the beak depth gene. Show all calculations. (Use p = frequency of allele D; q = frequency of allele d.)

Part C: A 1983 El Niño event brought heavy rainfall to the Galápagos, dramatically increasing the abundance of small soft seeds. By 1984, mean beak depth had shifted back toward smaller values.
Identify the type of natural selection acting on beak depth after the 1983 El Niño, and explain why small beak depth was favored.
Explain why this shift in beak depth does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance.

Part D: The large ground finch (Geospiza magnirostris) arrived on Daphne Major Island after 1982 and occupies a similar ecological niche to the medium ground finch. Explain the concept of competitive exclusion and predict what might happen to the medium ground finch population as a result of G. magnirostris's arrival. Describe ONE possible evolutionary outcome for the medium ground finch population that would allow coexistence.
stimulus:
Table 1: Mean beak depth (mm) of the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major Island, Galápagos

Year | Mean beak depth (mm) | Sample size | Notes
1976 |        9.42          |    642      | Pre-drought
1977 |        9.96          |    85       | During drought (severe dry season)
1978 |       10.07          |    388      | Post-drought recovery

Drought conditions (1976-1977): Small soft seeds became scarce first; large hard seeds remained available longer. Birds with larger, deeper beaks could crack large seeds that smaller-beaked birds could not process.

Survival: 85 of 642 birds survived the drought. Mean beak depth of survivors = 9.96 mm (significantly larger than pre-drought mean of 9.42 mm).

Table 2: Allele frequencies for a beak depth quantitative trait locus (simplified diploid model)
Allele D (associated with deeper beaks): frequency = 0.6
Allele d (associated with shallower beaks): frequency = 0.4

Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 population (N=642):
DD: 0.40 | Dd: 0.42 | dd: 0.18
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976, pre-drought) to 9.96 mm in drought survivors, and remained elevated at 10.07 mm by 1978. This reflects natural selection acting on pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth within the finch population (source of variation: beak depth varies among individual finches due to underlying genetic differences, i.e., standing genetic variation, prior to the drought). The selective agent was the drought-induced scarcity of small, soft seeds, which left only large, hard seeds available; birds needed sufficiently deep, strong beaks to crack these large hard seeds. This produced differential survival: only 85 of 642 birds survived the drought, and the survivors had a significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population mean (9.42 mm) — individuals with deeper beaks were better able to access/process the remaining large hard seeds and thus survived and reproduced at higher rates than shallow-beaked individuals. Because beak depth is heritable (passed from parents to offspring via genes), the surviving (deeper-beaked) birds' offspring inherited genes for deeper beaks, so the population's mean beak depth remained elevated (10.07 mm) into the next generation (1978) — this shift in the population's genetic/phenotypic composition, resulting from differential reproductive success of individuals with a heritable advantageous trait, is natural selection.

(b) Given allele frequencies p (allele D) = 0.6 and q (allele d) = 0.4, expected genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are: DD = p² = 0.36, Dd = 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48, dd = q² = 0.16. Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 (N=642) were: DD = 0.40, Dd = 0.42, dd = 0.18. Converting to counts: Expected counts — DD = 0.36×642 = 231.1, Dd = 0.48×642 = 308.2, dd = 0.16×642 = 102.7. Observed counts — DD = 0.40×642 ≈ 257, Dd = 0.42×642 ≈ 270, dd = 0.18×642 ≈ 116.
χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E = (257−231.1)²/231.1 + (270−308.2)²/308.2 + (116−102.7)²/102.7
= (25.9)²/231.1 + (−38.2)²/308.2 + (13.3)²/102.7
= 670.8/231.1 + 1459.2/308.2 + 176.9/102.7
≈ 2.90 + 4.73 + 1.72 = 9.35
With df = 1 (3 genotype classes − 1 − 1 estimated allele frequency parameter) and χ²_crit = 3.84 (p=0.05), the calculated χ² (9.35) exceeds χ²_crit (3.84), so we reject the null hypothesis of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium — the observed genotype frequencies deviate significantly from HWE expectations, meaning the 1976 population was NOT in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this locus (consistent with ongoing natural selection/nonrandom mating rather than the idealized HWE assumptions of no selection, random mating, no migration, no mutation, and infinite population size).

(c)(i) After the 1983 El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant, and mean beak depth shifted back toward smaller values by 1984 — this is directional selection (selection favoring one phenotypic extreme, shifting the population mean in one direction), here favoring SMALLER beak depth. Small, soft seeds require less force to crack open, so finches with smaller, more slender beaks could feed on them efficiently (with less energy expenditure/handling time) than deep-beaked finches, which are specialized for large, hard seeds but are less efficient at processing small soft seeds; with small soft seeds now abundant, smaller-beaked birds had a survival/foraging advantage, so directional selection shifted the population mean toward smaller beak depth.

(c)(ii) This shift does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance because no individual bird's beak physically changed in response to use or environmental conditions during its own lifetime and then passed that acquired change to offspring (which is what Lamarckian "inheritance of acquired characteristics" would require). Instead, the shift reflects a change in the population's allele frequencies due to natural selection acting on pre-existing heritable genetic variation: individuals that already happened to carry alleles for smaller beak depth had higher relative survival/reproduction under the new (post-El Niño) conditions, so those alleles increased in frequency in the next generation. The mechanism is differential reproductive success of pre-existing genotypes, not modification of an individual's traits during its lifetime followed by inheritance of that modification.

(d) The competitive exclusion principle states that two species cannot indefinitely coexist in the same community if they compete for exactly the same limiting resource(s) in the same way, because the more efficient competitor will eventually outcompete and exclude the other from that shared niche. G. magnirostris, with its larger beak, is a superior competitor for large, hard seeds compared to the medium ground finch. As G. magnirostris establishes itself on Daphne Major and competes for this same large-seed resource, medium ground finches (especially those individuals with larger beak depths, most similar in diet/niche to G. magnirostris) may experience increased competition for large seeds, potentially reducing their survival and reproductive success and causing a decline in the medium ground finch population (or at least in its large-beaked segment). A possible evolutionary outcome allowing coexistence is character displacement: natural selection could favor medium ground finches with smaller beak depths (shifting the population's beak-depth distribution away from overlap with G. magnirostris), resulting in niche partitioning where medium ground finches specialize increasingly on smaller seeds while G. magnirostris specializes on larger seeds — reducing direct resource competition and allowing the two species to coexist on the island.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Analyze beak depth data and explain the mechanism of natural selection — variation, selective agent, differential survival, heritability.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Data analysis: mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976) to 10.07 mm (1978), a shift of ~0.65 mm. This is directional selection toward deeper beaks. Four components: (1) Variation — natural heritable variation in beak depth existed in the 1976 population (beak depth is a heritable polygenic trait with continuous variation); (2) Selective agent — the 1977 drought depleted small soft seeds, leaving only large hard seeds available; birds with larger/deeper beaks had a survival advantage because they could crack large hard seeds; (3) Differential survival — only 85/642 birds survived (13%); survivors had significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population (9.42 mm) — evidence that large beaks conferred survival advantage; (4) Heritability — beak depth is heritable (genetic basis); surviving birds passed their deeper-beak alleles to offspring → 1978 post-drought population showed larger mean beak depth than 1976. Award 1 pt for correct data description (direction and evidence) + 1 pt for addressing at least 3 of the 4 evolutionary mechanism components.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Beak depth increased ~0.65mm from 1976 to 1978 due to directional selection: drought eliminated small seeds → only birds with deep beaks could crack large seeds → differential survival (only 13% survived, with larger mean beak depth) → heritable deep-beak alleles passed to offspring → population mean shifted.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using 1976 allele frequencies; show all calculations.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: p = 0.6 (freq D), q = 0.4 (freq d). Expected H-W genotype frequencies: p^2 = 0.36 (DD), 2pq = 0.48 (Dd), q^2 = 0.16 (dd). Observed frequencies: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18 (N=642). Chi-square requires counts, not raw proportions: Expected counts -- DD=0.36x642=231.1, Dd=0.48x642=308.2, dd=0.16x642=102.7. Observed counts -- DD=0.40x642=257, Dd=0.42x642=270, dd=0.18x642=116. Chi-square = (257-231.1)^2/231.1 + (270-308.2)^2/308.2 + (116-102.7)^2/102.7 = 2.90+4.73+1.72 = 9.35. With df=1, critical value=3.84. Since 9.35 > 3.84, REJECT the null hypothesis of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium -- the 1976 population was NOT in H-W equilibrium (consistent with the ongoing directional selection described in part a). 1 pt for correct expected genotype frequencies; 1 pt for converting to counts and computing chi-square correctly; 1 pt for the correct conclusion (reject H-W equilibrium).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Expected: DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16. Must convert to counts (N=642) before computing chi-square: chi-square=9.35 > 3.84 critical value -> reject H-W equilibrium; population was NOT in equilibrium.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Identify selection type after 1983 El Niño; explain why this is not Lamarckian.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) After El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant → small beaks efficient for small soft seeds → directional selection toward SMALLER beaks (opposite direction from drought). OR: if both small and large seeds abundant → stabilizing selection on intermediate beak depth. Most defensible: directional selection toward smaller beaks because small seeds are now abundant and favored. Small-beaked birds can efficiently process abundant small seeds; large seeds may now be scarce; smaller beaks may require less energy to maintain. (ii) Not Lamarckian because: Lamarckian inheritance requires that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime are directly inherited by offspring (use/disuse + inheritance of acquired characteristics). In this case: birds did not develop smaller beaks during their lifetime because seeds got smaller. Rather, birds with pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth (small beaks) happened to have higher fitness in the new environment → differential reproduction → their alleles increased in frequency. The beak size change in the population is due to differential reproduction of pre-existing variants, not inheritance of acquired traits. 1 pt per sub-part.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) Directional selection toward smaller beaks — El Niño brought small soft seeds, which small-beaked birds can exploit more efficiently. (ii) Not Lamarckian — birds did not shrink their own beaks in response to environment; rather, small-beaked individuals already in the population survived and reproduced more, passing their heritable alleles forward.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain competitive exclusion; predict outcome for medium ground finch; describe an evolutionary coexistence outcome.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Competitive exclusion principle: two species with identical ecological niches (same resource requirements) cannot coexist indefinitely; the superior competitor will exclude the inferior. G. magnirostris is larger with a deeper beak — better competitor for large hard seeds. If medium ground finch and G. magnirostris compete for the same large hard seeds: G. magnirostris may outcompete and exclude G. fortis → G. fortis population declines or goes locally extinct on Daphne Major. Evolutionary coexistence outcome (any ONE of): (1) Character displacement — natural selection favors G. fortis individuals with beaks different from G. magnirostris (e.g., smaller beaks focusing on small seeds that G. magnirostris cannot exploit efficiently) → two species diverge in beak size → resource partitioning → coexistence; (2) Niche differentiation — G. fortis specializes on different food resources (different seed types, different microhabitat); (3) Temporal partitioning — foraging at different times. Character displacement is the best-supported evolutionary mechanism. Note: actual documentation of character displacement in Galápagos finches is a classic case study. 1 pt for competitive exclusion definition + prediction; 1 pt for evolutionary coexistence mechanism.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist — G. magnirostris would outcompete G. fortis for large seeds → G. fortis may be excluded. Evolutionary coexistence: character displacement — selection favors G. fortis individuals with smaller beaks that exploit small seeds G. magnirostris cannot efficiently use → niche differentiation → stable coexistence.

A possible evolutionary outcome allowing coexistence is character displacement: natural selection could favor medium ground finches with smaller beak depths (shifting the population's beak-depth distribution away from overlap with G. magnirostris), resulting in niche partitioning where medium ground finches specialize increasingly on smaller seeds while G. magnirostris specializes on larger seeds — reducing direct resource competition and allowing the two species to coexist on the island.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Analyze beak depth data and explain the mechanism of natural selection — variation, selective agent, differential survival, heritability.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Data analysis: mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976) to 10.07 mm (1978), a shift of ~0.65 mm. This is directional selection toward deeper beaks. Four components: (1) Variation — natural heritable variation in beak depth existed in the 1976 population (beak depth is a heritable polygenic trait with continuous variation); (2) Selective agent — the 1977 drought depleted small soft seeds, leaving only large hard seeds available; birds with larger/deeper beaks had a survival advantage because they could crack large hard seeds; (3) Differential survival — only 85/642 birds survived (13%); survivors had significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population (9.42 mm) — evidence that large beaks conferred survival advantage; (4) Heritability — beak depth is heritable (genetic basis); surviving birds passed their deeper-beak alleles to offspring → 1978 post-drought population showed larger mean beak depth than 1976. Award 1 pt for correct data description (direction and evidence) + 1 pt for addressing at least 3 of the 4 evolutionary mechanism components.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Beak depth increased ~0.65mm from 1976 to 1978 due to directional selection: drought eliminated small seeds → only birds with deep beaks could crack large seeds → differential survival (only 13% survived, with larger mean beak depth) → heritable deep-beak alleles passed to offspring → population mean shifted.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using 1976 allele frequencies; show all calculations.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: p = 0.6 (freq D), q = 0.4 (freq d). p + q = 1.0 ✓. Expected H-W genotype frequencies: p² = (0.6)² = 0.36 (DD); 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48 (Dd); q² = (0.4)² = 0.16 (dd). Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. Comparison: DD observed (0.40) > expected (0.36); Dd observed (0.42) < expected (0.48); dd observed (0.18) > expected (0.16). Deviations are present. To formally test, χ²: (0.40-0.36)²/0.36 + (0.42-0.48)²/0.48 + (0.18-0.16)²/0.16 = 0.0044/0.36 + 0.0036/0.48 + 0.0004/0.16 = 0.012 + 0.0075 + 0.0025 = 0.022. With df=1 (for 2-allele), critical value ~3.84. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 → fail to reject H-W equilibrium (deviations not significant). Conclusion: population is approximately in H-W equilibrium. 1 pt for correct expected frequencies; 1 pt for comparison to observed and correct conclusion.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Expected: DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16. Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 critical value → population does not significantly deviate from H-W equilibrium.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Identify selection type after 1983 El Niño; explain why this is not Lamarckian.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) After El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant → small beaks efficient for small soft seeds → directional selection toward SMALLER beaks (opposite direction from drought). OR: if both small and large seeds abundant → stabilizing selection on intermediate beak depth. Most defensible: directional selection toward smaller beaks because small seeds are now abundant and favored. Small-beaked birds can efficiently process abundant small seeds; large seeds may now be scarce; smaller beaks may require less energy to maintain. (ii) Not Lamarckian because: Lamarckian inheritance requires that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime are directly inherited by offspring (use/disuse + inheritance of acquired characteristics). In this case: birds did not develop smaller beaks during their lifetime because seeds got smaller. Rather, birds with pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth (small beaks) happened to have higher fitness in the new environment → differential reproduction → their alleles increased in frequency. The beak size change in the population is due to differential reproduction of pre-existing variants, not inheritance of acquired traits. 1 pt per sub-part.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) Directional selection toward smaller beaks — El Niño brought small soft seeds, which small-beaked birds can exploit more efficiently. (ii) Not Lamarckian — birds did not shrink their own beaks in response to environment; rather, small-beaked individuals already in the population survived and reproduced more, passing their heritable alleles forward.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain competitive exclusion; predict outcome for medium ground finch; describe an evolutionary coexistence outcome.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Competitive exclusion principle: two species with identical ecological niches (same resource requirements) cannot coexist indefinitely; the superior competitor will exclude the inferior. G. magnirostris is larger with a deeper beak — better competitor for large hard seeds. If medium ground finch and G. magnirostris compete for the same large hard seeds: G. magnirostris may outcompete and exclude G. fortis → G. fortis population declines or goes locally extinct on Daphne Major. Evolutionary coexistence outcome (any ONE of): (1) Character displacement — natural selection favors G. fortis individuals with beaks different from G. magnirostris (e.g., smaller beaks focusing on small seeds that G. magnirostris cannot exploit efficiently) → two species diverge in beak size → resource partitioning → coexistence; (2) Niche differentiation — G. fortis specializes on different food resources (different seed types, different microhabitat); (3) Temporal partitioning — foraging at different times. Character displacement is the best-supported evolutionary mechanism. Note: actual documentation of character displacement in Galápagos finches is a classic case study. 1 pt for competitive exclusion definition + prediction; 1 pt for evolutionary coexistence mechanism.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist — G. magnirostris would outcompete G. fortis for large seeds → G. fortis may be excluded. Evolutionary coexistence: character displacement — selection favors G. fortis individuals with smaller beaks that exploit small seeds G. magnirostris cannot efficiently use → niche differentiation → stable coexistence.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: A student sets up the following experiment: potato (Solanum tuberosum) cylinders of equal mass are placed in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations for 24 hours. Mass change is recorded.
Using the data in Table 1, graph the percent mass change versus sucrose concentration (or describe the graph's decreasing trend and label the near-zero crossing between 0.3 M and 0.4 M).
Estimate the sucrose concentration at which the potato tissue is in osmotic equilibrium with the surrounding solution. Explain what this concentration tells you about the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue.
At the 0.2 M sucrose solution, predict and explain the direction of net water movement and the expected physical state of the potato cells.

Part B: Water potential determines the direction of water movement. A potato cell with solute potential of -7.0 bars is placed in an external pure-water solution for which water potential = 0 bars and pressure potential = 0 bars.
Define water potential and write the equation Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p, defining each term.
Calculate the pressure potential of the potato cell at equilibrium with the external pure-water solution. Explain what this value represents in the context of plant cell turgor.

Part C: Compare the response of a plant cell and an animal cell (e.g., a red blood cell) placed in each of the following solutions. Use appropriate terminology (plasmolysis, crenation, lysis, turgor, etc.):
A hypotonic solution
A hypertonic solution

Part D: Aquaporins are membrane protein channels that facilitate the movement of water across cell membranes. A researcher finds that certain plant cells in a drought-stressed leaf can reduce water loss by decreasing aquaporin expression.
Explain the mechanism by which aquaporins facilitate water movement without violating the passive nature of osmosis.
Predict the effect of aquaporin deletion on a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution, compared to a normal cell. Explain your prediction.
stimulus:
Table 1: Mass change of potato cylinders in sucrose solutions

Sucrose concentration (M) | Initial mass (g) | Final mass (g) | % Mass change
         0.0              |      5.00        |     5.42       |    +8.4%
         0.1              |      5.00        |     5.22       |    +4.4%
         0.2              |      5.00        |     5.08       |    +1.6%
         0.3              |      5.00        |     5.01       |    +0.2%
         0.4              |      5.00        |     4.99       |    −0.2%
         0.5              |      5.00        |     4.78       |    −4.4%
         0.6              |      5.00        |     4.55       |    −9.0%
         0.8              |      5.00        |     4.21       |    −15.8%

Note: All measurements at 22°C. Potato samples are from the same tuber.
canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Graph description: percent mass change starts strongly positive (+8.4%) at 0 M sucrose and decreases progressively (in a roughly linear, downward-sloping trend) as sucrose concentration increases, crossing from positive to negative between 0.3 M (+0.2%) and 0.4 M (−0.2%), and continuing to decline to a strongly negative value (−15.8%) at 0.8 M. Key points to label: the y-intercept at (0 M, +8.4%), the x-intercept (zero mass change) at approximately 0.35 M, and the endpoint at (0.8 M, −15.8%).

(a)(ii) The sucrose concentration at osmotic equilibrium (0% mass change) falls between 0.3 M (+0.2%) and 0.4 M (−0.2%); interpolating, this is approximately 0.35 M. This tells us that the internal solute concentration of the potato tissue is approximately 0.35 M (in sucrose-equivalent terms) — at this external concentration, water has no net tendency to move into or out of the cells because the internal and external solute (and thus water potential) concentrations are equal.

(a)(iii) At 0.2 M sucrose, the external solution (0.2 M) is hypotonic relative to the potato tissue (whose internal solute concentration is ~0.35 M) — the potato cells have a higher internal solute concentration than the surrounding solution. Net water movement will be INTO the potato cells, down the water potential gradient from the more dilute external solution (higher Ψ) to the more concentrated cell interior (lower Ψ), consistent with the observed mass gain (+1.6%). As water enters, the cells become more turgid: the protoplast swells and presses against the cell wall, increasing turgor pressure, but the rigid cell wall prevents lysis.

(b)(i) Water potential (Ψ) is a measure of the free energy of water per unit volume/area, which determines the direction water will move (water moves from regions of higher Ψ to regions of lower Ψ); it is measured in pressure units (bars or MPa). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, where Ψs (solute potential/osmotic potential) is the reduction in water potential caused by dissolved solutes (always ≤ 0, since solutes reduce the free energy/entropy available to water), and Ψp (pressure potential) is the physical pressure exerted on the water — in plant cells this is typically the turgor pressure created by the protoplast pushing against the rigid cell wall (positive when the cell is turgid).

(b)(ii) The potato tissue's Ψs = −7.0 bars. Placed in pure water, Ψ(outside) = 0 bars (Ψs = 0, Ψp = 0 for pure water). At equilibrium, water potential inside the cell equals water potential outside: Ψ(inside) = Ψ(outside) → Ψs + Ψp = 0 → (−7.0) + Ψp = 0 → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This positive pressure potential represents the turgor pressure built up inside the cell as water enters and the protoplast presses against the cell wall; the wall pushes back with an equal, opposing pressure. At equilibrium, this turgor pressure exactly counterbalances the tendency of water to keep entering due to the cell's negative solute potential (even though a concentration difference in solutes still exists), so net water movement stops — the cell is fully turgid.

(c) Hypotonic solution: Plant cell — water moves INTO the cell (down the water potential gradient, since the hypotonic solution has a higher Ψ than the cell); the rigid cellulose cell wall prevents the cell from bursting by generating counter (pressure) potential, so the cell becomes turgid (firm), which is beneficial for structural support. Animal cell (e.g., RBC) — water moves into the cell, but with no rigid wall to resist expansion and build counter-pressure, the cell can swell uncontrollably and undergo lysis (membrane rupture).
Hypertonic solution: Plant cell — water moves OUT of the cell (toward the lower-Ψ hypertonic external solution); the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall, a process called plasmolysis, and the cell becomes flaccid (loses turgor). Animal cell — water moves out and the cell shrinks/shrivels, a process called crenation.

(d)(i) Aquaporins are channel proteins that form water-permeable pores across the membrane, allowing water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer much more rapidly (facilitated diffusion) than by unassisted diffusion through the membrane alone. Aquaporins do not use ATP and cannot move water against its water-potential gradient — they simply provide a faster, lower-resistance pathway for water to move down the SAME gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) that would drive movement anyway. Because movement is still occurring passively down an existing free-energy gradient (aquaporins only increase the rate/permeability, not the direction or the thermodynamic favorability of movement), the process remains passive osmosis, not active transport.

(d)(ii) A cell with reduced/deleted aquaporin expression placed in a hypertonic solution will still lose water — net water movement will still be OUT of the cell, since the direction is dictated by the water potential gradient (unchanged by aquaporin presence) — but the RATE of water loss (and thus the rate of plasmolysis) will be SLOWER than in a normal cell, because water must now cross the membrane primarily via slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer itself rather than through the fast aquaporin channels. The final equilibrium extent of plasmolysis would eventually be similar to a normal cell, but the aquaporin-deficient cell would take longer to reach that equilibrium state.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Graphs or accurately describes the decreasing relationship between sucrose concentration and percent mass change, including the near-zero crossing between 0.3 M and 0.4 M.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predicts water movement into the potato at 0.2 M and the resulting turgid state of the potato cells.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Defines water potential and its components; calculates the potato cell pressure potential at equilibrium with the external pure-water solution.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: 1 point: defines water potential as determining direction of water movement and gives Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p with Psi_s and Psi_p defined. 1 point: uses the potato cell solute potential -7.0 bars and equilibrium with the external pure-water solution water potential 0 bars to calculate pressure potential +7.0 bars. 1 point: interprets +7.0 bars as turgor pressure from the cell wall opposing inward water movement.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Label water potential 0 bars and pressure potential 0 bars as values for the external pure-water solution, then show 0 = -7.0 + pressure potential so the potato cell pressure potential is +7.0 bars.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Compares plant-cell and animal-cell responses in both hypotonic and hypertonic solutions using correct terminology.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: 1 point for hypotonic comparison: plant cells take up water and become turgid because the cell wall prevents lysis, while animal cells take up water and may lyse. 1 point for hypertonic comparison: plant cells lose water and plasmolyze, while animal cells lose water and crenate.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: For full credit, describe both plant and animal cell responses in both hypotonic and hypertonic solutions, with turgor, lysis, plasmolysis, and crenation used correctly.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how aquaporins facilitate osmosis without violating passive transport; predict effect of aquaporin deletion in hypertonic solution.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Aquaporins facilitate osmosis by providing a hydrophilic channel for water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer rapidly and selectively. They do not provide energy or actively pump water — they only lower the activation energy barrier for water movement through the membrane by creating a pore lined with hydrophilic amino acids through which water molecules pass in single file via hydrogen bonding. Water movement through aquaporins is still driven entirely by the water potential gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) — the thermodynamic driving force is unchanged; only the rate (permeability) is increased. This is facilitated diffusion, not active transport. (ii) In hypertonic solution: normal cell — aquaporins allow rapid net efflux of water → cell rapidly loses water → plasmolysis occurs quickly. Aquaporin-deleted cell — water can still cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion (lipid bilayer has some intrinsic water permeability), but much more slowly → plasmolysis occurs more slowly (or is attenuated in rate) but the eventual equilibrium state is the same (still loses water to hypertonic solution). The final equilibrium is driven by thermodynamics, not kinetics — aquaporins affect RATE of water loss, not direction or final equilibrium. 1 pt for correct passive mechanism explanation; 1 pt for predicting slower (not absent) water loss with correct reasoning.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that aquaporins are passive hydrophilic channels that increase the rate of water movement down a water-potential gradient; then predict slower water loss/plasmolysis in hypertonic solution after deletion, not a reversed or active process.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Identify osmotic equilibrium concentration; explain water movement direction and cell state at 0.2 M.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Osmotic equilibrium: approximately 0.35–0.40 M sucrose (between 0.3 M where mass is nearly unchanged at +0.2% and 0.4 M where mass is slightly decreased at −0.2%). Interpolating: equilibrium is at approximately 0.35 M, where mass change = 0%. This concentration equals the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue — at this concentration, the water potential of the solution equals the water potential of the potato, so no net water movement. At 0.2 M sucrose: the solution is LESS concentrated than potato tissue (~0.35 M) → potato tissue has more negative water potential than the solution → water moves INTO the cells by osmosis. Potato cells gain water → cells become turgid (cell wall provides counter-pressure, preventing lysis). 1 pt for identifying equilibrium concentration with reasoning; 1 pt for correct direction of water movement at 0.2 M with explanation.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Equilibrium ≈ 0.35 M (where % mass change = 0). Potato tissue solute concentration ≈ 0.35 M. At 0.2 M: solution is hypotonic to potato → water moves INTO cells → cells become turgid/swell.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Define water potential and its components; calculate pressure potential at equilibrium in pure water.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Water potential (Ψ): the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water; determines direction of water movement (water moves from high Ψ to low Ψ). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Ψs (solute potential / osmotic potential): always ≤ 0 in solutions; becomes more negative as solute concentration increases; reflects the reduction in water potential due to dissolved solutes. Ψp (pressure potential / turgor pressure): can be positive (pressure from cell wall pushing back) or negative (tension in xylem); reflects the effect of physical pressure on water potential. (ii) At equilibrium with pure water (Ψwater = 0): Ψcell = 0. Ψ = Ψs + Ψp → 0 = −7.0 + Ψp → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This represents full turgor pressure — the cell wall is pushing back with +7.0 bars of pressure against the inward osmotic flow. The cell is fully turgid. 1 pt for correct definitions with equation; 1 pt for correct calculation and interpretation of Ψp = +7.0 bars as turgor pressure.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Compare plant cell and animal cell responses in hypotonic and hypertonic solutions.

Animal cell (RBC) — water enters by osmosis → cell swells → if sufficiently hypotonic, cell may burst (lyse/cytolysis) because no cell wall provides resistance; RBCs lyse in pure water. Animal cell (RBC) — water leaves by osmosis → cell shrinks → crenation (cell becomes spiky/star-shaped as membrane buckles). Key difference: plant cells have a cell wall that prevents lysis in hypotonic conditions; animal cells lack a cell wall and can lyse. 1 pt per correct comparison (hypotonic and hypertonic, with plant vs. animal distinction and correct terminology).

The final equilibrium is driven by thermodynamics, not kinetics — aquaporins affect RATE of water loss, not direction or final equilibrium. 1 pt for correct passive mechanism explanation; 1 pt for predicting slower (not absent) water loss with correct reasoning.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the data in Table 1, describe how reaction rate changes as substrate concentration increases, and explain why the rate reaches a maximum (saturates) at high substrate concentration even though more substrate is available.

Part B: Table 2 shows the same enzyme's activity in the presence of Inhibitor A and Inhibitor B, each tested across a range of substrate concentrations. Inhibitor A's effect can be substantially overcome by adding more substrate; Inhibitor B's effect cannot. Classify each inhibitor as competitive or noncompetitive and justify your classification using this evidence. Describe where each type of inhibitor binds (the active site vs. an allosteric site) and explain how binding there reduces enzyme activity.

Part C: Some enzymes are regulated by allosteric inhibitors that are end products of the metabolic pathway the enzyme participates in. Explain how this represents allosteric regulation. Include the difference between the allosteric site and the active site, and explain how binding at the allosteric site changes the enzyme's shape and activity.

Part D: Temperature affects enzyme activity in a characteristic bell-shaped curve.
Explain why enzyme activity increases from 0°C to the temperature optimum.
Explain why enzyme activity decreases sharply above the temperature optimum, connecting your answer to denaturation.
stimulus:
Table 1: Enzyme kinetics (no inhibitor)
[Substrate] μM | Reaction rate (μmol/min)
     10         |        10
     20         |        16.7
     40         |        25
     80         |        33.3
    160         |        40
    500         |        47.6
   1000         |        49.5
   5000         |        50.0

Table 2: Enzyme activity with inhibitors (1 mM each), at low vs. high substrate concentration
               | Rate at low [S] (μmol/min) | Rate at high [S] (μmol/min)
No inhibitor   |            10               |            50
Inhibitor A    |             4               |            48
Inhibitor B    |             5               |            25
canonical_answer_1:
(a) From Table 1, reaction rate approaches an asymptote near 50 μmol/min at high substrate concentrations (49.5–50.0 μmol/min at [S] = 1000–5000 μM), so Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min. Km is the substrate concentration at which reaction rate equals half of Vmax (25 μmol/min); the table shows rate = 25 μmol/min occurs exactly at [S] = 40 μM, so Km ≈ 40 μM.
Biological significance: Km is inversely related to the enzyme's apparent affinity for its substrate — a LOW Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a low substrate concentration, indicating HIGH affinity (the enzyme binds and processes substrate effectively even when substrate is scarce); a HIGH Km indicates lower affinity (more substrate is needed to achieve the same fractional saturation). Vmax reflects the maximum catalytic capacity of the enzyme population under the given conditions, once the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate — it depends on the total amount/concentration of enzyme present and each enzyme molecule's intrinsic turnover number (kcat, how quickly an individual enzyme molecule converts bound substrate to product).

(b)(i) Inhibitor A: Vmax unchanged (50, same as no inhibitor) but Km increased (120 vs. 40) → classified as a COMPETITIVE inhibitor. A higher apparent Km means more substrate is required to reach half-maximal velocity, consistent with the inhibitor competing with substrate for the same binding site — but because sufficiently high substrate concentration can still outcompete the inhibitor, the same Vmax can eventually be reached.
Inhibitor B: Vmax decreased (25 vs. 50) but Km unchanged (40, same as no inhibitor) → classified as a NONCOMPETITIVE inhibitor. Vmax is reduced because a fraction of enzyme molecules is rendered nonfunctional regardless of substrate concentration, but the affinity (Km) of the remaining active enzyme for substrate is unaffected, since this inhibitor does not compete at the active site.

(b)(ii) Competitive inhibitor (A): binds reversibly to the enzyme's active site itself, typically because it structurally resembles the substrate, physically blocking the substrate from binding there. Because this competition is reversible and concentration-dependent, sufficiently high substrate concentrations can outcompete/displace the inhibitor from the active site, so the reaction can still eventually reach the same Vmax as uninhibited enzyme (just requiring more substrate — a higher apparent Km).
Noncompetitive inhibitor (B): binds to a site on the enzyme distinct from the active site (an allosteric site), inducing a conformational change that impairs or abolishes the enzyme's catalytic activity regardless of how much substrate is bound. Because it does not compete with substrate for the active site, increasing substrate concentration cannot reverse this inhibition — the Vmax of the enzyme population is reduced (some fraction of enzyme is nonfunctional at any time), while the Km (affinity) of the still-active, uninhibited enzyme molecules remains unchanged.

(c) Threonine deaminase catalyzes the first committed step of the pathway converting threonine to isoleucine. Isoleucine, the pathway's end product, binds threonine deaminase at an allosteric site — a regulatory binding site physically and structurally distinct from the active site, where threonine itself binds and is chemically converted. When isoleucine binds this allosteric site, it induces a conformational change that is transmitted through the enzyme's tertiary/quaternary structure to the active site, distorting its shape so that it can no longer efficiently bind threonine or catalyze the reaction — reducing enzyme activity. This is feedback inhibition (end-product inhibition): the pathway's own final product inhibits an enzyme earlier in its own biosynthetic pathway, creating a self-regulating mechanism — as isoleucine accumulates to sufficient levels, it shuts down further isoleucine production by inhibiting threonine deaminase, preventing wasteful overproduction; as isoleucine is consumed/depleted, inhibition is relieved and the pathway resumes.

(d)(i) From 0°C up to the temperature optimum, increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules, increasing both the frequency and the energy of molecular collisions between them; this increases the rate at which enzyme–substrate complexes form and successfully proceed to products, so reaction rate increases with temperature in this range.
(d)(ii) Above the temperature optimum, reaction rate decreases sharply because excess thermal energy disrupts the weak, noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain the enzyme's precise tertiary/quaternary structure. The enzyme begins to denature (unfold from its native, catalytically functional conformation), progressively distorting or destroying the specific shape of the active site required for substrate binding and catalysis, so catalytic activity falls off rapidly as an increasing fraction of enzyme molecules become permanently denatured and nonfunctional.
(d)(iii) A thermophilic bacterium's enzyme would likely have structural features that create MORE and/or stronger stabilizing interactions holding its tertiary/quaternary structure together — e.g., more ionic bonds/salt bridges, more hydrogen bonds, more disulfide bonds, and/or tighter hydrophobic core packing — than the equivalent mesophilic enzyme. These additional stabilizing interactions allow the thermophilic protein to resist thermal denaturation and maintain its functional 3D conformation (and active-site shape) at the higher temperatures characteristic of the thermophile's environment, whereas the mesophilic enzyme's comparatively fewer/weaker stabilizing interactions cause it to denature at the lower temperatures typical of mesophilic environments.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain allosteric regulation by an end-product inhibitor, distinguishing the allosteric site from the active site.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Allosteric regulation: the enzyme has two distinct sites — the active site (where threonine binds and is converted to α-ketobutyrate, the first step toward isoleucine biosynthesis) and the allosteric (regulatory) site (where isoleucine binds as an inhibitor). These sites are physically separate and do not overlap. Feedback inhibition mechanism: when isoleucine accumulates (end product of the pathway), isoleucine binds the allosteric site of threonine deaminase → induces a conformational change in the enzyme's tertiary/quaternary structure → changes the shape of the active site → reduces affinity for threonine (or reduces kcat) → enzyme activity decreases → less isoleucine is produced. Significance: prevents overproduction of isoleucine; maintains metabolic balance without wasteful synthesis; response is rapid (no transcription needed — direct protein-level regulation). Difference from active site: allosteric site does not bind substrate and does not perform catalysis; it is a regulatory site that modulates active site conformation through cooperative conformational changes.

Isoleucine binding causes conformational change → active site shape altered → reduced threonine binding or catalysis → less isoleucine produced → negative feedback. Prevents overproduction.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the rise and fall of the temperature-activity curve, connecting the decline to denaturation.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Below optimum: increasing temperature increases average kinetic energy of both substrate and enzyme molecules → more frequent and energetic collisions between substrate and active site → more productive enzyme-substrate encounters per unit time → reaction rate increases. (ii) Above optimum: thermal energy exceeds the strength of non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds) holding the enzyme in its functional 3D shape → protein denatures (unfolds) → active site geometry is disrupted → enzyme loses catalytic function → activity drops sharply. This is irreversible denaturation (unlike reduced activity at low temperature, which is reversible). (iii) Thermophilic enzyme adaptations: more disulfide bonds (covalent, highly stable), more proline residues in loops (restricts backbone flexibility, reducing entropy-driven unfolding), denser hydrophobic core (more hydrophobic amino acids buried, stronger hydrophobic interactions), more ionic bonds (salt bridges) especially at surface, fewer flexible loops that can denature first. Functional result: higher energy (temperature) required to overcome the stabilizing forces → higher temperature optimum. 1 pt for molecular explanation of each side of the curve; 1 pt for thermophile adaptations.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Below optimum: more kinetic energy → faster substrate-enzyme collisions → higher rate. Above optimum: thermal energy breaks non-covalent bonds → denaturation → active site disrupted → activity lost irreversibly. Thermophile enzymes: more disulfide bonds, proline residues, denser hydrophobic core, salt bridges → resist denaturation at high temperature.
