stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: A pancreatic acinar cell synthesizes and secretes the digestive enzyme trypsinogen. Trace the complete pathway of a trypsinogen molecule from its synthesis to its secretion from the cell. Name each organelle or cellular structure involved and describe what happens to the protein at each step.

Part B: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) has functions distinct from the rough ER (RER). Describe THREE functions of the SER in a liver cell.

Part C: Lysosomes are membrane-bounded organelles containing digestive enzymes. Explain:
How the cell ensures its own digestive enzymes end up inside lysosomes rather than being secreted from the cell.
Why lysosomal enzymes do not destroy the lysosome's own membrane.
What happens when a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome.

Part D: A researcher treats cells with a drug that blocks vesicle budding from the Golgi apparatus. Predict and explain the effect of this treatment on: (i) secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein; (ii) delivery of digestive enzymes to lysosomes; (iii) the size and appearance of the ER in treated cells.
stimulus:
The endomembrane system consists of the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, and plasma membrane. The nuclear envelope is directly continuous with the ER. Most other compartments are functionally connected by vesicular transport.

Golgi apparatus: proteins are modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing), sorted, and packaged. The cis face receives vesicles from the ER; the trans face sends vesicles toward their destinations.
canonical_answer_1:
(a) mRNA encoding trypsinogen is translated by ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): a signal sequence on the growing polypeptide is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), directing the ribosome to dock at the RER membrane, and the polypeptide is threaded into the RER lumen as it is synthesized, where it begins folding (assisted by chaperone proteins) and is glycosylated. The protein is then packaged into COPII-coated transport vesicles that bud from the RER membrane and travel to and fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, releasing their contents into the Golgi lumen. Within the Golgi, the protein is further modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing) as it moves from the cis face through the medial cisternae toward the trans face, transported between Golgi cisternae. At the trans face, the mature trypsinogen is packaged into secretory vesicles, which bud off and travel to the plasma membrane, fusing with it (exocytosis) to release trypsinogen out of the pancreatic acinar cell into the pancreatic duct.

(b) Three functions of the smooth ER (SER) in a liver cell: (1) Detoxification of drugs and other lipid-soluble toxins — SER membranes contain enzymes (e.g., cytochrome P450 family enzymes) that chemically modify (e.g., hydroxylate) hydrophobic toxic compounds and drugs, increasing their water solubility so they can be excreted from the body. (2) Lipid and steroid synthesis — SER synthesizes membrane phospholipids, cholesterol, and (in steroid-hormone-producing cells) steroid hormones, as well as lipoprotein components. (3) Carbohydrate/glucose metabolism — SER contains the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate (generated by glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis), producing free glucose that can be transported out of the liver cell into the bloodstream to help regulate blood glucose levels (glucose-6-phosphate itself cannot cross the plasma membrane).
Molecular basis of detoxification: cytochrome P450 enzymes embedded in the SER membrane catalyze oxidation reactions (e.g., adding a hydroxyl group) to hydrophobic drug/toxin molecules, increasing their polarity and water solubility; this allows subsequent conjugation (e.g., with glucuronic acid) and excretion via bile or urine, preventing the accumulation of these lipid-soluble compounds within cell membranes.

(c)(i) Lysosomal (acid hydrolase) enzymes synthesized in the RER are tagged in the Golgi apparatus with a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) marker. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors located in the trans-Golgi network specifically recognize and bind M6P-tagged proteins, sorting them into clathrin-coated vesicles that are directed to lysosomes (or late endosomes that mature into lysosomes), rather than following the default pathway toward the plasma membrane for secretion — this specific tag-and-receptor recognition system targets lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes instead of being secreted out of the cell.

(c)(ii) Lysosomal acid hydrolases require the low (acidic, ~pH 5) internal pH of the lysosome (maintained by proton pumps in the lysosomal membrane) to be catalytically active; at the neutral pH of the cytosol, these enzymes are far less active, so even minor leakage into the cytosol would not significantly damage other cell components. Additionally, proteins on the inner (lumen-facing) surface of the lysosomal membrane are highly glycosylated, which helps shield/protect them from being degraded by the very enzymes contained within the lysosome.

(c)(iii) When a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome (a double-membrane vesicle that has engulfed damaged organelles or cytoplasmic material for recycling), it forms an autolysosome. The lysosome's acid hydrolases mix with and enzymatically digest the enclosed material — proteins, lipids, and damaged organelle components — breaking them down into their monomer building blocks (amino acids, fatty acids, sugars, nucleotides). These monomers are then transported out of the (auto)lysosome back into the cytosol, where the cell can recycle/reuse them for new biosynthesis or as an energy source.

(d) Brefeldin A disrupts COPI vesicle formation and causes the Golgi apparatus to collapse back into the ER.
(i) Secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein: would be blocked/severely decreased. With the Golgi structurally collapsed into the ER and normal ER→Golgi→plasma membrane vesicular traffic disrupted, the protein cannot be properly processed and packaged into secretory vesicles for exocytosis, so secretion out of the cell would stop or drop sharply.
(ii) Delivery of lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes: also blocked/severely impaired, because the trans-Golgi network (where lysosomal enzymes are normally M6P-tagged and sorted into lysosome-directed vesicles) is disrupted along with the rest of the Golgi — without a functional Golgi to apply this tag and sort the enzymes, they cannot be properly targeted to lysosomes.
(iii) ER morphology: the ER would appear enlarged/swollen and structurally abnormal, since Golgi membrane and its resident/cargo proteins are being redistributed back into (fused with) the ER, increasing the ER's membrane surface area and volume and altering its normal appearance — this collapse is the basis for using brefeldin A experimentally to study ER–Golgi trafficking.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Trace the trypsinogen pathway through the named organelles (ribosome/RER -> Golgi -> secretory vesicle -> plasma membrane) and describe what happens at each step.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Complete pathway: (1) Ribosome (on rough ER) — trypsinogen synthesized by ribosome; signal peptide directs ribosome to RER; polypeptide threaded into ER lumen as it is synthesized; signal peptide cleaved. (2) Rough ER lumen — initial N-linked glycosylation; protein folding assisted by chaperones (BiP/GRP78); disulfide bonds formed; quality control (misfolded proteins retained/degraded). (3) COPII vesicle buds from ER → transported to cis-Golgi. (4) Golgi apparatus (cis → medial → trans) — further glycosylation modifications; protein sorted and packaged in trans-Golgi network. (5) Secretory vesicle (dense-core or constitutive secretory vesicle) buds from trans-Golgi → transported to plasma membrane. (6) Exocytosis — vesicle fuses with plasma membrane; trypsinogen released into pancreatic duct lumen. Note: trypsinogen is secreted as an inactive zymogen (activated to trypsin in the small intestine by enteropeptidase) — accept if student notes this.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Ribosome on RER → ER lumen (signal peptide, glycosylation, folding) → COPII vesicle → Golgi (further modification) → secretory vesicle → exocytosis at plasma membrane.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe three SER functions (e.g. lipid synthesis, detoxification, calcium storage).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Three SER functions in liver cells: (1) Lipid synthesis — SER synthesizes phospholipids and cholesterol; enzymes embedded in SER membrane catalyze lipid synthesis using acetyl-CoA and fatty acid precursors. (2) Drug detoxification / xenobiotic metabolism — cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP450) in SER oxidize lipid-soluble drugs, toxins, and steroids → convert to more water-soluble forms for excretion (glucuronidation). Molecular basis: CYP450 enzymes use O₂ and NADPH to insert hydroxyl groups into hydrophobic substrates → increases polarity → facilitates conjugation reactions → more water-soluble metabolite excreted in bile or urine. (3) Glycogen metabolism — glucose-6-phosphatase embedded in SER membrane dephosphorylates glucose-6-phosphate → free glucose enters bloodstream. (4) Calcium storage/release — SER sequesters Ca²⁺; IP₃ signaling triggers Ca²⁺ release from SER. Any three with one molecular explanation earns full credit.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Three SER functions in liver: lipid synthesis; drug detoxification (CYP450 enzymes hydroxylate hydrophobic drugs → more water-soluble); glycogen metabolism (glucose-6-phosphatase). Molecular basis example: CYP450 uses O₂ + NADPH to hydroxylate lipophilic compounds → increases polarity → excreted.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain lysosomal enzyme targeting, why lysosomal enzymes do not digest the lysosome membrane, and what happens when a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Targeting: lysosomal hydrolases are glycoproteins synthesized in the RER and processed in the Golgi; a specific modification — addition of mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag — marks these enzymes as lysosomal. In the trans-Golgi, M6P receptors recognize the M6P tag and package enzymes into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for late endosomes/lysosomes rather than secretory vesicles. Without this tag (or with M6P receptor mutations), enzymes are secreted extracellularly instead. (ii) Membrane protection: lysosomal membrane lipids are heavily glycosylated on the luminal face (glycocalyx of the inner membrane) → carbohydrate coat protects membrane proteins and lipids from acid hydrolases; lysosomal membrane proteins (LAMPs, LIMPs) are specifically resistant to degradation; acidic pH is maintained by V-type H⁺-ATPase pumping protons in. Hydrolases require low pH to function — the neutral cytoplasm inactivates any leaked enzymes. frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict effects of blocking Golgi vesicle budding on secretion, lysosomal enzyme delivery, and ER appearance.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Secretion blocked: without COP-I vesicles and functional Golgi, proteins synthesized in RER cannot be transported to Golgi for processing, packaging, and sorting → secretory vesicles cannot form → newly synthesized extracellular proteins accumulate in ER and cannot be secreted. Any proteins already in Golgi would be retrograded to ER. Complete block of constitutive secretion. prior_canonical_answer_1:
(a) mRNA encoding trypsinogen is translated by ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): a signal sequence on the growing polypeptide is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), directing the ribosome to dock at the RER membrane, and the polypeptide is threaded into the RER lumen as it is synthesized, where it begins folding (assisted by chaperone proteins) and is glycosylated. The protein is then packaged into COPII-coated transport vesicles that bud from the RER membrane and travel to and fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, releasing their contents into the Golgi lumen. Within the Golgi, the protein is further modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing) as it moves from the cis face through the medial cisternae toward the trans face, transported between Golgi cisternae. At the trans face, the mature trypsinogen is packaged into secretory vesicles, which bud off and travel to the plasma membrane, fusing with it (exocytosis) to release trypsinogen out of the pancreatic acinar cell into the pancreatic duct.

(b) Three functions of the smooth ER (SER) in a liver cell: (1) Detoxification of drugs and other lipid-soluble toxins — SER membranes contain enzymes (e.g., cytochrome P450 family enzymes) that chemically modify (e.g., hydroxylate) hydrophobic toxic compounds and drugs, increasing their water solubility so they can be excreted from the body. (2) Lipid and steroid synthesis — SER synthesizes membrane phospholipids, cholesterol, and (in steroid-hormone-producing cells) steroid hormones, as well as lipoprotein components. (3) Carbohydrate/glucose metabolism — SER contains the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate (generated by glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis), producing free glucose that can be transported out of the liver cell into the bloodstream to help regulate blood glucose levels (glucose-6-phosphate itself cannot cross the plasma membrane).
Molecular basis of detoxification: cytochrome P450 enzymes embedded in the SER membrane catalyze oxidation reactions (e.g., adding a hydroxyl group) to hydrophobic drug/toxin molecules, increasing their polarity and water solubility; this allows subsequent conjugation (e.g., with glucuronic acid) and excretion via bile or urine, preventing the accumulation of these lipid-soluble compounds within cell membranes.

(c)(i) Lysosomal (acid hydrolase) enzymes synthesized in the RER are tagged in the Golgi apparatus with a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) marker. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors located in the trans-Golgi network specifically recognize and bind M6P-tagged proteins, sorting them into clathrin-coated vesicles that are directed to lysosomes (or late endosomes that mature into lysosomes), rather than following the default pathway toward the plasma membrane for secretion — this specific tag-and-receptor recognition system targets lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes instead of being secreted out of the cell.

(c)(ii) Lysosomal acid hydrolases require the low (acidic, ~pH 5) internal pH of the lysosome (maintained by proton pumps in the lysosomal membrane) to be catalytically active; at the neutral pH of the cytosol, these enzymes are far less active, so even minor leakage into the cytosol would not significantly damage other cell components. Additionally, proteins on the inner (lumen-facing) surface of the lysosomal membrane are highly glycosylated, which helps shield/protect them from being degraded by the very enzymes contained within the lysosome.

(c)(iii) When a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome (a double-membrane vesicle that has engulfed damaged organelles or cytoplasmic material for recycling), it forms an autolysosome. The lysosome's acid hydrolases mix with and enzymatically digest the enclosed material — proteins, lipids, and damaged organelle components — breaking them down into their monomer building blocks (amino acids, fatty acids, sugars, nucleotides). These monomers are then transported out of the (auto)lysosome back into the cytosol, where the cell can recycle/reuse them for new biosynthesis or as an energy source.

(d) Brefeldin A disrupts COPI vesicle formation and causes the Golgi apparatus to collapse back into the ER.
(i) Secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein: would be blocked/severely decreased. With the Golgi structurally collapsed into the ER and normal ER→Golgi→plasma membrane vesicular traffic disrupted, the protein cannot be properly processed and packaged into secretory vesicles for exocytosis, so secretion out of the cell would stop or drop sharply.
(ii) Delivery of lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes: also blocked/severely impaired, because the trans-Golgi network (where lysosomal enzymes are normally M6P-tagged and sorted into lysosome-directed vesicles) is disrupted along with the rest of the Golgi — without a functional Golgi to apply this tag and sort the enzymes, they cannot be properly targeted to lysosomes.
(iii) ER morphology: the ER would appear enlarged/swollen and structurally abnormal, since Golgi membrane and its resident/cargo proteins are being redistributed back into (fused with) the ER, increasing the ER's membrane surface area and volume and altering its normal appearance — this collapse is the basis for using brefeldin A experimentally to study ER–Golgi trafficking.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Trace trypsinogen from synthesis to secretion naming organelles, events, and vesicle types.

(2) Rough ER lumen — initial N-linked glycosylation; protein folding assisted by chaperones (BiP/GRP78); disulfide bonds formed; quality control (misfolded proteins retained/degraded). (5) Secretory vesicle (dense-core or constitutive secretory vesicle) buds from trans-Golgi → transported to plasma membrane. (6) Exocytosis — vesicle fuses with plasma membrane; trypsinogen released into pancreatic duct lumen. Note: trypsinogen is secreted as an inactive zymogen (activated to trypsin in the small intestine by enteropeptidase) — accept if student notes this.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe three SER functions in liver cells; explain molecular basis of one.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
Describe TWO OR THREE specific lines of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.

Part B: Describe the role of the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis. In your answer, explain: (i) the source of the proton gradient; (ii) how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase; and (iii) the general role of the electron transport chain complexes (supplied in the stimulus) in building that gradient.

Part C: A researcher adds the following compounds to isolated mitochondria respiring aerobically. For each compound, predict whether O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis will increase, decrease, or be unaffected, and explain your reasoning:
Rotenone (inhibits Complex I electron transfer)
Oligomycin (blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase)
Dinitrophenol / DNP (uncoupler — makes the inner membrane permeable to H⁺)

Part D: Heart muscle cells have unusually high numbers of mitochondria. Explain the functional reason for this, and describe the specific structural feature of mitochondria that maximizes ATP output.
stimulus:
Mitochondrial structure:
• Outer membrane: permeable to small molecules (porins)
• Intermembrane space: H⁺ accumulates here during electron transport
• Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae; contains electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase; impermeable to ions
• Matrix: contains Krebs cycle enzymes, mtDNA, mitochondrial ribosomes

The electron transport chain complexes in the inner membrane pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space as electrons pass through them; ATP synthase uses the resulting H⁺ gradient to synthesize ATP. Note: when the H⁺ gradient cannot be relieved by ATP synthase (e.g. if ATP synthase is blocked), electron flow through the chain and O₂ consumption also slow, because the chain works against the built-up gradient.
canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Four lines of evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria: (1) Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA genome (mtDNA), structurally similar to bacterial chromosomes (circular, not complexed with histones), distinct from the linear, histone-associated nuclear DNA of the eukaryotic host. (2) Mitochondria contain their own ribosomes, which resemble bacterial (70S-type) ribosomes in size and antibiotic sensitivity, rather than the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic host cell. (3) Mitochondria are bounded by a double membrane: the inner membrane is thought to derive from the original engulfed bacterium's own plasma membrane, while the outer membrane is thought to derive from the host cell's plasma membrane/engulfing vesicle formed during the initial phagocytic/endocytic event. (4) Mitochondria reproduce independently of the host cell cycle via binary fission, similar to how free-living bacteria divide, rather than being newly assembled by the cell each time. (Additional supporting evidence: phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial rRNA/protein sequences shows mitochondria are most closely related to a specific group of alpha-proteobacteria.)

(a)(ii) Over evolutionary time, most genes originally present in the free-living bacterial ancestor's genome were transferred from the mitochondrial genome to the host cell's nuclear genome (endosymbiotic/organellar gene transfer); the corresponding proteins are now synthesized in the cytosol by cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported back into the mitochondrion via specific protein-targeting signal sequences. Retaining most genes in the nucleus is advantageous because it allows the cell to centrally coordinate/regulate mitochondrial protein production together with the rest of the cell's needs, benefits from the nucleus's more robust and accurate DNA repair/recombination machinery (mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate and less effective repair), and reduces genomic redundancy — the mitochondrial genome now retains only a small number of genes, typically those encoding highly hydrophobic membrane proteins (e.g., core electron transport chain subunits) that are difficult to import from the cytosol after synthesis.

(b) The source of the proton gradient is the electron transport chain: as electrons from NADH (and FADH2) are passed sequentially through Complexes I, III, and IV, the energy released by these electron transfers is used by each complex to actively pump H+ ions from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, creating a higher H+ concentration (and more positive charge/lower pH) in the intermembrane space than in the matrix — an electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force). This gradient drives ATP synthesis via chemiosmosis: because the inner membrane is impermeable to ions except through specific channels, H+ can flow back down its concentration gradient (from intermembrane space into the matrix) only through the F0 channel of ATP synthase; this proton flow spins the F0 rotor, driving conformational changes in the F1 head that catalyze phosphorylation of ADP + Pi to form ATP.
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, passing the released electrons into the electron transport chain, and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex III (cytochrome bc1): continues passing electrons along the chain and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): accepts electrons from cytochrome c and transfers them to the final electron acceptor, O2, reducing it (with H+ from the matrix) to H2O, and pumps 2 additional H+ into the intermembrane space.
ATP synthase (Complex V): uses the energy of protons flowing back through its F0 channel down the electrochemical gradient to drive the rotary catalytic mechanism of its F1 head, synthesizing ATP from ADP and Pi.

(c)(i) Rotenone (inhibits Complex I): electrons from NADH can no longer enter the electron transport chain at Complex I, blocking electron flow through the chain from that entry point. O2 consumption DECREASES (electrons can no longer reach Complex IV via this pathway at the normal rate), and ATP synthesis DECREASES correspondingly (the proton gradient can no longer be adequately maintained, reducing ATP synthase activity).

(c)(ii) Oligomycin (blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase): protons can no longer flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, so ATP synthesis DECREASES/stops directly. Because the proton gradient can no longer be dissipated through ATP synthase, H+ accumulates in the intermembrane space, increasing the gradient's magnitude/"back pressure" against further proton pumping; this makes continued pumping by the ETC complexes energetically less favorable, so electron transport (and thus O2 consumption) also DECREASES — both O2 consumption and ATP synthesis decrease.

(c)(iii) DNP (uncoupler; makes the inner membrane permeable to H+): protons leak directly back into the matrix across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase entirely, so the proton gradient cannot build up (it is continuously dissipated as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP) — ATP synthesis DECREASES, since protons no longer need to flow through ATP synthase to return to the matrix. However, because the gradient never builds up significant "back pressure," the ETC complexes can pump protons essentially unimpeded, and the cell/mitochondrion compensates for the lost ATP output by increasing the rate of electron transport — so O2 consumption INCREASES, even though little of that respiratory energy is captured as ATP (most is released as heat).

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high ATP demands: cardiac muscle cells must contract continuously throughout life to pump blood, requiring constant ATP for the actin–myosin contractile machinery, and neurons require large amounts of ATP to maintain ion gradients (via the Na+/K+ ATPase) for generating and propagating action potentials and for synaptic transmission (neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle trafficking/recycling) — both cell types are highly metabolically active and depend heavily on the efficient, high-ATP-yield process of oxidative phosphorylation. The specific structural feature that maximizes ATP output is the highly folded inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae): these folds greatly increase the surface area of inner membrane available to house electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase molecules, allowing many more of these proteins to be packed into a given mitochondrial volume, maximizing the rate of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production per mitochondrion.
A drug inhibiting mitochondrial fission would be especially harmful to neurons compared to rapidly dividing cells like skin fibroblasts because neurons are post-mitotic (non-dividing, terminally differentiated) cells with very long axonal and dendritic processes (sometimes over a meter long) that depend on mitochondrial fission (together with fusion) to distribute healthy mitochondria along their length to distant synaptic terminals, where local ATP supply is essential for synaptic function, and fission is also required for mitochondrial quality control (isolating damaged mitochondrial segments for removal via mitophagy). Because neurons cannot dilute or replace damaged/undistributed mitochondria through cell division (unlike rapidly dividing fibroblasts, which continually produce new daughter cells that each receive a fresh partitioned complement of mitochondria during division), blocking fission would cause neurons to progressively accumulate large, dysfunctional, poorly distributed mitochondria that cannot reach distant synapses or be properly quality-controlled, severely impairing neuronal ATP supply and function over time — a problem that dividing fibroblasts are comparatively protected from due to their shorter, simpler geometry and ongoing mitochondrial redistribution through cell division.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe two or three lines of evidence for endosymbiosis (double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Four lines of evidence: (1) Size and shape: mitochondria are similar in size (~1-2 μm) and shape to alpha-proteobacteria; (2) Double membrane: mitochondria have two membranes — the outer membrane likely derived from the phagocytic vacuole; the inner membrane is the original bacterial plasma membrane with bacterial-type lipid composition (cardiolipin); (3) Mitochondrial DNA: circular, naked DNA (like bacterial chromosomes) located in the matrix; not associated with histones; encodes rRNA, tRNA, and some proteins; (4) Mitochondrial ribosomes: 70S ribosomes (bacterial type) sensitive to antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes (chloramphenicol, erythromycin) but not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (5) Binary fission: mitochondria divide by binary fission, not mitosis; (6) Phylogenetic similarity: mitochondrial rRNA sequences are closely related to alpha-proteobacteria (specifically Rickettsia-like organisms). Any four with correct explanation. (ii) Gene transfer to nucleus: over evolutionary time, most ancestral bacterial genes were transferred to the host cell nucleus (endosymbiotic gene transfer). This is adaptive because: nuclear genes can be regulated by eukaryotic gene expression machinery; nuclear DNA is protected by repair mechanisms; reduced mtDNA reduces the risk of harmful mutations in the energy-producing organelle; nuclear-encoded proteins are imported post-translationally into mitochondria via TOM/TIM complexes.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Four evidence: (1) size/shape similar to bacteria; (2) double membrane (inner = bacterial membrane with cardiolipin); (3) circular naked mitochondrial DNA; (4) 70S ribosomes (sensitive to bacterial antibiotics). Gene transfer: most mitochondrial genes transferred to nucleus over evolution (endosymbiotic gene transfer) for better regulation, protection, and coordination.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain (i) proton gradient source, (ii) how it drives ATP synthase, (iii) the general role of ETC complexes in building the gradient -- score (i)/(ii)/(iii) separately.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Source of proton gradient: NADH and FADH₂ (from glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle) donate electrons to the ETC. As electrons pass through the complexes, the energy released is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space: Complex I pumps 4H⁺, Complex III pumps 4H⁺, Complex IV pumps 2H⁺. This creates an electrochemical proton gradient (high H⁺/low pH in intermembrane space vs. matrix) = proton-motive force. ATP synthesis: H⁺ cannot freely cross the inner membrane (impermeable). H⁺ flows back down its electrochemical gradient through the F₀ channel of ATP synthase (the only route). H⁺ flow drives rotation of the F₀ rotor → mechanical rotation transmitted to F₁ catalytic subunits → conformational changes in F₁ catalyze ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi (rotary catalysis). Specific roles: Complex I — accepts electrons from NADH → passes to ubiquinone, pumps 4H⁺; Complex III — accepts electrons from reduced ubiquinone (QH₂) via Q-cycle → passes to cytochrome c, pumps 4H⁺; Complex IV — accepts electrons from cytochrome c → reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor), pumps 2H⁺; ATP synthase — H⁺ gradient drives F₀ rotation → F₁ synthesizes ATP (chemiosmosis).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: H⁺ pumped from matrix to intermembrane space by Complexes I (4H⁺), III (4H⁺), IV (2H⁺) as electrons flow. Proton gradient (proton-motive force) drives H⁺ back through ATP synthase F₀ channel → F₁ rotation → ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi. Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict rotenone (decreases both), oligomycin (ATP synthesis decreases; O2 consumption also decreases per the stimulus note on coupled electron flow, or unaffected with sound reasoning accepted), and DNP (O2 consumption increases, ATP synthesis decreases) with reasoning for each.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Rotenone (blocks Complex I): electron flow from NADH through Complex I is blocked → electrons cannot enter the ETC from NADH → H⁺ pumping by Complexes I, III, IV stops → proton gradient collapses → ATP synthesis stops. O₂ consumption DECREASES (Complex IV cannot receive electrons; O₂ is not reduced). ATP synthesis DECREASES (no gradient). (ii) Oligomycin (blocks F₀ of ATP synthase): H⁺ cannot flow through ATP synthase → H⁺ accumulates in intermembrane space → proton gradient INCREASES (back-pressure) → this back-pressure slows H⁺ pumping by Complexes → electron flow through ETC slows → O₂ consumption DECREASES. ATP synthesis DECREASES (synthase blocked). Classic observation: oligomycin paradoxically reduces O₂ consumption by back-pressure on the ETC. (iii) DNP (uncoupler): makes inner membrane permeable to H⁺ → H⁺ flows back into matrix bypassing ATP synthase → proton gradient dissipated as heat → no ATP synthesized. But now there is no back-pressure on the ETC → ETC pumps H⁺ as fast as possible to try to maintain gradient → O₂ consumption INCREASES dramatically. ATP synthesis DECREASES (to zero — all gradient dissipated as heat). DNP causes hyperthermia (was used as a diet drug — dangerously). 1 pt per any two correctly predicted and explained.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Rotenone: O₂ decreases (ETC blocked at Complex I), ATP decreases. Oligomycin: O₂ decreases (back-pressure stops ETC), ATP decreases. DNP: O₂ increases (no back-pressure, ETC runs faster), ATP decreases (gradient dissipated as heat).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why heart cells need many mitochondria and describe cristae as the structural feature that maximizes ATP output.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: High energy demand cells: heart muscle and neurons are continuously active and cannot undergo anaerobic metabolism for sustained periods. They require constant high-rate ATP production (heart: ~30 kg ATP/day; neurons: cannot tolerate even brief energy deficits). More mitochondria = more ETC surface area = more ATP. Structural feature: cristae (inner membrane folds) dramatically increase the surface area of the inner membrane → more ETC complexes and ATP synthases per mitochondrion → greater ATP output per organelle. Fission inhibition in neurons vs. fibroblasts: mitochondria must be distributed throughout the cell to local sites of energy demand — in neurons, this means delivering mitochondria to synapses (far from the cell body, up to 1 meter in motor neurons). Mitochondrial fission allows small mitochondria to be transported along microtubules to distant synaptic sites. Without fission: mitochondria become elongated and cannot be transported into dendrites and axons → synapses lack local energy supply → synaptic transmission fails → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and rapidly dividing; mitochondria can be inherited by daughter cells even without efficient transport; fibroblasts are less dependent on precise organelle localization. 1 pt for heart/neurons high demand + cristae explanation; 1 pt for fission/transport mechanism in neurons.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Heart/neurons have high continuous ATP demand → many mitochondria; cristae (inner membrane folds) increase surface area for ETC/ATP synthase. Fission inhibition: neurons need small mitochondria transported to distant synapses via microtubules; without fission, elongated mitochondria cannot enter axons/dendrites → synapses lack ATP → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and divide frequently — less dependent on mitochondrial transport.

(c)(ii) Oligomycin (blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase): protons can no longer flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, so ATP synthesis DECREASES/stops directly. Because the proton gradient can no longer be dissipated through ATP synthase, H+ accumulates in the intermembrane space, increasing the gradient's magnitude/"back pressure" against further proton pumping; this makes continued pumping by the ETC complexes energetically less favorable, so electron transport (and thus O2 consumption) also DECREASES — both O2 consumption and ATP synthesis decrease.

(c)(iii) DNP (uncoupler; makes the inner membrane permeable to H+): protons leak directly back into the matrix across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase entirely, so the proton gradient cannot build up (it is continuously dissipated as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP) — ATP synthesis DECREASES, since protons no longer need to flow through ATP synthase to return to the matrix. However, because the gradient never builds up significant "back pressure," the ETC complexes can pump protons essentially unimpeded, and the cell/mitochondrion compensates for the lost ATP output by increasing the rate of electron transport — so O2 consumption INCREASES, even though little of that respiratory energy is captured as ATP (most is released as heat).

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high ATP demands: cardiac muscle cells must contract continuously throughout life to pump blood, requiring constant ATP for the actin–myosin contractile machinery, and neurons require large amounts of ATP to maintain ion gradients (via the Na+/K+ ATPase) for generating and propagating action potentials and for synaptic transmission (neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle trafficking/recycling) — both cell types are highly metabolically active and depend heavily on the efficient, high-ATP-yield process of oxidative phosphorylation. The specific structural feature that maximizes ATP output is the highly folded inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae): these folds greatly increase the surface area of inner membrane available to house electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase molecules, allowing many more of these proteins to be packed into a given mitochondrial volume, maximizing the rate of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production per mitochondrion.
A drug inhibiting mitochondrial fission would be especially harmful to neurons compared to rapidly dividing cells like skin fibroblasts because neurons are post-mitotic (non-dividing, terminally differentiated) cells with very long axonal and dendritic processes (sometimes over a meter long) that depend on mitochondrial fission (together with fusion) to distribute healthy mitochondria along their length to distant synaptic terminals, where local ATP supply is essential for synaptic function, and fission is also required for mitochondrial quality control (isolating damaged mitochondrial segments for removal via mitophagy). Because neurons cannot dilute or replace damaged/undistributed mitochondria through cell division (unlike rapidly dividing fibroblasts, which continually produce new daughter cells that each receive a fresh partitioned complement of mitochondria during division), blocking fission would cause neurons to progressively accumulate large, dysfunctional, poorly distributed mitochondria that cannot reach distant synapses or be properly quality-controlled, severely impairing neuronal ATP supply and function over time — a problem that dividing fibroblasts are comparatively protected from due to their shorter, simpler geometry and ongoing mitochondrial redistribution through cell division.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe four lines of evidence for endosymbiosis; explain gene transfer to nucleus.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Four lines of evidence: (1) Size and shape: mitochondria are similar in size (~1-2 μm) and shape to alpha-proteobacteria; (2) Double membrane: mitochondria have two membranes — the outer membrane likely derived from the phagocytic vacuole; the inner membrane is the original bacterial plasma membrane with bacterial-type lipid composition (cardiolipin); (3) Mitochondrial DNA: circular, naked DNA (like bacterial chromosomes) located in the matrix; not associated with histones; encodes rRNA, tRNA, and some proteins; (4) Mitochondrial ribosomes: 70S ribosomes (bacterial type) sensitive to antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes (chloramphenicol, erythromycin) but not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (5) Binary fission: mitochondria divide by binary fission, not mitosis; (6) Phylogenetic similarity: mitochondrial rRNA sequences are closely related to alpha-proteobacteria (specifically Rickettsia-like organisms). Any four with correct explanation. (ii) Gene transfer to nucleus: over evolutionary time, most ancestral bacterial genes were transferred to the host cell nucleus (endosymbiotic gene transfer). This is adaptive because: nuclear genes can be regulated by eukaryotic gene expression machinery; nuclear DNA is protected by repair mechanisms; reduced mtDNA reduces the risk of harmful mutations in the energy-producing organelle; nuclear-encoded proteins are imported post-translationally into mitochondria via TOM/TIM complexes.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Four evidence: (1) size/shape similar to bacteria; (2) double membrane (inner = bacterial membrane with cardiolipin); (3) circular naked mitochondrial DNA; (4) 70S ribosomes (sensitive to bacterial antibiotics). Gene transfer: most mitochondrial genes transferred to nucleus over evolution (endosymbiotic gene transfer) for better regulation, protection, and coordination.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe proton gradient source, ATP synthesis mechanism, and roles of Complexes I, III, IV, and ATP synthase.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Source of proton gradient: NADH and FADH₂ (from glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle) donate electrons to the ETC. As electrons pass through the complexes, the energy released is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space: Complex I pumps 4H⁺, Complex III pumps 4H⁺, Complex IV pumps 2H⁺. This creates an electrochemical proton gradient (high H⁺/low pH in intermembrane space vs. matrix) = proton-motive force. ATP synthesis: H⁺ cannot freely cross the inner membrane (impermeable). H⁺ flows back down its electrochemical gradient through the F₀ channel of ATP synthase (the only route). H⁺ flow drives rotation of the F₀ rotor → mechanical rotation transmitted to F₁ catalytic subunits → conformational changes in F₁ catalyze ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi (rotary catalysis). Specific roles: Complex I — accepts electrons from NADH → passes to ubiquinone, pumps 4H⁺; Complex III — accepts electrons from reduced ubiquinone (QH₂) via Q-cycle → passes to cytochrome c, pumps 4H⁺; Complex IV — accepts electrons from cytochrome c → reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor), pumps 2H⁺; ATP synthase — H⁺ gradient drives F₀ rotation → F₁ synthesizes ATP (chemiosmosis).
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: H⁺ pumped from matrix to intermembrane space by Complexes I (4H⁺), III (4H⁺), IV (2H⁺) as electrons flow. Proton gradient (proton-motive force) drives H⁺ back through ATP synthase F₀ channel → F₁ rotation → ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi. Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor).

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis for rotenone, oligomycin, and DNP.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Rotenone (blocks Complex I): electron flow from NADH through Complex I is blocked → electrons cannot enter the ETC from NADH → H⁺ pumping by Complexes I, III, IV stops → proton gradient collapses → ATP synthesis stops. O₂ consumption DECREASES (Complex IV cannot receive electrons; O₂ is not reduced). ATP synthesis DECREASES (no gradient). (ii) Oligomycin (blocks F₀ of ATP synthase): H⁺ cannot flow through ATP synthase → H⁺ accumulates in intermembrane space → proton gradient INCREASES (back-pressure) → this back-pressure slows H⁺ pumping by Complexes → electron flow through ETC slows → O₂ consumption DECREASES. ATP synthesis DECREASES (synthase blocked). Classic observation: oligomycin paradoxically reduces O₂ consumption by back-pressure on the ETC. (iii) DNP (uncoupler): makes inner membrane permeable to H⁺ → H⁺ flows back into matrix bypassing ATP synthase → proton gradient dissipated as heat → no ATP synthesized. But now there is no back-pressure on the ETC → ETC pumps H⁺ as fast as possible to try to maintain gradient → O₂ consumption INCREASES dramatically. ATP synthesis DECREASES (to zero — all gradient dissipated as heat). DNP causes hyperthermia (was used as a diet drug — dangerously). 1 pt per any two correctly predicted and explained.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Rotenone: O₂ decreases (ETC blocked at Complex I), ATP decreases. Oligomycin: O₂ decreases (back-pressure stops ETC), ATP decreases. DNP: O₂ increases (no back-pressure, ETC runs faster), ATP decreases (gradient dissipated as heat).

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why heart/neurons need many mitochondria; describe cristae; explain fission inhibition harm to neurons.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: High energy demand cells: heart muscle and neurons are continuously active and cannot undergo anaerobic metabolism for sustained periods. They require constant high-rate ATP production (heart: ~30 kg ATP/day; neurons: cannot tolerate even brief energy deficits). More mitochondria = more ETC surface area = more ATP. Structural feature: cristae (inner membrane folds) dramatically increase the surface area of the inner membrane → more ETC complexes and ATP synthases per mitochondrion → greater ATP output per organelle. Fission inhibition in neurons vs. fibroblasts: mitochondria must be distributed throughout the cell to local sites of energy demand — in neurons, this means delivering mitochondria to synapses (far from the cell body, up to 1 meter in motor neurons). Mitochondrial fission allows small mitochondria to be transported along microtubules to distant synaptic sites. Without fission: mitochondria become elongated and cannot be transported into dendrites and axons → synapses lack local energy supply → synaptic transmission fails → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and rapidly dividing; mitochondria can be inherited by daughter cells even without efficient transport; fibroblasts are less dependent on precise organelle localization. 1 pt for heart/neurons high demand + cristae explanation; 1 pt for fission/transport mechanism in neurons.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Heart/neurons have high continuous ATP demand → many mitochondria; cristae (inner membrane folds) increase surface area for ETC/ATP synthase. Fission inhibition: neurons need small mitochondria transported to distant synapses via microtubules; without fission, elongated mitochondria cannot enter axons/dendrites → synapses lack ATP → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and divide frequently — less dependent on mitochondrial transport.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Describe, in general terms, how a glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is broken down through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle, and identify at which of these stages CO₂ is released.

Part B: For one molecule of glucose completely oxidized through aerobic respiration, explain which stages produce NADH and FADH₂, and explain how these electron carriers are used in the electron transport chain to ultimately produce ATP.

Part C: The actual ATP yield from one glucose molecule is lower than the theoretical maximum. Explain why, describing at least TWO general reasons the process is not perfectly efficient.

Part D: A cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Using the data in Table 1, which shows glucose consumption rates, explain why glucose consumption increases dramatically under anaerobic conditions. Your answer should connect the cell's ATP needs, the lower ATP yield of fermentation compared to aerobic respiration, and the need to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.
stimulus:
Table 1: Glucose consumption in yeast cells
Condition     | Glucose consumed (mmol/hr/g cells)
Aerobic       |        0.5
Anaerobic     |        4.2

General ATP yield summary:
Glycolysis: net 2 ATP (substrate-level), 2 NADH
Pyruvate oxidation: 0 ATP, 2 NADH
Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 2 ATP (GTP), 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂
Each NADH and FADH₂ used in the electron transport chain contributes to ATP production, but not with perfect efficiency.
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Carbon trace: Glycolysis splits glucose (6C) into 2 pyruvate (3C each); no carbon is lost as CO2 in glycolysis, so all 6 carbons remain in the 2 pyruvate molecules. In pyruvate oxidation, each pyruvate (3C) is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA (2C) plus 1 CO2, releasing 2 CO2 total (one per pyruvate) and leaving 4 carbons in the two acetyl groups. In the Krebs cycle, each acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate; over one turn, 2 CO2 are released via two decarboxylation steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase). Since the cycle turns twice (once per acetyl-CoA), 4 CO2 are released total. Overall CO2 accounting: 2 CO2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 4 CO2 (Krebs, 2 turns) = 6 CO2, accounting for all 6 original glucose carbons.

(b) Electron carriers produced per glucose: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH (cytoplasmic). Pyruvate oxidation produces 2 NADH (mitochondrial matrix, one per pyruvate). The Krebs cycle (2 turns) produces 6 NADH and 2 FADH2. Total = 10 NADH (2 cytoplasmic + 8 mitochondrial) and 2 FADH2. Mitochondrial NADH donates its electrons to Complex I of the electron transport chain, pumping protons at Complexes I, III, and IV (~2.5 ATP equivalent each). FADH2 donates electrons to Complex II, bypassing Complex I, so it only drives proton pumping at Complexes III and IV (~1.5 ATP equivalent each). The 2 cytoplasmic NADH from glycolysis cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly and must be shuttled in via the malate-aspartate shuttle (delivers electrons to mitochondrial NAD+, yielding the full ~2.5 ATP equivalent) or the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (delivers electrons to FAD, yielding only ~1.5 ATP equivalent).

(c) Three reasons actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical ~30-32 ATP: (1) Proton leak — some protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane through channels other than ATP synthase, dissipating part of the proton-motive force as heat rather than using it to synthesize ATP. (2) Shuttle costs — cytoplasmic NADH shuttled via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers electrons to FAD instead of NAD+, losing about 1 ATP equivalent per cytoplasmic NADH compared to the theoretical maximum that assumes full NADH-level input. (3) The proton gradient is used for purposes other than ATP synthesis, such as powering the transport of ADP into and ATP out of the mitochondrial matrix (via the adenine nucleotide translocase) and importing inorganic phosphate and pyruvate, which consumes some of the gradient's energy without directly producing ATP.

(d) The Pasteur effect: without O2, there is no terminal electron acceptor for the electron transport chain, so oxidative phosphorylation stops and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+ via the ETC. Glycolysis absolutely requires a continuous supply of NAD+ (used by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase); under anaerobic conditions this NAD+ is regenerated instead by fermentation (reducing pyruvate to lactate or acetaldehyde to ethanol), which allows glycolysis to keep running. However, anaerobic glycolysis alone nets only 2 ATP per glucose via substrate-level phosphorylation, versus ~30 ATP aerobically — roughly a 15-fold drop in efficiency. To meet the same cellular energy demand, the cell must dramatically increase glycolytic flux, consistent with Table 1 showing glucose consumption jumping from 0.5 to 4.2 mmol/hr/g (about 8x) under anaerobic conditions. This increase is driven by regulation of phosphofructokinase (PFK), the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme: ATP and citrate (both more abundant when the Krebs cycle/ETC are active) are allosteric inhibitors of PFK, while AMP and ADP (more abundant when ATP production falls under anaerobic conditions) are allosteric activators. Anaerobically, falling ATP/citrate and rising AMP/ADP relieve PFK inhibition and activate it, ramping up glycolytic rate to compensate for the far lower ATP yield per glucose molecule.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe glucose breakdown through the three stages in general terms and identify CO2-releasing steps.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Glucose (6C): Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 6C glucose → 2× 3C pyruvate. No CO₂ released in glycolysis. All 6 carbons in 2 pyruvate. Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix): each 3C pyruvate → 1 CO₂ released + 2C acetyl-CoA (per pyruvate); 2 pyruvate → 2 CO₂ released + 2 acetyl-CoA. Running total: 2 CO₂ out (2 carbons); 4 carbons remain in 2 acetyl-CoA. Krebs cycle (×2 turns per glucose): each acetyl-CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → 2 CO₂ released per turn → oxaloacetate (4C) regenerated. Per turn: 2 CO₂ released. Two turns: 4 CO₂ released. Running total CO₂: 2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 4 (Krebs) = 6 CO₂ total. All 6 carbons from glucose accounted for as CO₂ released. Oxaloacetate is regenerated (not consumed net) and cycles continuously. 1 pt for correct carbon accounting through pyruvate oxidation; 1 pt for Krebs cycle carbon accounting with correct total CO₂.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Glycolysis: 6C glucose → 2× 3C pyruvate (no CO₂). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 pyruvate → 2 CO₂ + 2 acetyl-CoA (2C). Krebs ×2: 2 acetyl-CoA → 4 CO₂. Total: 6 CO₂ = all 6 glucose carbons accounted for.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Identify which stages produce NADH/FADH2 and explain their general role feeding the ETC.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Per glucose molecule: Glycolysis: 2 NADH (cytoplasm). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH (mitochondrial matrix). Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ (mitochondrial matrix). Total: 10 NADH (2 cytoplasmic + 8 mitochondrial) + 2 FADH₂. Use in ETC: Mitochondrial NADH → Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase); NADH donates 2 electrons to FMN prosthetic group → electrons passed to ubiquinone (Q); 4 H⁺ pumped per NADH. FADH₂ → Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, embedded in inner membrane) → electrons enter Q pool directly; no H⁺ pumped by Complex II → fewer ATP per FADH₂. Cytoplasmic NADH: must transfer electrons across inner membrane via shuttles: malate-aspartate shuttle → mitochondrial NADH → ~2.5 ATP; glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle → FADH₂ equivalent → ~1.5 ATP. All electron carriers ultimately deliver electrons to O₂ via Complex IV. 1 pt for complete count of NADH/FADH₂ by stage; 1 pt for correct ETC use with Complex assignments.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Glycolysis: 2 NADH (cytoplasm). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH (matrix). Krebs ×2: 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ (matrix). Total: 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂. Mitochondrial NADH → Complex I (4H⁺/NADH). FADH₂ → Complex II (no H⁺ pumped). Cytoplasmic NADH: shuttle dependent (2.5 or 1.5 ATP equiv).
accepted_variants: Complex II FADH2 no H+ pumped

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain at least two general reasons actual ATP yield is lower than theoretical maximum.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Three reasons actual < theoretical: (1) Proton leak: the inner mitochondrial membrane is not perfectly impermeable; some H⁺ leaks back across without passing through ATP synthase → energy dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP → fewer ATP per NADH/FADH₂. (2) ATP transport cost: ATP synthesized in the mitochondrial matrix must be exported by the ATP-ADP translocase (adenine nucleotide translocator, ANT) using a H⁺ cotransport mechanism → importing ADP and exporting ATP consumes some of the proton-motive force that could otherwise drive ATP synthesis. (3) Cytoplasmic NADH shuttle cost: glycolytic NADH cannot directly enter the mitochondria; malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttles are needed → shuttle type determines effective ATP yield (malate-aspartate shuttle gives ~2.5 ATP per cytoplasmic NADH, but some cells use the less efficient glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle giving ~1.5 ATP). (4) H⁺/ATP ratio uncertainty: the number of H⁺ required to synthesize 1 ATP by ATP synthase (the P/O ratio) is not exactly an integer (~2.7 H⁺/ATP experimentally), creating inherent inefficiency versus theoretical integer assumptions. Accept any three mechanistically correct explanations. 1 pt per 2 explanations, max 2 pts.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Three reasons: (1) proton leak across inner membrane dissipates gradient as heat; (2) ATP-ADP translocase uses part of proton gradient to export ATP; (3) cytoplasmic NADH must use less efficient shuttles (glycerol-3-phosphate gives fewer ATP); (4) non-integer P/O ratio for ATP synthase.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain increased anaerobic glucose consumption via ATP needs, fermentation's lower yield, and NAD+ regeneration.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Pasteur effect: aerobic conditions → low glucose consumption; anaerobic → 8× higher glucose consumption to maintain same ATP production rate. Mechanism: Under aerobic conditions: pyruvate enters Krebs/ETC → ~30-32 ATP per glucose; glycolysis is regulated at phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) — allosterically inhibited by high ATP/citrate levels → glycolysis slows when ATP is plentiful → low glucose consumption. Under anaerobic conditions: ETC cannot function (no O₂ as terminal electron acceptor) → no oxidative phosphorylation → only 2 ATP per glucose from glycolysis. To compensate: cell must consume 15-16× more glucose to generate the same ATP. But also: without ETC, NADH (from glycolysis) cannot be oxidized → NAD⁺ becomes depleted → glycolysis would halt at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step (requires NAD⁺). Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ (by reducing pyruvate using NADH) → allows glycolysis to continue rapidly. PFK-1 is no longer inhibited (low ATP → low inhibition) → glycolysis runs at maximum rate. Net: high glucose consumption rate required to generate sufficient ATP from inefficient glycolysis alone.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Pasteur effect: anaerobic = 8× more glucose consumed. Aerobic: ETC produces ~30 ATP/glucose; high ATP inhibits PFK-1 → glycolysis slows. Anaerobic: no ETC → only 2 ATP/glucose; low ATP → PFK-1 uninhibited → glycolysis runs fast; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis going. Net: must consume much more glucose to maintain ATP.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Compare alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation, and explain the metabolic purpose both pathways share.

Part B: A claim states that fermentation directly produces ATP from the reactions shown in the stimulus. Evaluate this claim: identify which step, if any, produces ATP directly, and clarify where most of a cell's ATP actually comes from when oxygen is available.

Part C: Using Table 1, explain the CO₂ production values under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, explain why the anaerobic rate is higher, and predict the CO₂ production rate for the aerobic + cyanide condition, given that cyanide blocks the electron transport chain.

Part D: A common claim is that lactic acid directly causes the burning sensation in fatigued muscles. Evaluate this claim and explain what most directly causes muscle fatigue during intense anaerobic exercise.
stimulus:
Table 1: CO₂ production by yeast
Condition                    | CO₂ production (mmol/hr/g)
Aerobic (glucose)            |        3.0
Anaerobic (glucose)          |        8.5
Aerobic (glucose + cyanide)  |        ?

Alcoholic fermentation reactions:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase)
2 Acetaldehyde + 2 NADH → 2 ethanol + 2 NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase)

Lactic acid fermentation:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 lactate (lactate dehydrogenase)
(No CO₂ produced in lactic acid fermentation)
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation) and 2 NADH. Pyruvate decarboxylase removes a carboxyl group from each pyruvate, releasing CO2 and forming acetaldehyde. Alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ in the process. Net reaction: glucose to 2 ethanol + 2 CO2. Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): glycolysis proceeds identically (2 ATP, 2 NADH). Lactate dehydrogenase directly reduces pyruvate to lactate, oxidizing NADH to NAD+; no CO2 is released. In both pathways, the enzyme catalyzing the final, defining step is lactate dehydrogenase (muscle) or alcohol dehydrogenase (yeast), and the metabolic purpose in both cases is identical: regenerate NAD+ so that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in glycolysis can keep functioning, allowing glycolysis (the only ATP-producing step available without O2) to continue.

(b) The claim is false/misleading. The reduction of pyruvate/acetaldehyde to lactate/ethanol (the fermentation step itself) produces zero ATP — it is purely a redox (NADH to NAD+) reaction with no phosphorylation of ADP. The actual ATP-producing step is glycolysis, specifically the substrate-level phosphorylation reactions catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, which occur before fermentation and do not themselves require O2 or fermentation. Fermentation's real function is to regenerate the NAD+ consumed by glycolysis, indirectly sustaining ATP production by keeping glycolysis running. The distinction matters because it correctly locates anaerobic ATP synthesis in glycolysis (substrate-level phosphorylation), not in the fermentation reaction, which is bioenergetically neutral for ATP.

(c)(i) Yeast produce CO2 aerobically via two decarboxylation-based processes: pyruvate oxidation (pyruvate to acetyl-CoA + CO2) and the Krebs cycle (isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps). Anaerobically, yeast produce CO2 via pyruvate decarboxylase in alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate to acetaldehyde + CO2).
(ii) The anaerobic CO2 rate is higher because anaerobic ATP yield per glucose (2 ATP via glycolysis) is far lower than the aerobic yield (~30 ATP), so to meet the same energy demand yeast must process glucose at a much higher rate anaerobically. Even though aerobic respiration releases more CO2 per glucose molecule (6 CO2 vs. 2 CO2 in fermentation), the much higher glucose flux anaerobically results in a higher overall CO2 production rate per unit time.
(iii) Cyanide blocks Complex IV, halting electron flow and stopping oxidative phosphorylation even in the presence of O2. Yeast would respond as if anaerobic: glycolytic flux would increase (loss of ATP/citrate-mediated PFK inhibition) and cells would shift to alcoholic fermentation to regenerate NAD+. CO2 production would initially drop (loss of the 6 CO2/glucose from pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle) but then rise again, approaching anaerobic-like rates, as fermentation-driven glycolytic flux increases and CO2 is produced via pyruvate decarboxylase.

(d) The coach's claim is not supported by current physiology. Lactate itself is not a metabolic "waste" that directly damages muscle; it can even be used as fuel by muscle and other tissues (e.g., the heart, liver via the Cori cycle). Muscle fatigue during intense exercise is caused primarily by: accumulation of H+ ions from rapid ATP hydrolysis (metabolic acidosis), which interferes with calcium binding to troponin and cross-bridge cycling; accumulation of inorganic phosphate (Pi), which disrupts calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and impairs cross-bridge force generation; and depletion of phosphocreatine/ATP stores along with disturbances in potassium ion balance across the muscle membrane, which reduce membrane excitability. Lactate production and fatigue are correlated (both increase during intense anaerobic exercise) because they share the same underlying cause — high rates of anaerobic glycolysis — but lactate itself is not the causal agent of fatigue.

frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): glucose -> 2 pyruvate -> 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO2 -> 2 ethanol + 2 NAD+; net C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + 2 ATP; CO2 is a byproduct. (ii) Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): glucose -> 2 pyruvate -> 2 lactate + 2 NAD+; net C6H12O6 -> 2 C3H6O3 + 2 ATP; no CO2 produced; lactate can be exported to the liver (Cori cycle). Purpose shared by both pathways: regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP anaerobically -- not to make lactate/ethanol as an end in itself. 1 pt for correct pathway/products for both types; 1 pt for correctly stating the shared metabolic purpose as NAD+ regeneration.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Evaluate the claim that fermentation directly produces ATP; clarify which step produces ATP.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The claim is INCORRECT as stated. ATP is produced by GLYCOLYSIS (substrate-level phosphorylation at phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps), NOT by the fermentation reactions themselves. The fermentation reactions (pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂, or pyruvate → lactate) produce NO ATP directly — they are redox reactions that recycle NAD⁺ by oxidizing NADH. The purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue to operate and produce ATP. Without NAD⁺ regeneration, the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis would halt (requires NAD⁺ as electron acceptor) → glycolysis stops → no more ATP from glycolysis. Distinction matters: the ATP comes from glycolysis; fermentation is a supporting reaction that enables glycolysis to keep running by preventing NADH accumulation. This is why some students confuse fermentation with energy production — it enables energy production (glycolysis) rather than performing it directly.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain CO₂ under both conditions; explain higher anaerobic rate; predict cyanide effect.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) CO₂ sources: Aerobic — CO₂ released in pyruvate oxidation (1 CO₂ per pyruvate) and Krebs cycle (2 CO₂ per acetyl-CoA × 2 turns = 4 CO₂ total). Anaerobic — CO₂ released only in pyruvate → acetaldehyde step (1 CO₂ per pyruvate; 2 per glucose) by pyruvate decarboxylase. No CO₂ from lactic acid fermentation. Yeast do alcoholic fermentation, so CO₂ is produced anaerobically. (ii) Higher CO₂ anaerobically (8.5 vs. 3.0 mmol/hr/g): despite less ATP per glucose (2 vs. ~30), yeast must consume ~4× more glucose per hour to maintain adequate ATP production → more glucose molecules processed → more total fermentative CO₂ released per hour → higher CO₂ production rate. (iii) Cyanide (Complex IV inhibitor): blocks O₂ from being reduced → ETC halts → aerobic respiration stops → yeast switch to fermentation → CO₂ production would INCREASE toward anaerobic levels (Pasteur effect in reverse); the yeast, now functionally anaerobic, ferment glucose rapidly → high CO₂ output.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) Aerobic CO₂: pyruvate oxidation + Krebs. Anaerobic CO₂: pyruvate decarboxylase only (alcoholic fermentation). (ii) Higher anaerobic CO₂: need 4× more glucose to generate ATP → more decarboxylation steps → more CO₂ per hour. (iii) Cyanide: ETC blocked → forced anaerobic → CO₂ increases to anaerobic levels.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Evaluate "lactic acid burns muscle" claim; explain actual cause of muscle fatigue.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The claim is OUTDATED and largely incorrect. Current understanding: lactate (lactic acid) itself does not cause muscle fatigue or burning sensation. Lactate is a fuel that can be oxidized by heart and oxidative muscle fibers, and the Cori cycle converts lactate to glucose in the liver. Actual causes of muscle fatigue during intense exercise: (1) Inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation: Pi released from ATP hydrolysis accumulates in the muscle; Pi inhibits cross-bridge cycling (reduces force per cross-bridge) and may block calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → reduced force production; (2) Acidosis: excess H⁺ (from ATP hydrolysis: ATP → ADP + Pi + H⁺) lowers intracellular pH → inhibits enzyme activity and reduces calcium sensitivity of troponin → reduced force. The burning sensation is from H⁺ (acid), not lactate per se. (3) Depletion of phosphocreatine and glycogen; (4) ADP accumulation. Lactate correlates with fatigue (produced alongside H⁺ under anaerobic conditions) but does not cause it. Some evidence suggests lactate may actually buffer acidosis by consuming H⁺ in the LDH reaction. 1 pt for correctly identifying the claim as outdated/incorrect; 1 pt for explaining actual fatigue mechanisms (H⁺, Pi accumulation).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Claim outdated: lactate does not cause muscle fatigue. Actual causes: H⁺ accumulation (from ATP hydrolysis, not from lactate) lowers pH → inhibits enzymes, reduces Ca²⁺ sensitivity; inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation impairs cross-bridge cycling; phosphocreatine depletion. Lactate itself may buffer acidosis.
