stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the information provided, describe the mechanism by which insulin binding triggers GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane. Trace the signaling pathway from insulin binding at the receptor through to glucose uptake.

Part B: Compare the insulin/receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathway to the epinephrine/G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) pathway described. For each pathway, identify: the receptor type and location, the primary second messenger or amplification step, and one physiological effect.

Part C: Suppose a mutation causes the insulin receptor to be constitutively (continuously) active, even in the absence of insulin. Predict THREE consequences of this mutation for the cell, addressing metabolic effects, cell proliferation, and gene expression.

Part D: Several distinct mutations can produce excessive, insulin-independent growth signaling in cancer cells. For EACH of the following, explain how the described change leads to chronic activation of a growth-signaling pathway:
(i) Overexpression of the HER2 receptor
(ii) A Ras protein locked in its GTP-bound form
(iii) Loss-of-function mutation in the PTEN gene
stimulus:
Insulin signaling pathway:
• Insulin binds → receptor α-subunits change conformation
• β-subunit cytoplasmic tails auto-phosphorylate tyrosines (kinase activation)
• IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) binds and is phosphorylated by receptor
• PI3K recruited → phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3
• PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt → PDK1 phosphorylates/activates Akt
• Active Akt phosphorylates downstream targets:
  – Phosphorylates AS160 → GLUT4 vesicle fusion with plasma membrane
  – Phosphorylates and inhibits GSK-3 → activates glycogen synthase
  – Activates mTOR → promotes protein synthesis
  – Phosphorylates and inactivates FOXO transcription factors

GPCR comparison:
• β-adrenergic receptor + epinephrine → Gα-GTP → adenylyl cyclase activated
• cAMP produced → PKA activated → multiple downstream phosphorylations
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Insulin binds the alpha-subunits of the insulin receptor, causing a conformational change that activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the beta-subunits; the beta-subunits trans-autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. These phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites that recruit and phosphorylate IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1). Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits PI3K via SH2 domains; PI3K phosphorylates membrane PIP2 to PIP3. PIP3 recruits both PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the plasma membrane, where PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. Active Akt phosphorylates AS160, inhibiting its normal suppression of Rab GTPases; this permits GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting GLUT4 glucose transporters and enabling glucose uptake.

(b) Insulin/RTK pathway: receptor type is a single-pass transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase located on the cell surface; the primary second messenger/amplifier is the PI3K to PIP3 to Akt phosphorylation cascade; physiological effect includes GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake (also glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis via mTOR). Epinephrine/GPCR (beta-adrenergic) pathway: receptor type is a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface, coupled to a Gs protein; the second messenger is cyclic AMP (cAMP), produced by adenylyl cyclase and activating protein kinase A (PKA); physiological effect includes glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) in liver/muscle via PKA-mediated activation of glycogen phosphorylase kinase, raising blood glucose as part of the fight-or-flight response.

(c) Three consequences of a constitutively active insulin receptor: (1) Metabolic effects — continuous Akt activation drives ongoing GLUT4 translocation and glycogen synthase activation (via GSK-3 inhibition), causing excessive, insulin-independent glucose uptake and storage, risking hypoglycemia and disrupted glucose homeostasis. (2) Cell proliferation — sustained activation of Akt/mTOR (and likely the parallel Ras/MAPK branch downstream of the RTK) promotes continuous protein synthesis and cell growth signals, potentially driving uncontrolled proliferation. (3) Gene expression effects — continuous phosphorylation and inactivation of FOXO transcription factors (which normally activate genes for gluconeogenesis and stress response/apoptosis when unphosphorylated) suppresses these FOXO target genes, altering glucose production pathways and reducing normal apoptotic/stress responses, which could favor unchecked cell survival.

(d)(i) HER2 overexpression: more receptor molecules on the cell surface increases the likelihood of ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, chronically activating downstream growth pathways (Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt) even without normal levels of growth factor, driving continuous proliferation signaling.
(ii) Ras locked in GTP-bound form: Ras normally functions as a molecular switch, active when GTP-bound and inactivated when it hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (assisted by GAPs); a mutation that prevents GTP hydrolysis leaves Ras permanently active, continuously stimulating the MAPK/ERK cascade and driving persistent proliferation signals to the nucleus regardless of upstream receptor activation.
(iii) PTEN loss-of-function: PTEN normally converts PIP3 back to PIP2, acting as a brake on the PI3K/Akt pathway; without functional PTEN, PIP3 accumulates unchecked, causing constitutive Akt activation and continuous pro-growth, pro-survival, anti-apoptotic signaling that drives uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe insulin → RTK → IRS-1 → PI3K → Akt → GLUT4 pathway in sequence.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Correct pathway sequence: (1) Insulin binds to the extracellular α-subunit of the insulin receptor → conformational change. (2) β-subunit cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domains auto-phosphorylate each other (transautophosphorylation) → kinase becomes active. (3) Activated receptor phosphorylates IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) on multiple tyrosines. (4) Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits and activates PI3K (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase). (5) PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3 at inner leaflet of plasma membrane. (6) PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the membrane; PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. (7) Active Akt phosphorylates AS160 (a GTPase-activating protein for Rab GTPases) → inactivates AS160 → Rab GTPases remain GTP-bound → GLUT4-containing vesicles traffic to and fuse with plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake. 1 pt for RTK activation mechanism (auto-phosphorylation, IRS-1 phosphorylation); 1 pt for PI3K→PIP3→Akt→GLUT4 mechanism.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Insulin binds receptor → RTK auto-phosphorylation → IRS-1 phosphorylated → PI3K activated → PIP2→PIP3 → Akt (PKB) activated → AS160 phosphorylated → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with plasma membrane → glucose uptake.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Compare RTK (insulin) and GPCR (epinephrine) pathways on receptor type, second messenger, and physiological effect.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Insulin receptor (RTK): (i) Transmembrane receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; single-pass (dimer) transmembrane; extracellular ligand-binding domain + intracellular kinase domain. (ii) Primary amplifier: PIP3 (membrane phospholipid second messenger) → activates Akt; no classical second messenger like cAMP; amplification through phosphorylation cascade. (iii) Physiological effect in liver: GLUT4 insertion → increased glucose uptake; glycogen synthase activated → glycogen synthesis; protein synthesis via mTOR. β-adrenergic receptor (GPCR): (i) 7-transmembrane receptor coupled to G-protein; no intrinsic catalytic activity; activates associated Gα protein. (ii) Primary second messenger: cAMP (produced by adenylyl cyclase activated by Gα-GTP) → activates PKA (protein kinase A) → phosphorylates multiple targets. (iii) Physiological effect in skeletal muscle: PKA activates phosphorylase kinase → activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) → glucose-1-phosphate → glycolysis → ATP for fight-or-flight. 1 pt per pathway with all 3 elements correct.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: RTK (insulin): intrinsic tyrosine kinase, PIP3/Akt amplification, effect = glucose uptake / glycogen synthesis. GPCR (epinephrine): 7-TM receptor, Gα → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA, effect = glycogenolysis / fight-or-flight response.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict three consequences of constitutively active insulin receptor.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: cells would constitutively import glucose (GLUT4 always at surface in insulin-sensitive cells) → increased glycolysis and glycogen synthesis → hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) as cells deplete blood glucose even in fasting state; excess acetyl-CoA → lipogenesis → excess fat storage. (2) Cell proliferation: Akt constitutively active → phosphorylates and inactivates GSK-3 → β-catenin accumulates → activates Wnt target genes promoting cell division; mTOR constitutively active → enhanced protein synthesis and cell growth; FOXO transcription factors constitutively inactivated → reduced expression of p27 (CDK inhibitor) and other cell cycle brakes → excessive cell proliferation → potential tumor formation. (3) Gene expression: constitutive Akt inactivates FOXO → reduced FOXO-dependent transcription (genes for gluconeogenesis, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis suppressed); mTOR promotes ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis genes; constitutive growth signals mimic oncogenic transformation. Award 1 pt per two well-explained consequences, max 2 pts.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: hypoglycemia, excess glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis even without food. (2) Proliferation: mTOR and Akt constitutively active → cell growth, reduced apoptosis, tumor-like proliferation. (3) Gene expression: FOXO transcription factors constitutively inhibited → reduced gluconeogenesis genes, reduced apoptosis genes.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how HER2 overexpression, Ras-GTP lock, and PTEN loss each contribute to cancer.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) HER2 overexpression: HER2 (ErbB2) is an RTK that forms dimers with other EGF family receptors; overexpression increases probability of spontaneous dimerization and auto-phosphorylation even without growth factor binding → constitutive downstream signaling (Ras→MAPK, PI3K→Akt) → constant proliferation signal. Also, more receptors means stronger amplified response to any ligand. Targeted by trastuzumab (Herceptin) antibody therapy. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: Ras is a small GTPase; normally GTP-Ras is active and stimulates proliferation (through MAPK cascade); Ras-GAP proteins hydrolyze GTP → GDP to inactivate Ras. A mutation preventing GTP hydrolysis (e.g., G12V mutation in KRAS) locks Ras in the active GTP-bound state → constitutive MAPK activation → continuous proliferation signal regardless of whether growth factor receptor is active. ~30% of human cancers have Ras mutations. (iii) PTEN loss: PTEN is a phosphatase that converts PIP3 back to PIP2 (antagonizes PI3K). Loss-of-function mutation → PIP3 accumulates constitutively → Akt constitutively active → mTOR always on → cell growth, survival, proliferation unchecked → tumor suppressor function lost (PTEN is a tumor suppressor). 1 pt per any two mechanisms with correct molecular detail.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) HER2 overexpression: spontaneous dimerization → constitutive kinase activity → continuous RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling without growth factor. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: cannot hydrolyze GTP → always active → constitutive MAPK → proliferation. (iii) PTEN loss: cannot convert PIP3→PIP2 → PIP3 accumulates → Akt always active → mTOR → proliferation (lost tumor suppressor).

(a) Insulin binds the alpha-subunits of the insulin receptor, causing a conformational change that activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the beta-subunits; the beta-subunits trans-autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. These phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites that recruit and phosphorylate IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1). Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits PI3K via SH2 domains; PI3K phosphorylates membrane PIP2 to PIP3. PIP3 recruits both PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the plasma membrane, where PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. Active Akt phosphorylates AS160, inhibiting its normal suppression of Rab GTPases; this permits GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting GLUT4 glucose transporters and enabling glucose uptake.

(b) Insulin/RTK pathway: receptor type is a single-pass transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase located on the cell surface; the primary second messenger/amplifier is the PI3K to PIP3 to Akt phosphorylation cascade; physiological effect includes GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake (also glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis via mTOR). Epinephrine/GPCR (beta-adrenergic) pathway: receptor type is a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface, coupled to a Gs protein; the second messenger is cyclic AMP (cAMP), produced by adenylyl cyclase and activating protein kinase A (PKA); physiological effect includes glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) in liver/muscle via PKA-mediated activation of glycogen phosphorylase kinase, raising blood glucose as part of the fight-or-flight response.

(c) Three consequences of a constitutively active insulin receptor: (1) Metabolic effects — continuous Akt activation drives ongoing GLUT4 translocation and glycogen synthase activation (via GSK-3 inhibition), causing excessive, insulin-independent glucose uptake and storage, risking hypoglycemia and disrupted glucose homeostasis. (2) Cell proliferation — sustained activation of Akt/mTOR (and likely the parallel Ras/MAPK branch downstream of the RTK) promotes continuous protein synthesis and cell growth signals, potentially driving uncontrolled proliferation. (3) Gene expression effects — continuous phosphorylation and inactivation of FOXO transcription factors (which normally activate genes for gluconeogenesis and stress response/apoptosis when unphosphorylated) suppresses these FOXO target genes, altering glucose production pathways and reducing normal apoptotic/stress responses, which could favor unchecked cell survival.

(d)(i) HER2 overexpression: more receptor molecules on the cell surface increases the likelihood of ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, chronically activating downstream growth pathways (Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt) even without normal levels of growth factor, driving continuous proliferation signaling.
(ii) Ras locked in GTP-bound form: Ras normally functions as a molecular switch, active when GTP-bound and inactivated when it hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (assisted by GAPs); a mutation that prevents GTP hydrolysis leaves Ras permanently active, continuously stimulating the MAPK/ERK cascade and driving persistent proliferation signals to the nucleus regardless of upstream receptor activation.
(iii) PTEN loss-of-function: PTEN normally converts PIP3 back to PIP2, acting as a brake on the PI3K/Akt pathway; without functional PTEN, PIP3 accumulates unchecked, causing constitutive Akt activation and continuous pro-growth, pro-survival, anti-apoptotic signaling that drives uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe insulin → RTK → IRS-1 → PI3K → Akt → GLUT4 pathway in sequence.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Correct pathway sequence: (1) Insulin binds to the extracellular α-subunit of the insulin receptor → conformational change. (2) β-subunit cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domains auto-phosphorylate each other (transautophosphorylation) → kinase becomes active. (3) Activated receptor phosphorylates IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) on multiple tyrosines. (4) Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits and activates PI3K (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase). (5) PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3 at inner leaflet of plasma membrane. (6) PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the membrane; PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. (7) Active Akt phosphorylates AS160 (a GTPase-activating protein for Rab GTPases) → inactivates AS160 → Rab GTPases remain GTP-bound → GLUT4-containing vesicles traffic to and fuse with plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake. 1 pt for RTK activation mechanism (auto-phosphorylation, IRS-1 phosphorylation); 1 pt for PI3K→PIP3→Akt→GLUT4 mechanism.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Insulin binds receptor → RTK auto-phosphorylation → IRS-1 phosphorylated → PI3K activated → PIP2→PIP3 → Akt (PKB) activated → AS160 phosphorylated → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with plasma membrane → glucose uptake.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Compare RTK (insulin) and GPCR (epinephrine) pathways on receptor type, second messenger, and physiological effect.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Insulin receptor (RTK): (i) Transmembrane receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; single-pass (dimer) transmembrane; extracellular ligand-binding domain + intracellular kinase domain. (ii) Primary amplifier: PIP3 (membrane phospholipid second messenger) → activates Akt; no classical second messenger like cAMP; amplification through phosphorylation cascade. (iii) Physiological effect in liver: GLUT4 insertion → increased glucose uptake; glycogen synthase activated → glycogen synthesis; protein synthesis via mTOR. β-adrenergic receptor (GPCR): (i) 7-transmembrane receptor coupled to G-protein; no intrinsic catalytic activity; activates associated Gα protein. (ii) Primary second messenger: cAMP (produced by adenylyl cyclase activated by Gα-GTP) → activates PKA (protein kinase A) → phosphorylates multiple targets. (iii) Physiological effect in skeletal muscle: PKA activates phosphorylase kinase → activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) → glucose-1-phosphate → glycolysis → ATP for fight-or-flight. 1 pt per pathway with all 3 elements correct.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: RTK (insulin): intrinsic tyrosine kinase, PIP3/Akt amplification, effect = glucose uptake / glycogen synthesis. GPCR (epinephrine): 7-TM receptor, Gα → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA, effect = glycogenolysis / fight-or-flight response.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict three consequences of constitutively active insulin receptor.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: cells would constitutively import glucose (GLUT4 always at surface in insulin-sensitive cells) → increased glycolysis and glycogen synthesis → hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) as cells deplete blood glucose even in fasting state; excess acetyl-CoA → lipogenesis → excess fat storage. (2) Cell proliferation: Akt constitutively active → phosphorylates and inactivates GSK-3 → β-catenin accumulates → activates Wnt target genes promoting cell division; mTOR constitutively active → enhanced protein synthesis and cell growth; FOXO transcription factors constitutively inactivated → reduced expression of p27 (CDK inhibitor) and other cell cycle brakes → excessive cell proliferation → potential tumor formation. (3) Gene expression: constitutive Akt inactivates FOXO → reduced FOXO-dependent transcription (genes for gluconeogenesis, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis suppressed); mTOR promotes ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis genes; constitutive growth signals mimic oncogenic transformation. Award 1 pt per two well-explained consequences, max 2 pts.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: hypoglycemia, excess glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis even without food. (2) Proliferation: mTOR and Akt constitutively active → cell growth, reduced apoptosis, tumor-like proliferation. (3) Gene expression: FOXO transcription factors constitutively inhibited → reduced gluconeogenesis genes, reduced apoptosis genes.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how HER2 overexpression, Ras-GTP lock, and PTEN loss each contribute to cancer.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) HER2 overexpression: HER2 (ErbB2) is an RTK that forms dimers with other EGF family receptors; overexpression increases probability of spontaneous dimerization and auto-phosphorylation even without growth factor binding → constitutive downstream signaling (Ras→MAPK, PI3K→Akt) → constant proliferation signal. Also, more receptors means stronger amplified response to any ligand. Targeted by trastuzumab (Herceptin) antibody therapy. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: Ras is a small GTPase; normally GTP-Ras is active and stimulates proliferation (through MAPK cascade); Ras-GAP proteins hydrolyze GTP → GDP to inactivate Ras. A mutation preventing GTP hydrolysis (e.g., G12V mutation in KRAS) locks Ras in the active GTP-bound state → constitutive MAPK activation → continuous proliferation signal regardless of whether growth factor receptor is active. ~30% of human cancers have Ras mutations. (iii) PTEN loss: PTEN is a phosphatase that converts PIP3 back to PIP2 (antagonizes PI3K). Loss-of-function mutation → PIP3 accumulates constitutively → Akt constitutively active → mTOR always on → cell growth, survival, proliferation unchecked → tumor suppressor function lost (PTEN is a tumor suppressor). 1 pt per any two mechanisms with correct molecular detail.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) HER2 overexpression: spontaneous dimerization → constitutive kinase activity → continuous RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling without growth factor. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: cannot hydrolyze GTP → always active → constitutive MAPK → proliferation. (iii) PTEN loss: cannot convert PIP3→PIP2 → PIP3 accumulates → Akt always active → mTOR → proliferation (lost tumor suppressor).

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The pedigree in Figure 1 shows the inheritance of a trait across three generations. Affected individuals are shaded. Determine the most likely mode of inheritance and justify your answer by identifying at least TWO pedigree observations that support your conclusion. Assign genotypes to individuals I-1, I-2, II-3 (an affected male), and II-4 (an unaffected female who has an affected son). Calculate the probability that a child of II-4 and II-3 will be an affected female.

Part B: Males with X-linked recessive conditions are affected at a much higher frequency than females. Explain the molecular and genetic basis for this sex difference, using hemizygosity in your explanation.

Part C: Explain X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) in female mammals. Describe when X-inactivation occurs in development and how the choice of which X is inactivated is made. Describe the molecular mechanism of X-inactivation, naming the gene responsible and the RNA molecule involved. Explain why X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited.

Part D: A tortoiseshell cat has patches of orange and black fur. The gene for orange/black fur color is X-linked. Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female. Explain why the patches of orange and black fur are large rather than a uniform blended color. Predict the coat color pattern of a female cat that is homozygous for the orange allele.
stimulus:
Pedigree — Figure 1 (described):
Generation I:   I-1 (unaffected male) × I-2 (unaffected female)
Generation II:  II-1 (unaffected female), II-2 (unaffected male),
                II-3 (AFFECTED male), II-4 (unaffected female),
                II-5 (unaffected male)
Generation III: III-1 (AFFECTED male, son of II-4 and II-5)
                III-2 (unaffected female, daughter of II-4 and II-5)

Note: No affected females in pedigree.
Affected: II-3 (male), III-1 (male, son of II-4 and unaffected II-5)

X-linked gene notation:
• X^A = dominant / unaffected allele
• X^a = recessive / affected allele
• Females: X^A X^A (normal), X^A X^a (carrier), X^a X^a (affected)
• Males: X^A Y (normal), X^a Y (affected)
canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Most likely mode of inheritance: X-linked recessive. Two supporting pedigree observations: (1) only males are affected (no affected females appear anywhere in the pedigree), consistent with a recessive allele on the X chromosome where males need only one copy (hemizygous) to be affected while females need two copies; (2) the trait appears to skip a generation through an unaffected carrier female (II-4, unaffected, yet has an affected son III-1), which is the classic X-linked recessive pattern of transmission through unaffected carrier mothers rather than direct parent-to-offspring transmission in every generation.
(ii) Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y (unaffected male); I-2 = X^A X^a (obligate carrier, since she must have transmitted the recessive allele that appears in affected descendants); II-3 = X^a Y (affected male); II-4 = X^A X^a (unaffected carrier female, confirmed by having an affected son).
(iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a, carrier female) x II-3 (X^a Y, affected male) gives offspring: 1/4 X^A X^a (carrier female), 1/4 X^a X^a (affected female), 1/4 X^A Y (unaffected male), 1/4 X^a Y (affected male). The probability of an affected female (X^a X^a) is 1/4 (25%): the affected father II-3 always contributes X^a to every daughter, and the carrier mother II-4 contributes X^a to half of her offspring, so a daughter is affected only if she also receives X^a from her mother -- 1/2 (mother's X^a) x 1 (father's obligate X^a) = 1/4.

(b) Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes -- they have only a single X chromosome (paired with a Y chromosome that lacks a homologous allele for most X-linked genes), so a single copy of a recessive allele is sufficient to produce the affected phenotype in males, with no second allele to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes, so a single recessive allele is typically masked by a normal dominant allele on the other X chromosome (heterozygous carrier females are unaffected); females must inherit the recessive allele from both parents to be affected, which is much less likely, especially for rare alleles, explaining the much higher frequency of affected males.

(c)(i) X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development, around the blastocyst stage (approximately day 5-6 in humans), independently in each cell of the female embryo. The choice of which X chromosome (maternal or paternal) is inactivated in each cell is random.
(ii) The Xist gene, located on the X chromosome destined to be inactivated, is upregulated and transcribes a long non-coding RNA (Xist RNA) that coats that X chromosome in cis; this recruits chromatin-modifying complexes that establish heterochromatin (histone deacetylation and methylation, DNA methylation), condensing that chromosome into a transcriptionally silent Barr body.
(iii) X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited because once a given cell inactivates a specific X chromosome, the epigenetic marks (including DNA methylation patterns) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and passed on to all of that cell's mitotic descendants, so each clonal lineage of cells maintains the same inactivated X, producing stable patches of tissue expressing only one parental X allele.

(d)(i) Tortoiseshell cats are almost always female because the orange/black coat color gene is X-linked; a heterozygous female undergoes random X-inactivation, creating two populations of cells -- some expressing the orange allele, others the black allele -- producing a patched, two-color coat. Males are hemizygous (XY) and carry only one allele, so they are uniformly either orange or black (except in rare XXY males).
(ii) The patches are large rather than finely blended because X-inactivation happens early in development when the embryo consists of relatively few cells; each of those early cells' clonal descendants (forming a large contiguous patch of tissue) all inherit the same inactivated X, so entire regions of skin trace back to a single early progenitor with one particular X active, producing large, blocky patches rather than a fine intermixed pattern.
(iii) A female homozygous for the orange allele would be entirely orange, with no black patches, because every cell expresses the orange allele regardless of which X chromosome is inactivated.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Determine mode of inheritance; assign genotypes; calculate probability of affected female offspring.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) X-linked recessive. Evidence: (1) Only males are affected (II-3, III-1) — X-linked recessive affects males more frequently than females because males are hemizygous; (2) Affected son III-1 was born to two unaffected parents (II-4 and II-5) → trait skipped a generation → characteristic of recessive; (3) Affected II-3 had an unaffected father (I-1) — this rules out Y-linked (which would affect all sons of affected fathers); (4) I-2 must be a carrier (unaffected female with affected son II-3). Also rules out autosomal: autosomal recessive would give equal sex ratios; autosomal dominant would show affected in every generation if parents are affected. (ii) Genotypes: I-1: X^A Y (unaffected male, no allele to give son affected); I-2: X^A X^a (carrier female — must carry X^a to pass to affected son II-3); II-3: X^a Y (affected male); II-4: X^A X^a (carrier — must carry X^a to have affected son III-1, and her husband II-5 is X^A Y unaffected so son must have gotten X^a from her). (iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a) × II-3 (X^a Y): Possible offspring: X^A X^a (carrier female), X^a X^a (affected female), X^A Y (normal male), X^a Y (affected male). Probability affected female = X^a X^a = 1/4 = 25%.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: X-linked recessive. Evidence: only males affected; skip-generation transmission; unaffected parents have affected sons. Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y; I-2 = X^A X^a; II-3 = X^a Y; II-4 = X^A X^a. Probability affected female = 1/4 (25%).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain molecular basis of higher male frequency for X-linked recessive traits using hemizygosity.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Hemizygosity: males have only one X chromosome and one Y chromosome (XY). The Y chromosome does not carry most genes present on the X chromosome (the non-pseudoautosomal region of Y is distinct). Therefore, for X-linked genes, males have only ONE copy of the allele (hemizygous) — there is no second allele on a homolog to mask the recessive allele's phenotypic effect. For X-linked recessive conditions: a male who inherits even one copy of the recessive allele (X^a Y) will be affected, because there is no corresponding dominant allele on the Y to compensate. For females: they have two X chromosomes (XX), so a female with one recessive allele (X^A X^a) is a heterozygous CARRIER — the dominant X^A allele produces sufficient functional protein to mask the recessive phenotype. A female must be homozygous recessive (X^a X^a) to be affected, requiring inheritance of the recessive allele from BOTH parents. This is much less probable than a male inheriting a single recessive allele. Example: red-green color blindness affects ~8% of males but only ~0.5% of females because female frequency ≈ (male frequency)² (Hardy-Weinberg).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes (only one X, no second allele on Y). A single recessive allele causes expression in males. Females (XX) need two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous) to be affected. Single-carrier females are unaffected. Therefore males affected much more frequently.
accepted_variants: Y does not carry X-linked alleles
single recessive allele expresses in males
dominant allele masks recessive in heterozygous female

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain X-inactivation: timing, choice, molecular mechanism, and clonal inheritance.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Timing and choice: X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development — in placental mammals, around days 12-16 in humans (at the blastocyst → post-implantation stage, around the time of gastrulation; some texts say 100-cell stage). In each somatic cell of the early embryo, ONE X chromosome is randomly inactivated — either the maternal X or the paternal X is chosen with equal probability. (Note: in extra-embryonic cells like trophoblast, the paternal X is preferentially inactivated — imprinted X-inactivation.) After the initial choice is made independently in each cell, it is maintained in all descendants. (ii) Molecular mechanism: the XIST gene (X-Inactive Specific Transcript) on the X chromosome to be inactivated is transcribed and produces a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) called XIST (or Xist in mice). XIST RNA coats the inactive X chromosome in cis (spreads along the chromosome it is transcribed from). XIST RNA recruits chromatin-remodeling proteins (Polycomb group proteins) → histone modifications (H3K27 methylation, H3K9 methylation, loss of H3 acetylation) → heterochromatin formation → DNA methylation of CpG islands at gene promoters → gene silencing. The inactive X condenses into a dense structure called the Barr body (sex chromatin). (iii) Permanence and clonal inheritance: once X is inactivated, epigenetic marks (DNA methylation and histone modifications) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and cell division → every daughter cell inherits the same inactive X → the inactivation pattern is clonally inherited for the lifetime of the organism. The XIST RNA continues to be expressed from the inactive X to maintain silencing. This is why X-inactivation is an irreversible epigenetic modification in somatic cells. 1 pt per two sub-parts correctly addressed.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Timing: early embryo (~day 12-16), random choice in each cell (maternal or paternal X). Mechanism: XIST gene transcribes lncRNA that coats inactive X → recruits Polycomb proteins → histone methylation → DNA methylation → Barr body. Clonal: epigenetic marks copied at each cell division → all daughter cells have same inactive X.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain tortoiseshell cat genetics: female only; large patches; homozygous orange prediction.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Tortoiseshell always female: the coat color gene is X-linked (O = orange, o = black). Males (XY) are hemizygous → can only be orange (X^O Y) or black (X^o Y), never both. Females (XX) can be heterozygous (X^O X^o) → carry one orange and one black allele. X-inactivation causes random inactivation of one X in each somatic cell → some cells express orange, others express black → patches of each color. Very rarely, tortoiseshell males occur due to XXY karyotype (Klinefelter syndrome in cats). (ii) Large patches: X-inactivation occurs early in development (small number of cells), and once a cell's X is inactivated, all descendants inherit the same inactive X (clonal inheritance). By the time the cat's coat develops, each early embryonic cell has produced millions of descendants, all with the same X active → large coherent patches of one color. If inactivation were re-randomized at every cell division, colors would be uniformly blended (like a mix of paint) instead of patchy. The large patches are direct evidence of clonal expansion from early X-inactivation events. (iii) Homozygous orange female: X^O X^O → both X chromosomes carry the orange allele. X-inactivation still occurs (one X silenced in each cell), but both X chromosomes carry orange allele → all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated → cat is uniformly solid orange (no black patches). 1 pt for (i) with hemizygosity explanation; 1 pt for (ii) + (iii).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) Tortoiseshell = heterozygous female (X^O X^o); males hemizygous cannot have both alleles; rare tortoiseshell males are XXY. (ii) Large patches = clonal expansion from early X-inactivation; each patch descended from one early cell with same inactive X. (iii) Homozygous orange female (X^O X^O) = solid orange; all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated.
accepted_variants: X^O X^O solid orange all cells

(iii) Permanence and clonal inheritance: once X is inactivated, epigenetic marks (DNA methylation and histone modifications) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and cell division → every daughter cell inherits the same inactive X → the inactivation pattern is clonally inherited for the lifetime of the organism. The XIST RNA continues to be expressed from the inactive X to maintain silencing. This is why X-inactivation is an irreversible epigenetic modification in somatic cells. 1 pt per two sub-parts correctly addressed.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Timing: early embryo (~day 12-16), random choice in each cell (maternal or paternal X). Mechanism: XIST gene transcribes lncRNA that coats inactive X → recruits Polycomb proteins → histone methylation → DNA methylation → Barr body. Clonal: epigenetic marks copied at each cell division → all daughter cells have same inactive X.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain tortoiseshell cat genetics: female only; large patches; homozygous orange prediction.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Tortoiseshell always female: the coat color gene is X-linked (O = orange, o = black). Males (XY) are hemizygous → can only be orange (X^O Y) or black (X^o Y), never both. Females (XX) can be heterozygous (X^O X^o) → carry one orange and one black allele. X-inactivation causes random inactivation of one X in each somatic cell → some cells express orange, others express black → patches of each color. Very rarely, tortoiseshell males occur due to XXY karyotype (Klinefelter syndrome in cats). (ii) Large patches: X-inactivation occurs early in development (small number of cells), and once a cell's X is inactivated, all descendants inherit the same inactive X (clonal inheritance). By the time the cat's coat develops, each early embryonic cell has produced millions of descendants, all with the same X active → large coherent patches of one color. If inactivation were re-randomized at every cell division, colors would be uniformly blended (like a mix of paint) instead of patchy. The large patches are direct evidence of clonal expansion from early X-inactivation events. (iii) Homozygous orange female: X^O X^O → both X chromosomes carry the orange allele. X-inactivation still occurs (one X silenced in each cell), but both X chromosomes carry orange allele → all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated → cat is uniformly solid orange (no black patches). 1 pt for (i) with hemizygosity explanation; 1 pt for (ii) + (iii).
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: (i) Tortoiseshell = heterozygous female (X^O X^o); males hemizygous cannot have both alleles; rare tortoiseshell males are XXY. (ii) Large patches = clonal expansion from early X-inactivation; each patch descended from one early cell with same inactive X. (iii) Homozygous orange female (X^O X^O) = solid orange; all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated.
accepted_variants: X^O X^O solid orange all cells

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Eukaryotic gene expression requires the coordinated action of transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and chromatin remodeling. Describe the sequence of events that leads to the assembly of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) at a eukaryotic promoter and name TWO general transcription factors and their roles. Explain how an enhancer element located 10,000 base pairs upstream of a gene can stimulate transcription at the gene's promoter, including the role of activator proteins and Mediator.

Part B: Chromatin structure regulates access to DNA. Using Figure 1 (which shows the same gene in euchromatin vs. heterochromatin states): Describe the structural difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin at the level of histone modification. Explain how histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) have opposite effects on transcription, including the mechanism by which acetylation opens chromatin. A researcher adds trichostatin A (an HDAC inhibitor) to cells. Predict and explain the effect on global gene expression.

Part C: Experiment: The researcher fuses the DNA-binding domain of a transcription factor to different activation domains and measures target gene expression. Results are shown in Table 1. What does the DNA-binding domain alone demonstrate about gene activation? What do the activation domain results reveal about how transcription is activated? The researcher finds that activation domain 3 interacts physically with the Mediator complex. Explain how this interaction could lead to increased transcription.

Part D: Explain how the following two mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression in a multicellular organism that has one genome but hundreds of distinct cell types: Combinatorial control by transcription factors and epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states.
stimulus:
Figure 1 (described):
• Euchromatin: beads-on-a-string appearance; histones visible as individual nucleosomes; 30nm fiber partially unfolded; gene accessible to RNA polymerase → gene ON
• Heterochromatin: highly compact; 300nm fiber; DNA wound tightly; gene inaccessible → gene OFF

Table 1: Transcription factor domain fusion experiment
Construct                    | Target gene expression (relative units)
DBD alone                    |         1 (baseline)
DBD + Activation Domain 1    |        45
DBD + Activation Domain 2    |        12
DBD + Activation Domain 3    |        87
DBD + AD1 + AD3              |       203

Note: DBD = DNA-binding domain; all constructs bind the same promoter sequence.
canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Pre-initiation complex (PIC) assembly: TFIID (via its TBP subunit) binds the TATA box in the promoter and bends the DNA, nucleating assembly of the complex; this recruits TFIIA and TFIIB, which stabilize TFIID binding and help correctly position RNA Polymerase II at the transcription start site. RNA Pol II is recruited together with TFIIF; TFIIE and TFIIH then join the complex. TFIIH has both helicase activity (unwinds the DNA at the start site, forming the transcription bubble) and kinase activity (phosphorylates the C-terminal domain, CTD, of RNA Pol II), which triggers promoter escape and the start of transcription. Two general transcription factors and their roles: TFIID (binds the TATA box via TBP, nucleates PIC assembly) and TFIIH (unwinds promoter DNA and phosphorylates the Pol II CTD to initiate transcription).
(ii) Enhancers act at a distance through DNA looping: activator proteins bind the enhancer sequence; the Mediator complex physically bridges these DNA-bound activators with the general transcription machinery (including RNA Pol II and the general transcription factors) assembled at the promoter, causing the intervening DNA to loop out so the enhancer and promoter come into close physical proximity despite being far apart in linear sequence. This interaction stabilizes PIC assembly at the promoter and increases the rate of transcription initiation.

(b)(i) Euchromatin has hyperacetylated histones, is loosely packed in a "beads-on-a-string" (10 nm fiber) conformation with accessible DNA. Heterochromatin has hypoacetylated (deacetylated) and often methylated histones (for example, H3K9 trimethylation), and is tightly compacted (30 nm+ fiber), rendering the DNA inaccessible.
(ii) Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) add acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, neutralizing their positive charge; this weakens the electrostatic attraction between the histones and the negatively charged DNA backbone, loosening chromatin structure and increasing accessibility for transcription factors and RNA polymerase, thereby activating transcription. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove these acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge on histones, tightening histone-DNA interactions, condensing chromatin, and repressing transcription.
(iii) Trichostatin A inhibits HDACs, causing acetyl groups to accumulate on histones (global hyperacetylation). Chromatin becomes more open and accessible throughout the genome, which generally increases global gene expression, since more promoters and regulatory regions become accessible to transcription factors and RNA polymerase.

(c)(i) The DNA-binding domain alone produces only baseline expression (about 1), demonstrating that binding to the promoter DNA is necessary but not sufficient to activate transcription — the DBD can locate and occupy the target sequence but cannot itself recruit the machinery needed to activate transcription without an activation domain.
(ii) The different activation domains produce very different levels of activation (45, 12, 87), showing that activation is modular and that activation domains vary substantially in their ability to recruit and stimulate the transcriptional machinery, likely reflecting differences in the specific protein-protein interactions each domain can make with coactivators, chromatin remodelers, or Mediator. The combined AD1 + AD3 result (203) exceeding either domain alone demonstrates a synergistic (more than additive) effect when multiple activation domains act together.
(iii) Because Activation Domain 3 physically interacts with the Mediator complex, it can directly recruit Mediator to the promoter region; Mediator in turn helps recruit and stabilize RNA Polymerase II and the general transcription factors at the promoter, increasing the efficiency of PIC assembly and the rate of transcription initiation, explaining AD3's strong activation of gene expression (87 relative units).

(d)(i) Combinatorial control: different cell types express different combinations of transcription factors. A given gene's regulatory elements often require a specific combination of multiple transcription factors bound simultaneously to be activated, so the gene is only expressed in cell types that happen to express that particular combination of factors; this allows a relatively limited number of transcription factors to generate many distinct, cell-type-specific gene expression patterns combinatorially.
(ii) Epigenetic inheritance: the chromatin state (DNA methylation patterns and histone modifications) established at specific genes during differentiation is stably maintained and copied through successive rounds of DNA replication and mitosis, so a differentiated cell's daughter cells retain the same pattern of active and silenced genes as the parent cell — this preserves cell-type identity across many cell divisions without requiring the pattern of gene expression to be re-established from scratch in every generation of cells.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe PIC assembly at eukaryotic promoter naming two GTFs; explain enhancer-Mediator mechanism.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) PIC assembly: (1) A pioneer transcription factor or general factor recognizes the TATA box (core promoter element ~25 bp upstream of TSS) → TFIID (containing TBP, TATA-Binding Protein) binds the TATA box; TBP bends DNA. (2) TFIIA and TFIIB are recruited → TFIIB positions RNA pol II. (3) TFIIF enters with RNA pol II → stabilizes RNA pol II at promoter. (4) TFIIE and TFIIH join → TFIIH has helicase activity to unwind DNA at TSS (open complex formation) and kinase activity to phosphorylate the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA pol II → triggers elongation. Two GTFs to name: TFIID (TBP subunit recognizes TATA box), TFIIH (helicase opens DNA and CTD kinase activates polymerase). (ii) Enhancer mechanism: activator proteins bind the enhancer element via their DNA-binding domains. The activation domains of activators recruit coactivators and Mediator complex. The chromatin between enhancer and promoter loops around (enhancer-promoter looping, mediated by cohesin and CTCF proteins) → brings the activator-Mediator complex into contact with the PIC at the promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → stimulates transcription initiation rate. This looping explains action at a distance (10 kb away). 1 pt for PIC assembly with two GTFs and roles; 1 pt for enhancer-looping-Mediator mechanism.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: TFIID (TBP binds TATA box) and TFIIH (helicase opens DNA, CTD kinase activates RNA pol II) assemble PIC. Enhancer: activators bind → DNA loops (cohesin/CTCF) → enhancer contacts promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → increased transcription.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe euchromatin/heterochromatin histone modifications; HAT/HDAC mechanisms; predict HDAC inhibitor effect.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Euchromatin vs. heterochromatin at histone level: Euchromatin — histones are hyperacetylated (acetyl groups on lysine residues of H3 and H4 N-terminal tails) and have active histone methylation marks (H3K4me3 at promoters); chromatin is loose and accessible. Heterochromatin — histones are hypoacetylated (deacetylated), have repressive methylation marks (H3K9me3, H3K27me3); histone H1 (linker histone) compacts chromatin further; chromatin is condensed, DNA inaccessible. (ii) HAT/HDAC mechanism: HATs (histone acetyltransferases) add acetyl groups to histone lysine residues → neutralizes positive charge of lysine → reduces attraction between histones and negatively charged DNA → chromatin loosens (nucleosome-DNA interaction weakened) → DNA more accessible to transcription machinery → transcription increases. HDACs (histone deacetylases) remove acetyl groups → lysines revert to positive charge → stronger histone-DNA interactions → chromatin compacts → transcription decreases. (iii) Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor) effect: HDACs cannot remove acetyl groups → histones remain hyperacetylated → chromatin stays loose/open → global increase in transcription of many genes, including genes normally kept silenced. Genes under active repression via deacetylation would be de-repressed. Effect: widespread upregulation of gene expression; some previously silenced genes (tumor suppressors, differentiation genes) may be reactivated. This is why HDAC inhibitors are investigated as cancer therapies. 1 pt for euchromatin/heterochromatin marks with mechanism; 1 pt for correct HDAC inhibitor prediction with reasoning.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Euchromatin: hyperacetylated histones (H3K4me3), loose chromatin. Heterochromatin: deacetylated histones (H3K9me3, H3K27me3), compact. HATs acetylate lysines → neutralize charge → looser chromatin → more transcription. HDACs remove acetyl → compact. HDAC inhibitor → all histones remain acetylated → global gene upregulation → silenced genes de-repressed.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Interpret domain fusion experiment data; explain Mediator interaction mechanism.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) DBD alone (expression = 1, baseline): the DNA-binding domain alone can bind the promoter but does NOT activate transcription — it shows that DNA binding is necessary but not sufficient for transcription activation. Simply recruiting a protein to the DNA does not stimulate RNA pol II. Transcriptional activation requires a separate activation domain. (ii) Activation domain results: activation domains differ in strength (AD3 > AD1 > AD2); the activation domain is the functional module responsible for stimulating transcription, independent of what DNA it is bound to (domain swap experiment works). Combining AD1 + AD3 gives superadditive (synergistic) activation (203 > 45+87 = 132) — demonstrates that multiple activation domains can work cooperatively (combinatorial activation), perhaps by recruiting different coactivators simultaneously. (iii) Mediator interaction of AD3: if AD3 physically contacts the Mediator complex, AD3 recruits Mediator to the promoter → Mediator acts as a bridge between activators and the general transcription machinery → Mediator interacts with RNA pol II CTD → stimulates assembly of the PIC or transition from initiation to productive elongation (CTD phosphorylation) → increased transcription. AD3's stronger activation could be because it makes particularly favorable contacts with Mediator subunits. 1 pt for correct interpretations of DBD alone + AD results; 1 pt for Mediator mechanism.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: DBD alone: binding DNA insufficient for activation. ADs differ in strength; AD3 > AD1 > AD2. AD1+AD3 synergistic (203 > 132) = combinatorial activation. AD3-Mediator interaction: recruits Mediator to promoter → bridges activator to RNA pol II → stimulates PIC assembly or CTD phosphorylation → increased transcription.
accepted_variants: Mediator bridges activator to RNA pol II

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain cell-type-specific expression via combinatorial TF control and epigenetic inheritance.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors: different cell types express different subsets of transcription factors; the combination of TFs present in a cell determines which genes are active. Gene A may require TF1 + TF2 + TF3 to be activated; Gene B requires TF1 + TF4. A neuron expresses TF1+TF2+TF3 (→ Gene A on, Gene B off); a muscle cell expresses TF1+TF4 (→ Gene A off, Gene B on). With as few as 10 different TFs, the combinatorial possibilities (2^10 = 1024 combinations) can specify hundreds of distinct cell identities. The same promoter is interpreted differently depending on which TFs are present → same genome, different expression profiles. (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states: once a cell commits to a lineage, its chromatin state (which regions are euchromatic vs. heterochromatic, DNA methylation at CpG islands, Polycomb/Trithorax marks on histones) is faithfully copied at each cell division. Maintenance methyltransferases (DNMT1) re-methylate hemimethylated DNA after replication. Histone modifications are self-perpetuating (Polycomb group proteins recognize their own mark → spread to newly deposited histones). This ensures that a liver cell's daughter cells remain liver cells and do not become neurons — the gene expression program is inherited epigenetically without changes in DNA sequence. 1 pt per mechanism correctly explained with cellular specificity logic.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Combinatorial TF control: different cell types have different TF combinations; each gene requires a specific TF combination; same genome interpreted differently per cell type. Epigenetic inheritance: chromatin marks (DNA methylation, H3K27me3) copied at each division; liver cell daughters remain liver cells; self-perpetuating chromatin states stabilize cell identity.
accepted_variants: different TF combinations per cell type

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies due to chance events. Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs mechanistically from natural selection as a cause of reduced genetic diversity. A cheetah population experienced a severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago. Today, all cheetahs are nearly genetically identical and can accept skin grafts from any other cheetah without rejection. Explain what this reveals about the level of genetic diversity in the cheetah population. The northern elephant seal population dropped to ~20 individuals in the 1890s due to hunting and has since recovered to ~170,000 individuals. Despite this large census size, genetic diversity remains very low. Using the bottleneck effect, explain this paradox: why did the recovery of census size not restore genetic diversity?

Part B: Inbreeding is common in small populations and can lead to inbreeding depression. Explain the molecular mechanism of inbreeding depression by including the roles of heterozygosity and recessive deleterious alleles. Table 1 shows genetic data for two Florida panther populations. Explain what the data indicate about genetic diversity and predict the fitness consequences for Population B.

Part C: A conservation manager introduces 8 Texas pumas (a different subspecies) into the Florida panther population as a genetic rescue strategy. Explain the mechanism by which genetic rescue increases fitness in an inbred population. Predict TWO risks of this genetic rescue strategy and explain why each is a concern. Five years after the introduction, the manager measures the heterozygosity and cub survival rate of offspring of puma-panther crosses versus pure panther offspring. Predict the outcome and the mechanism.

Part D: Conservation biologists have observed that populations with very low genetic diversity remain at elevated risk even when census size is large. Explain why low genetic diversity reduces a population's ability to respond to a new pathogen or a changing climate. Describe ONE additional risk, besides disease or climate vulnerability, that low genetic diversity poses to a population's long-term survival.
stimulus:
Table 1: Florida panther genetic data
                      | Population A (1994, before rescue) | Population B (captive, inbred)
Mean heterozygosity   |         0.04                       |         0.01
Allelic richness      |         3.2 alleles/locus          |         1.8 alleles/locus
Kinked tail frequency |         50%                        |         85%
Cryptic testes freq.  |         55%                        |         90%

Cheetah fact: In lab skin graft experiments, cheetah-to-cheetah skin grafts survive indefinitely. Human-to-human grafts from unrelated donors are rejected within days.

Genetic rescue context: 8 Texas pumas released into Florida in 1995; subsequent panther population showed:
- Increased heterozygosity
- Increased cub survival from 20% to 50%
- Reduced frequency of morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes)
canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) A bottleneck is a sudden, drastic reduction in population size that leaves only a small, random subset of the original gene pool; which alleles survive is a matter of chance, unrelated to their fitness effects, so rare alleles are often lost regardless of whether they were helpful, harmful, or neutral. Natural selection instead changes allele frequencies in a consistent, fitness-driven direction: alleles that improve survival/reproduction become more common and alleles that reduce fitness become less common. A bottleneck reduces diversity non-directionally; selection changes frequencies directionally based on adaptive value.
(a)(ii) That cheetahs can accept skin grafts from virtually any unrelated cheetah shows they are genetically extremely similar to one another -- the self-recognition proteins on their cells are nearly identical across the population, so the immune system does not detect transplanted tissue as foreign. This is the signature of a population that lost most of its genetic variation in a severe bottleneck; a genetically diverse population would reject grafts between unrelated individuals.
(a)(iii) Genetic diversity is set by how many different alleles were present among the individuals who actually contributed offspring, which for the elephant seals was capped at roughly 20 survivors during the bottleneck. Regaining numbers afterward does not add back alleles that were already lost -- diversity can only be recovered slowly, through new mutation accumulating over many generations, not simply by the population growing larger. The modern population, despite its size, still carries only the reduced genetic variation of the ~20 individuals that founded its recovery.

(b)(i) Inbreeding increases the chance that an offspring inherits two identical copies of the same allele (one from each related parent), raising homozygosity across the genome. Most seriously harmful alleles are recessive and normally masked in heterozygotes; increased homozygosity exposes these recessive deleterious alleles in the phenotype, lowering fitness (survival, fertility) -- this is inbreeding depression.
(b)(ii) Population B has much lower mean heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04) and lower allelic richness (1.8 vs. 3.2 alleles/locus) than Population A, along with far higher rates of kinked tails (85% vs. 50%) and cryptic testes (90% vs. 55%). This pattern indicates Population B has undergone substantially more inbreeding. Predicted consequences: reduced male fertility (cryptic testes impair sperm production), possible impaired mobility from the tail defect, and lower overall reproductive success and offspring survival -- the expected signs of inbreeding depression.

(c)(i) Genetic rescue works by breeding in unrelated individuals carrying different alleles than the inbred population. Offspring of these crosses are heterozygous at many loci where residents were homozygous, so functional alleles from the immigrants mask the residents' harmful recessive alleles, producing a fitness increase (heterosis/hybrid vigor) that offsets inbreeding depression.
(c)(ii) Two risks: (1) Outbreeding depression -- the introduced subspecies may carry alleles or trait combinations adapted to a different environment, so hybrid offspring may be less well-suited to Florida conditions than pure-bred residents. (2) Loss of local genetic distinctiveness ("genetic swamping") -- if introduced alleles spread widely, the unique genetic identity of the original Florida subspecies could be diluted or lost.
(c)(iii) Hybrid (puma x panther) offspring should show higher heterozygosity and higher cub survival than pure panther offspring, because the puma parent's alleles mask homozygous deleterious recessive alleles inherited from the inbred panther lineage (heterosis). This matches the historical data: cub survival rose from 20% to 50% after the 1995 introduction.

(d)(i) Genetic diversity is the raw material selection needs to respond to change: when a new pathogen or environmental shift occurs, a genetically diverse population is more likely to already contain individuals whose alleles happen to confer resistance or tolerance, allowing selection to increase those alleles' frequency so the population adapts. A population with very low genetic diversity has few alternative alleles available, so if the existing alleles are poorly suited to the new challenge, the population has little capacity to adapt and faces a much higher risk of decline.
(d)(ii) One additional risk of low genetic diversity: continued inbreeding depression -- with little variation left, most matings are effectively between genetically similar individuals, so harmful recessive alleles keep being exposed in homozygous offspring, suppressing fertility and survival even without any new environmental threat.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs from natural selection; interpret the cheetah skin grafts as evidence of near-zero genetic variation; explain the elephant seal census-vs-diversity paradox using the bottleneck effect.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Bottleneck vs. selection: bottleneck randomly reduces diversity regardless of fitness; selection changes frequencies directionally by fitness. Cheetah skin grafts: near-identical self-recognition proteins from a severe bottleneck explain graft acceptance (no MHC terminology required). Elephant seal paradox: current diversity reflects the ~20 bottleneck survivors; regained census size does not restore lost alleles, only new mutation over generations does. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly explained.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Bottleneck = random loss of alleles regardless of fitness. Cheetah grafts: near-identical self-recognition proteins from a bottleneck. Elephant seals: diversity still reflects ~20 founders; census recovery alone does not restore it.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism of inbreeding depression via heterozygosity and recessive deleterious alleles; interpret the panther data; predict fitness consequences for Population B.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Inbreeding depression mechanism: increased homozygosity from mating between relatives exposes recessive deleterious alleles, reducing fitness. Population B data: lower heterozygosity (0.01 vs 0.04), lower allelic richness (1.8 vs 3.2), higher kinked-tail (85% vs 50%) and cryptic-testes (90% vs 55%) frequencies indicate severe inbreeding; predicted consequences include reduced male fertility and lower reproductive success/offspring survival. Do not require MHC-allele-count claims -- the stimulus table supplies no such data.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Inbreeding depression: homozygosity exposes recessive deleterious alleles. Population B: lower heterozygosity/allelic richness, higher defect frequencies -> predicted reduced fertility and reproductive success.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain genetic rescue mechanism; predict two risks; predict outcome of hybrid vs. pure offspring.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Rescue mechanism: outbred immigrants raise heterozygosity, masking residents' recessive deleterious alleles (heterosis). Two risks: (1) outbreeding depression (maladapted introduced alleles); (2) genetic swamping (loss of local genetic distinctiveness). Hybrid offspring prediction: higher heterozygosity, higher cub survival than pure offspring, consistent with the 20%->50% cub-survival data.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Rescue: outbred alleles mask residents' recessive alleles (heterosis). Risks: outbreeding depression; genetic swamping. Hybrids: higher heterozygosity and cub survival than pure offspring.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why low genetic diversity reduces a population's ability to respond to a new pathogen or changing climate; describe one additional genetic risk of low diversity.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Explains that genetic diversity provides the raw material for selection to act on when a new pathogen or climate shift occurs, so low-diversity populations have little capacity to adapt. Describes one additional risk beyond disease/climate vulnerability -- continued inbreeding depression is the expected answer, but any well-reasoned genetic (not demographic-only) risk of low diversity should be credited.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Diversity = raw material for adaptation to new pathogens/climate. One more risk: continued inbreeding depression from residual low diversity.
accepted_variants: Ne ideal population genetic drift rate
