prior_canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) The bottleneck effect is a sudden, drastic reduction in population size (caused by a random event such as a natural disaster, disease outbreak, or intense hunting) that causes a random subset of the original population's genetic diversity to survive purely by chance, regardless of the survivors' fitness; allele frequencies in the survivors may differ greatly from the original population simply due to random sampling, and rare alleles can be lost entirely. This differs mechanistically from natural selection, which changes allele frequencies based on differential survival and reproduction linked to fitness (a non-random process with respect to the alleles' effects), whereas a bottleneck's effect on allele frequencies results from random chance sampling of a small surviving group, unrelated to the fitness value of the alleles involved.
(ii) This is remarkable because, in normal outbred populations, an individual's immune system would recognize and reject transplanted tissue from an unrelated donor as foreign (based on differences in MHC and other self-recognition proteins). The fact that cheetahs can accept skin grafts from virtually any other cheetah (comparable to grafts between identical twins in other species) reveals that cheetahs have extremely low genetic diversity, especially at MHC loci — nearly all cheetahs are genetically very similar to one another, a hallmark signature of a severe historical population bottleneck.
(iii) Effective population size (Ne) — the size of an idealized, randomly mating population that would experience the same rate of genetic drift as the actual population — can remain very low even after census size (N) recovers, because genetic diversity lost during a severe bottleneck (when Ne was extremely small, around 20 individuals) is not regained simply by population growth in numbers; new mutations that could restore diversity arise very slowly. So although the elephant seal population now numbers about 170,000, its genetic diversity still reflects the small gene pool of the roughly 20 bottleneck survivors, illustrating that census size and effective/genetic population size can diverge substantially, especially in the aftermath of a severe bottleneck.

(b)(i) Inbreeding (mating between close relatives) increases the probability that offspring inherit two copies of the same allele that are identical by descent at a given locus, increasing homozygosity across the genome. Because many deleterious alleles are recessive and normally masked in heterozygous individuals, this increased homozygosity raises the chance that offspring are homozygous for harmful recessive alleles, reducing fitness (inbreeding depression). The purging hypothesis proposes that if a population experiences sustained, gradual inbreeding, natural selection can progressively remove (purge) the most severely deleterious recessive alleles from the gene pool as they become increasingly exposed in homozygous form and selected against, potentially reducing genetic load over many generations, though this process comes with a high fitness cost and does not work as well following a sudden, severe bottleneck.
(ii) Population B (captive, inbred) has much lower mean heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04), lower allelic richness, fewer MHC alleles, and much higher frequencies of morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes) than Population A, indicating that Population B has experienced substantially more inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity. This predicts that Population B will show significantly reduced fitness: lower fertility/reproductive success (consistent with the high frequency of cryptic testes affecting male fertility), greater susceptibility to disease (fewer MHC alleles limit the breadth of immune recognition), and generally reduced viability and survival — the classic signs of inbreeding depression.

(c)(i) Genetic rescue works by introducing new, unrelated genetic variation from a different, more genetically diverse population or subspecies into an inbred population through interbreeding; this increases heterozygosity in the resulting offspring (masking previously homozygous deleterious recessive alleles with new functional alleles from the introduced lineage) and restores lost genetic variation, producing a fitness benefit (heterosis, or hybrid vigor) that reverses inbreeding depression.
(ii) Two risks: (1) outbreeding depression — if the introduced population is too genetically divergent or locally adapted to different conditions, hybrid offspring may have disrupted co-adapted gene complexes or may be poorly suited to the local environment, potentially reducing rather than improving fitness; (2) loss of local adaptation or genetic/taxonomic distinctiveness — introducing genes from a different subspecies could dilute or swamp out alleles that were specifically adapted to the local environment of the original population, and could blur the genetic distinctiveness of the endangered population or subspecies, raising conservation and taxonomic concerns (genetic swamping).
(iii) Predicted outcome: the hybrid (puma-panther cross) offspring would show higher heterozygosity and higher cub survival rate compared to pure panther offspring. Mechanism: hybrid offspring inherit one allele from the less-related Texas puma parent and one allele from the Florida panther parent at many loci, increasing heterozygosity and masking deleterious recessive alleles that were homozygous and expressed in the inbred pure panther lineage; this heterosis effect improves overall fitness and survival, consistent with the historical Florida panther genetic rescue data showing cub survival increasing from 20% to 50% after the 1995 introduction of Texas pumas.

(d)(i) Effective population size (Ne) is the size of an idealized, randomly mating population that would experience the same rate of genetic drift (the same rate of loss of heterozygosity and random allele frequency change) as the actual population being studied. Ne is almost always smaller than census size (N) because real populations deviate from the idealized assumptions: unequal sex ratios (fewer breeding males or females than the total population), high variance in reproductive success among individuals (some individuals, such as dominant males, produce disproportionately more offspring than others), fluctuating population size over time (Ne is weighted more heavily toward the smallest historical population size, such as after a bottleneck), and non-random mating or overlapping generations — all of these reduce the effective number of individuals actually contributing genes to the next generation relative to the total census count.
(ii) Two genetic risks that threaten populations below the minimum viable population threshold: (1) increased genetic drift, causing random loss of genetic diversity and potential fixation of harmful alleles purely by chance in a small population; (2) increased inbreeding, since fewer potential unrelated mates are available, raising the likelihood of mating between relatives, which leads to inbreeding depression and the accumulation of homozygous deleterious recessive alleles.
(iii) Maintaining genetic diversity is important for a species' long-term survival because it provides the raw material upon which natural selection can act to enable adaptation to future or changing environmental conditions, such as new diseases, climate change, or habitat shifts. A population with low genetic diversity has fewer alternative alleles available that might confer resistance or tolerance to new challenges, making it more vulnerable to decline or extinction if conditions change, since there is less standing genetic variation available for evolutionary rescue.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs from natural selection; interpret the cheetah skin grafts as evidence of near-zero genetic variation; explain the elephant seal census-vs-diversity paradox using the bottleneck effect.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Bottleneck vs. selection: Bottleneck = random sampling event; when a population is dramatically reduced, only a small random sample of the original gene pool survives. Rare alleles are lost by chance regardless of their fitness value — loss is not based on phenotypic benefit/cost. Natural selection, by contrast, changes allele frequencies in a direction determined by fitness — it increases frequency of beneficial alleles and decreases frequency of harmful alleles. Bottleneck reduces diversity non-directionally (random alleles fixed or lost); selection changes diversity directionally (adaptive alleles favored). Result: a post-bottleneck population has low diversity across the genome, including at immune loci; post-selection population has adaptive alleles at high frequency but may retain diversity at neutral loci. (ii) Cheetah skin grafts: MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) genes determine self/non-self recognition in the immune system. Normally, unrelated individuals of the same species differ at MHC loci → immune cells detect MHC mismatch → reject transplanted tissue. Cheetahs can accept grafts from any other cheetah because the bottleneck reduced MHC diversity to near-zero — all cheetahs carry essentially the same MHC alleles → no immune mismatch → graft accepted. This reveals extreme genetic homogeneity; cheetahs are nearly as similar to each other as identical twins. This makes them vulnerable to epidemics. (iii) Elephant seal Ne paradox: Census size N = 170,000, but effective population size Ne was ~20 during the bottleneck. Ne is based on the breeding individuals and variance in reproductive success; the genetic diversity in the current population reflects the diversity that existed when Ne was at its minimum (~20 breeders). A population recovered from a recent bottleneck retains the low diversity of its bottleneck founders regardless of census size — recovery of numbers does not restore genetic variation lost during the bottleneck; only mutation over generations and gene flow can restore it. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly explained.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Bottleneck = random loss of alleles regardless of fitness (not directional). Selection = directional loss/gain based on fitness. Cheetah skin grafts: MHC diversity near zero → all cheetahs same MHC → no immune rejection. Elephant seal Ne paradox: current Ne still reflects the ~20 bottleneck founders; census size recovery does not restore genetic diversity lost during bottleneck.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism of inbreeding depression via heterozygosity and recessive deleterious alleles; interpret the panther data; predict fitness consequences for Population B.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Inbreeding depression mechanism: inbreeding (mating between relatives) increases the probability that an individual inherits the same allele from both parents (identity by descent) → increased homozygosity genome-wide. Most deleterious alleles are recessive and rare in outbred populations — they are mostly present in heterozygous individuals where the dominant allele masks the effect. In inbred individuals, probability of homozygosity for recessive deleterious alleles increases dramatically → deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (growth, fertility, survival, immunity). Purging hypothesis: in populations with prolonged inbreeding, the most severely deleterious recessive alleles may be "purged" — exposed in homozygotes and eliminated by natural selection. Mildly deleterious alleles are less efficiently purged because they have small fitness effects. (ii) Data interpretation for Population B: Population B has lower heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04), fewer alleles/locus (1.8 vs. 3.2), only 1 MHC allele (vs. 2), and higher frequency of morphological defects (kinked tail 85% vs. 50%; cryptic testes 90% vs. 55%). This indicates severe inbreeding. Predicted fitness consequences: high frequency of cryptic (undescended) testes → reduced male fertility → lower reproductive success; kinked tails (morphological defect, possibly spinal) → possible locomotion impairment in a predatory species; only 1 MHC allele → cannot recognize a diverse pathogen array → high susceptibility to infectious disease; low MHC diversity → poor immune response → epidemic vulnerability. Overall: inbreeding depression → low cub survival, poor reproductive performance, disease susceptibility.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Inbreeding depression: increased homozygosity exposes recessive deleterious alleles → reduced fitness. Purging removes most severe alleles. Population B: lower heterozygosity, fewer alleles, 1 MHC allele, 85-90% morphological defects → predicted reduced fertility (cryptic testes), possible locomotion issues, severe disease susceptibility from single MHC allele.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain genetic rescue mechanism; predict two risks; predict outcome of hybrid vs. pure offspring.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Genetic rescue mechanism: introducing individuals from an outbred population provides new alleles not present in the inbred population. Crosses between inbred resident and outbred immigrant → offspring are heterozygous at many loci where residents are homozygous → dominant alleles mask previously exposed recessive deleterious alleles → fitness increases (heterosis/hybrid vigor). Also restores functional diversity at immune loci (MHC) → improved pathogen resistance. Effectively reverses inbreeding depression without changing the genome. (ii) Two risks: (1) Outbreeding depression: the introduced subspecies may carry alleles adapted to different Texas environments (different climate, prey, pathogens) that are maladaptive in Florida conditions; co-adapted gene complexes may be disrupted by hybridization → offspring less adapted to local environment than pure residents. (2) Genetic swamping: if Texas pumas are introduced in large numbers and have higher fitness (due to heterosis), their alleles could eventually replace the Florida panther genome entirely → the unique local adaptations and genetic identity of the Florida subspecies could be lost → "genetic extinction" even if population persists. (iii) Hybrid vs. pure offspring prediction: Hybrid offspring (puma × panther) will have higher heterozygosity than pure panther offspring → expect higher cub survival, fewer morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes), better immune function. This is heterosis (hybrid vigor) — the mechanism is complementation: the Texas puma alleles complement the Florida panther's recessive deleterious alleles, so the harmful homozygous recessive phenotypes are not expressed. Data from the 1995 introduction confirms: cub survival increased from 20% to 50%; defects declined dramatically. 1 pt for rescue mechanism; 1 pt for two risks OR hybrid prediction.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Rescue mechanism: outbred immigrants → heterozygosity → recessive alleles masked → heterosis/hybrid vigor; new MHC alleles → better immunity. Risks: (1) outbreeding depression (maladapted Texas alleles in Florida); (2) genetic swamping (Florida genome replaced). Hybrid offspring: higher heterozygosity → heterosis → better survival, fewer defects; complementation masks deleterious recessive alleles.

prior_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why low genetic diversity reduces a population's ability to respond to a new pathogen or changing climate; describe one additional genetic risk of low diversity.
prior_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Effective population size (Ne): the size of an ideal panmictic population (random mating, equal sex ratio, equal reproductive success, no migration) that would experience the same rate of genetic drift (allele frequency change) as the actual population. Ne is almost always much smaller than census size N because: unequal sex ratio (e.g., 1 breeding male + 99 females → Ne ≈ 4, not 100); variance in reproductive success (dominant individuals breed much more than others → many individuals contribute no offspring → only a fraction effectively breed); fluctuating population sizes (Ne is dominated by the lowest N across generations — harmonic mean of past Ns); overlapping generations and age structure; geographic subdivision reducing effective breeding population. Typical Ne/N ratio in wildlife: 0.10–0.11. (ii) Two genetic risks below MVP: (1) Inbreeding depression: small populations have high relatedness → mating between relatives → homozygosity → recessive deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (fertility, immunity, survival). (2) Loss of adaptive potential (genetic erosion): genetic drift is strongest in small populations → neutral and mildly beneficial alleles lost by chance → allelic diversity decreases → population has fewer alleles available to respond to new selection pressures (disease outbreaks, climate change, new predators) → extinction risk increases. (iii) Genetic diversity for future change: a population with high genetic diversity has more heritable variation → when the environment changes (new pathogen, climate shift, habitat alteration), some individuals may already carry pre-existing alleles that confer survival advantage → natural selection can rapidly increase frequency of those alleles → population adapts and survives. A genetically uniform population (after bottleneck) has no variation for selection to act on → cannot adapt → high extinction risk. Genetic diversity = evolutionary raw material for adaptation. 1 pt per two of the four sub-parts correctly explained.
prior_criteria.minimum_fix: Ne = effective population size (ideal population with same genetic drift rate). Ne < N due to: unequal sex ratio, variance in reproductive success, past bottlenecks (harmonic mean). Two genetic risks: inbreeding depression + genetic erosion (drift removes adaptive variation). Diversity for future: provides variation for selection to act on new challenges (disease, climate) → adaptation and survival.
accepted_variants: Ne ideal population genetic drift rate

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Explain the relationship between habitat area and the population size (and therefore genetic diversity) that habitat can support, using the concept of carrying capacity. Predict what happens to a population's carrying capacity if its habitat area is halved.

Part B: Habitat fragmentation reduces the size of the population that can be supported in each remaining fragment. Explain THREE ecological consequences of small, fragmented populations for long-term persistence, including genetic drift and the bottleneck effect.

Part C: A study examined two patches of black-footed ferrets, a critically endangered species dependent on prairie dog colonies (as described in the stimulus): Patch A (connected by a corridor to a larger prairie dog complex, allowing gene flow) and Patch C (completely isolated, no gene flow). After 20 years, Patch A had a stable population while Patch C's population had declined to extinction. Using concepts of gene flow, genetic drift, and extinction risk, explain why Patch A succeeded while Patch C failed.

Part D: Explain how climate change can increase extinction risk for species living in isolated habitats such as mountaintops. Describe TWO conservation strategies that could reduce this risk.
stimulus:
Black-footed ferret facts:
• North America's most endangered mammal; dependent on prairie dog colonies for food and burrows
• Current population: ~300 individuals in the wild from reintroduction programs beginning 1991
• Highly sensitive to sylvatic plague (Yersinia pestis) — a single outbreak can eliminate an entire ferret and prairie dog colony, illustrating extinction risk in a small, fragmented population
canonical_answer_1:
(a) A larger habitat area can support a larger population because it provides more food, space, and other resources -- this maximum sustainable population size is the habitat's carrying capacity. A larger population retains more genetic diversity and is less vulnerable to genetic drift and stochastic extinction than a small one. If habitat area is halved, the resources available are roughly halved as well, so carrying capacity is expected to decrease correspondingly -- the population the habitat can sustain shrinks, which in turn increases the population's vulnerability to genetic drift, inbreeding, and chance demographic/environmental events that can drive a small population extinct.

(b) Three ecological consequences of small, fragmented populations for long-term persistence: (1) Increased genetic drift -- in a small population, allele frequencies change substantially from generation to generation by chance alone, and rare alleles are easily lost, reducing genetic diversity faster than in a large population. (2) Bottleneck-like founder effects -- when a fragment supports only a small population, the diversity present is capped by however many individuals happen to be in that fragment, similar to a bottleneck, and that reduced diversity persists even if the fragment's population later grows. (3) Increased inbreeding -- with fewer potential mates available within an isolated fragment, related individuals are more likely to breed with each other, increasing homozygosity and the expression of harmful recessive alleles (inbreeding depression). Together, these genetic and demographic effects make small fragmented populations more vulnerable to decline and local extinction than a single large, continuous population of the same total size.

(c) Patch A, connected by a corridor to the larger prairie dog complex, keeps receiving individuals through gene flow: this prevents inbreeding, preserves heterozygosity, and allows the population to be replenished (a rescue effect) if it declines. Patch C, though initially similar in size, is fully isolated, so no immigration can replenish or diversify it. With a small, isolated founding population and no gene flow, Patch C's ferrets are especially vulnerable to genetic drift and inbreeding depression -- increased mating among relatives raises homozygosity of deleterious recessive alleles, reducing fertility, disease resistance, and offspring survival -- compounding demographic problems (such as vulnerability to a single sylvatic plague outbreak wiping out the colony, as described in the stimulus) and driving the population to extinction, exactly as the connected-versus-isolated comparison predicts.

(d)(i) Mountaintop habitats function like islands of suitable habitat surrounded by a climatically unsuitable lowland "sea." As climate warms, the montane climate zone a species needs shifts upslope, but because mountains taper toward their summit, the available habitat area shrinks as elevation increases -- so species are pushed into progressively smaller, more isolated patches, and eventually run out of mountain entirely with no higher ground left to colonize. Unlike lowland species, mountaintop species cannot simply shift latitude across a large, continuous landmass.
(d)(ii) As the suitable thermal zone shifts upslope, individuals or populations at the lower (trailing) edge of the species' current range experience increasingly unsuitable conditions, causing increased mortality and reduced reproduction there, while newly suitable habitat may open up at the upper (leading) edge. The population avoids net decline only if individuals (or, for plants, seeds/pollen) can disperse upslope fast enough to track the shifting climate zone; if dispersal is too slow relative to the pace of warming, the population suffers a net range contraction and increased extinction risk.
(d)(iii) Two climate-aware conservation strategies: (1) Establish or protect habitat corridors along elevational and latitudinal gradients so species can physically track shifting climate conditions over time. (2) Use assisted migration/translocation -- deliberately moving individuals or propagules beyond their natural dispersal range into newly climatically suitable habitat they could not reach on their own.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain carrying capacity's dependence on habitat area and predict the effect of halving that area.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Larger habitat area -> more resources -> higher carrying capacity -> larger sustainable population -> more retained genetic diversity, lower drift/extinction vulnerability. Halving area is predicted to roughly halve available resources and correspondingly reduce carrying capacity, increasing vulnerability to drift and demographic/environmental stochasticity. No species-area equation is supplied or required.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Smaller area -> lower carrying capacity -> smaller population -> more drift/extinction risk. Halving area roughly halves carrying capacity.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain three consequences of fragmentation for small populations, including drift and bottleneck effects.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Three genetic/demographic consequences of fragmentation, framed around drift and the bottleneck effect: (1) increased genetic drift in small fragment populations; (2) bottleneck-like founder effects capping diversity at whatever the fragment happens to hold; (3) increased inbreeding from a restricted local mate pool, causing inbreeding depression.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Three effects: increased drift; bottleneck-like founder effect; increased inbreeding (inbreeding depression) in small fragments.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why the connected patch succeeded and the isolated patch failed using gene flow, drift, and extinction risk.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Patch A + corridor: (1) Rescue effect: corridor to the larger prairie dog complex allows immigration of new individuals -> if the Patch A population declines, individuals from the larger population can recolonize/supplement it, lowering extinction probability; (2) Gene flow: the corridor allows exchange of individuals and alleles -> prevents inbreeding; heterozygosity maintained -> inbreeding depression avoided -> higher survival/reproduction. Patch C isolated: (1) No rescue effect: if a decline or local extinction occurs (e.g. a sylvatic plague outbreak per the stimulus), no immigration is possible -> the population cannot recover; (2) Small, isolated population -> genetic drift + inbreeding -> reduced genetic diversity -> reduced disease resistance/fitness -> population decline; (3) Demographic stochasticity: with a small isolated population, chance events (sex-ratio imbalance, loss of breeding individuals) further threaten persistence. The corridor gives Patch A a rescue effect and gene flow that Patch C lacks entirely -> Patch C functions as a true ecological island with no immigration -> expected outcome: extinction following any perturbation. 1 pt for Patch A connectivity advantages (rescue effect + gene flow); 1 pt for Patch C isolation failure mechanisms.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Patch A success: corridor to the larger prairie dog complex provides a rescue effect (recolonization if population declines) and gene flow (prevents inbreeding, maintains fitness). Patch C failure: no immigration possible -> no rescue effect; inbreeding -> fitness decline; demographic stochasticity + disease outbreak (sylvatic plague) -> extinction with no recovery.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the mountaintop climate-change extinction risk and describe two conservation strategies.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: (i) Mountaintop species and island biogeography: as temperatures warm, suitable habitat shifts upslope -> high-elevation species must track their thermal niche by moving upslope. Mountaintops function like islands of suitable habitat surrounded by an unsuitable warm lowland "sea." As the suitable zone shifts up, the area of habitat available SHRINKS (mountains taper toward the summit), so fewer individuals/species can be supported and extinction risk increases; eventually the suitable zone disappears off the summit entirely -> complete habitat loss. Unlike lowland species, mountaintop species cannot shift latitude across a large, continuous landmass once they run out of elevation. (ii) General demographic consequence: the trailing (lower) edge of the range becomes unsuitable and declines, while the leading (upper) edge may gain new suitable habitat if dispersal keeps pace; if dispersal is too slow relative to the rate of warming, the population's range contracts net, increasing extinction risk. (iii) Two climate-aware conservation strategies: (1) assisted migration/translocation -- deliberately moving individuals or propagules beyond their natural dispersal range into newly climatically suitable habitat; (2) climate-adaptive reserve networks/corridors along elevational and latitudinal gradients, allowing natural range tracking. 1 pt for mountaintop island biogeography explanation; 1 pt for demographic consequence OR two strategies.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Mountaintops: suitable habitat shrinks as the thermal zone shifts up (species-area) -> fewer individuals supported; no habitat beyond the summit -> extinction risk. Demographic consequence: trailing edge declines, leading edge may expand if dispersal keeps pace; too-slow dispersal -> net range contraction. Strategies: (1) assisted migration; (2) elevation/latitudinal corridors.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the data in the table, describe how reaction rate changes as substrate concentration increases, and explain why the rate levels off at high substrate concentration even though substrate is not limiting.

Part B: A competitive inhibitor is added at a fixed concentration and the experiment is repeated. Predict whether the maximum reaction rate reached at very high substrate concentration would change relative to the uninhibited reaction, and explain why, based on where a competitive inhibitor binds relative to the substrate.

Part C: Researchers raise the substrate concentration to 50 times the original level used in Part A, in the presence of the same competitive inhibitor. Predict what happens to reaction rate relative to the uninhibited maximum rate, and explain your reasoning.

Part D: Propose a modification to the experiment that would distinguish a competitive inhibitor from a noncompetitive inhibitor using only reaction-rate data, and explain what result would confirm each mechanism.
stimulus:
A biochemist measures the initial reaction rate of an enzyme at increasing substrate concentrations, holding enzyme concentration, pH, and temperature constant.

Substrate concentration (mM) | Initial reaction rate (micromol/min)
0.5                          | 12
1.0                          | 20
2.0                          | 30
4.0                          | 40
8.0                          | 46
16.0                         | 49
32.0                         | 50

criteria.learner_facing_text: Estimate Vmax and Km from the data; explain enzyme saturation.
Predict and explain how Vmax and Km change with competitive inhibitor.
Predict reaction rate at 50× Km with competitive inhibitor present.
Propose experiment to distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition.

canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Vmax: the reaction rate plateaus at very high substrate concentration, approaching ≈50 μmol/min (rates of 49 and 50 at 16 and 32 mM). Km (substrate concentration at half-Vmax, i.e., at a rate of ~25 μmol/min): the data show a rate of 20 at 1.0 mM and 30 at 2.0 mM, so the rate of 25 falls about halfway between, giving an estimated Km ≈ 1.5 mM.
(ii) At high substrate concentration the enzyme becomes saturated — essentially every active site is occupied by substrate at all times, so there is no free enzyme available to bind additional substrate molecules. The reaction rate is then limited not by substrate availability/collision frequency but by the enzyme's intrinsic catalytic turnover rate (kcat, how fast each occupied active site can convert substrate to product and release it), which is constant regardless of how much more substrate is added, producing the plateau.

(b) A competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax UNCHANGED but increases the apparent Km. Mechanism: a competitive inhibitor binds reversibly at the same active site as the substrate, competing with substrate for occupancy. It does not alter the enzyme's intrinsic catalytic rate once substrate is bound (kcat is unchanged), and because the competition is reversible, adding enough substrate can always out-compete the inhibitor for active sites, so the same Vmax is still reachable at sufficiently high [S]. However, because the inhibitor is occupying some active sites, more substrate is required to reach half-maximal velocity, so the apparent Km increases.

(c) At [S] = 50×Km with the competitive inhibitor still present, the reaction rate would approach (nearly equal) the original uninhibited Vmax. At such a large excess of substrate relative to inhibitor, substrate molecules vastly outnumber inhibitor molecules competing for the active site, effectively out-competing/displacing the inhibitor from most active sites, so nearly all enzyme becomes substrate-bound and catalytically active — competitive inhibition can always be overcome by sufficiently raising substrate concentration, unlike noncompetitive inhibition.

(d) Modification: repeat the initial-rate assay across a range of substrate concentrations (as in the original experiment) at a fixed inhibitor concentration, and construct/compare a rate-vs-[S] curve (or a Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot) against the uninhibited curve, examining how Vmax and Km change. Result confirming COMPETITIVE inhibition: Vmax is the SAME as the uninhibited reaction (the curve reaches the same plateau at sufficiently high [S]), while the apparent Km is INCREASED (more substrate needed to reach half-Vmax). Result confirming NONCOMPETITIVE inhibition: Vmax is DECREASED relative to uninhibited (the maximum rate can never be recovered even at saturating substrate, because the inhibitor binds a separate allosteric site independent of substrate concentration), while Km is UNCHANGED (the inhibitor doesn't affect substrate-binding affinity, so half-maximal rate is reached at the same [S], just at a reduced overall scale).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe the saturation trend and explain why rate plateaus (active sites become fully occupied).

criteria.learner_facing_text: Estimate Vmax and Km from the data; explain enzyme saturation.
Predict and explain how Vmax and Km change with competitive inhibitor.
Predict reaction rate at 50× Km with competitive inhibitor present.
Propose experiment to distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition.

prior_canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) Vmax: the reaction rate plateaus at very high substrate concentration, approaching ≈50 μmol/min (rates of 49 and 50 at 16 and 32 mM). Km (substrate concentration at half-Vmax, i.e., at a rate of ~25 μmol/min): the data show a rate of 20 at 1.0 mM and 30 at 2.0 mM, so the rate of 25 falls about halfway between, giving an estimated Km ≈ 1.5 mM.
(ii) At high substrate concentration the enzyme becomes saturated — essentially every active site is occupied by substrate at all times, so there is no free enzyme available to bind additional substrate molecules. The reaction rate is then limited not by substrate availability/collision frequency but by the enzyme's intrinsic catalytic turnover rate (kcat, how fast each occupied active site can convert substrate to product and release it), which is constant regardless of how much more substrate is added, producing the plateau.

(b) A competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax UNCHANGED but increases the apparent Km. Mechanism: a competitive inhibitor binds reversibly at the same active site as the substrate, competing with substrate for occupancy. It does not alter the enzyme's intrinsic catalytic rate once substrate is bound (kcat is unchanged), and because the competition is reversible, adding enough substrate can always out-compete the inhibitor for active sites, so the same Vmax is still reachable at sufficiently high [S]. However, because the inhibitor is occupying some active sites, more substrate is required to reach half-maximal velocity, so the apparent Km increases.

(c) At [S] = 50×Km with the competitive inhibitor still present, the reaction rate would approach (nearly equal) the original uninhibited Vmax. At such a large excess of substrate relative to inhibitor, substrate molecules vastly outnumber inhibitor molecules competing for the active site, effectively out-competing/displacing the inhibitor from most active sites, so nearly all enzyme becomes substrate-bound and catalytically active — competitive inhibition can always be overcome by sufficiently raising substrate concentration, unlike noncompetitive inhibition.

(d) Modification: repeat the initial-rate assay across a range of substrate concentrations (as in the original experiment) at a fixed inhibitor concentration, and construct/compare a rate-vs-[S] curve (or a Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot) against the uninhibited curve, examining how Vmax and Km change. stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The lac operon in bacteria is repressed by default and is induced (turned on) when the inducer allolactose is present. Predict the activity pattern of a Strain 3 mutant (operator deletion) across a range of inducer concentrations (0 mM, 0.1 mM, 1.0 mM, 10.0 mM). Explain why your predictions differ from the wild-type strain.

Part B: In Strain 2, the repressor protein is mutated so that it cannot bind to the inducer molecule (allolactose). Evaluate whether the Strain 2 experimental data support this hypothesis. Discuss what this mutation would mean for the cell's ability to regulate lactose-metabolizing gene expression in response to inducer availability.

Part C: Explain why the wild-type strain exhibits low reporter activity (low transcription) when inducer is absent and increased reporter activity when inducer is added. In your answer, describe the role of the repressor protein and explain how the inducer molecule interacts with the repressor to cause its release from the operator.

Part D: Describe how reporter activity changes across different inducer concentrations for the wild-type strain and explain what this dose-dependent response indicates about the sensitivity of the operon to inducer levels.
stimulus:
Researchers engineer a bacterial operon in which the structural gene is replaced with a reporter gene whose enzyme activity is easily measured. Three strains are grown in increasing concentrations of inducer molecule, and reporter enzyme activity is measured after 2 hours.

Inducer (mM) | Wild-type activity (units) | Strain 2 activity (units)
0            | 5                          | 4
0.1          | 40                         | 5
1.0          | 95                         | 6
10.0         | 98                         | 5
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Strain 3 (operator deleted): predicted high reporter activity at ALL inducer concentrations, including 0 mM, because without an operator sequence the repressor protein has nowhere to bind, regardless of whether it is bound to inducer or not; RNA polymerase can access the promoter and transcribe the gene continuously (constitutively), unaffected by inducer presence or absence. This differs from the wild-type strain, whose activity rises from low (5 units, no inducer) to high (95-98 units, saturating) as inducer increases, because the wild-type repressor can still bind and release the (intact) operator in response to inducer.

(b) The data support the hypothesis. Strain 2 activity stays low and essentially flat across all inducer concentrations (4-6 units), showing no meaningful induction response, unlike the wild type's rise from 5 to 98 units. This is consistent with a repressor that can still bind the operator (matching the wild-type baseline near 0 mM) but can no longer be released by inducer, since it never responds to rising inducer concentration -- it stays bound to the operator and continues blocking RNA polymerase regardless of how much inducer is present.

(c) Without inducer, the repressor protein is in its active, operator-binding conformation and binds tightly to the operator, which is positioned so that a bound repressor blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the reporter gene -- so transcription (and reporter activity) stays low. When inducer (allolactose) is added, it binds allosterically to the repressor, changing the repressor's shape so it can no longer bind the operator; the repressor releases from the operator, freeing the promoter region so RNA polymerase can bind and transcribe the gene, sharply increasing reporter activity as inducer concentration rises.

(d) As inducer concentration increases from 0 to 10.0 mM, wild-type reporter activity increases (from 5 to 98 units), then levels off (plateaus) between 1.0 and 10.0 mM (95 to 98 units) -- a positive, saturating dose-response relationship. This shows the operon is highly sensitive to low/moderate inducer levels (large activity increase between 0 and 1.0 mM) but becomes saturated at higher concentrations, where essentially all repressor molecules are already inducer-bound and released from the operator, so additional inducer has little further effect.

stem: Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in the thylakoid membrane drives production of ATP and NADPH during the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
stimulus: A diagram shows the thylakoid membrane with Photosystem II, the electron transport chain, Photosystem I, and ATP synthase.
canonical_answer_1: Water is split at PSII, and the released electrons move through PSII, cytochrome b6f, and PSI before reducing NADP+ to NADPH.
canonical_answer_2: As electrons pass through the thylakoid membrane, proton pumping builds a gradient that powers ATP synthase to make ATP and reduces NADP+ to NADPH.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Trace the path of electrons from water to NADP+ during the light-dependent reactions, naming at least two electron carriers or complexes.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Water is split at PSII releasing electrons; electrons flow through plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f complex, plastocyanin; reach PSI; re-energized; transferred via ferredoxin to NADP+ reductase to reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Electrons from water oxidation at PSII flow through the electron transport chain to PSI, then reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
accepted_variants: water to PSII to ETC to PSI to NADPH

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is established and how it drives ATP synthesis.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: H+ accumulates in thylakoid lumen from water splitting and ETC proton pumping; electrochemical gradient drives H+ through ATP synthase back into stroma; flow powers phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Electron transfer pumps H+ into the thylakoid lumen; the resulting concentration gradient drives H+ through ATP synthase, powering ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.

stem: A diploid organism with chromosome number 2n = 6 undergoes cell division under different conditions.
stimulus: A table compares the number of divisions, ploidy of resulting cells, and occurrence of crossing over in mitosis versus meiosis.
canonical_answer_1: Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells with 2n = 6, while meiosis produces four haploid cells with n = 3.
canonical_answer_2: Crossing over during prophase I exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations in the gametes.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Compare the chromosome number of cells produced by mitosis to the chromosome number of cells produced at the end of meiosis II for this organism.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Mitosis produces 2 diploid cells each with 6 chromosomes (2n = 6). Meiosis II produces 4 haploid cells each with 3 chromosomes (n = 3).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Mitosis yields cells with 6 chromosomes (2n = 6); meiosis II yields cells with 3 chromosomes (n = 3).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how crossing over during meiosis I increases genetic variation among offspring.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and exchange chromosome segments at chiasmata; new combinations of alleles on chromatids are created that were not present in either parent, increasing allele diversity in gametes and offspring.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes during prophase I, creating new combinations of alleles on chromatids that differ from either parental chromosome.

stem: In a hypothetical plant species, purple flower color (allele A) is dominant over white flower color (allele a). Two heterozygous plants are crossed.
stimulus: Parental cross: Aa x Aa. Students predict offspring phenotypes and genotypes.
canonical_answer_1: Aa x Aa gives a 3 purple : 1 white phenotype ratio, so 25% of offspring are white.
canonical_answer_2: This follows the law of segregation: during meiosis I the two alleles separate so each gamete gets only one allele of the gene.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Construct a Punnett square for the Aa x Aa cross and predict the expected phenotypic ratio in the offspring.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Correct 2x2 Punnett square showing AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Phenotypic ratio: 3 purple : 1 white (or 75% purple, 25% white).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The Punnett square gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (AA:Aa:aa) and a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (purple:white).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: State the principle of segregation and explain how meiosis accounts for it at the cellular level.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Principle of Segregation: the two alleles for a gene separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one allele. Meiosis accounts for this because homologous chromosomes (each carrying one allele) separate during meiosis I, placing one allele into each gamete.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The principle of segregation states alleles separate during gamete formation; homologous chromosomes separate at meiosis I, delivering one allele to each gamete.

stem: In eukaryotic cells, the primary RNA transcript undergoes several modifications in the nucleus before export to the cytoplasm for translation.
stimulus: A diagram shows a pre-mRNA with labeled exons (E1, E2, E3) and introns (I1, I2) before processing, and two alternative mature mRNA products after splicing.
canonical_answer_1: The pre-mRNA is capped (a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap is added to protect the mRNA and assist ribosome binding) and polyadenylated (a poly-A tail is added to the 3' end to protect from degradation and aid export), in addition to being spliced. During splicing, different combinations of exons can be included in or excluded from the mature mRNA in different cell types or developmental stages -- this is alternative splicing. As shown in the diagram, the same pre-mRNA (exons E1, E2, E3 and introns I1, I2) can be spliced in more than one way to produce different mature mRNA products. Because each alternatively spliced mRNA has a different exon composition, each is translated into a different polypeptide with a different amino acid sequence and potentially a different function -- allowing a single gene to encode multiple different proteins.
canonical_answer_2: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA, so one gene can produce multiple proteins with different amino acid sequences.

canonical_answer_2: The inner membrane of mitochondria is the site of the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis, analogous to the bacterial plasma membrane.

stem: A plant cell is placed in a highly concentrated salt solution.
canonical_answer_1: The cell loses water by osmosis, causing the central vacuole to shrink and the plasma membrane to pull away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).
canonical_answer_2: Unlike animal cells, plant cells do not burst in hypotonic solutions because the rigid cell wall provides turgor pressure support.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describe what happens to the plant cell in the concentrated salt solution and explain the mechanism.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the cell loses water by osmosis (water moves to higher solute outside); describes the vacuole shrinking and plasmolysis.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Water exits by osmosis to the hypertonic salt solution, the central vacuole shrinks, and the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why a plant cell does not burst when placed in a hypotonic (dilute) solution.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the cell wall resists expansion; as turgor pressure builds against the wall, it prevents further water intake.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The rigid cell wall resists swelling; as water enters and turgor pressure increases, the wall pushes back, preventing bursting.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain, in terms of fatty acid tail structure, why Bilayer B is more fluid than Bilayer A at the same temperature.

(b) Explain how the presence of cholesterol affects membrane fluidity in each bilayer at 20°C versus 40°C.
stimulus: A researcher compares the fluidity of two synthetic phospholipid bilayers at 20°C: Bilayer A is composed of phospholipids with saturated fatty acid tails, and Bilayer B is composed of phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails. Bilayer B is measured to be substantially more fluid than Bilayer A at the same temperature. The researcher then re-tests both bilayers with cholesterol embedded in the membrane, comparing fluidity at 20°C and at 40°C.
canonical_answer_1: Unsaturated fatty acid tails have kinks from double bonds, preventing tight packing and keeping the membrane fluid at lower temperatures.
canonical_answer_2: Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer: at high temperatures it restricts movement; at low temperatures it prevents crystallization.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why unsaturated fatty acids increase membrane fluidity.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the double bond creates a kink in the tail, preventing tight packing of phospholipids, so the membrane remains fluid.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The double bond bends the hydrocarbon tail, preventing phospholipids from packing tightly, which increases membrane fluidity.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of cholesterol in maintaining membrane fluidity across a range of temperatures.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States cholesterol stabilizes fluidity: restricts movement at high temp (prevents too fluid) and prevents packing at low temp (prevents solidifying).
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Cholesterol reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents solidification at low temperatures, acting as a fluidity buffer.

stem: A student compares ATP production in aerobic respiration versus fermentation in yeast under different oxygen conditions.

canonical_answer_2: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue but yields only 2 ATP per glucose.

stem: In peas, yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y) and round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). Two dihybrid plants (YyRr x YyRr) are crossed.
canonical_answer_1: Independent assortment produces four phenotypic classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio when genes are on different chromosomes.
canonical_answer_2: Each gene segregates independently; the probability of each phenotypic combination is the product of individual gene probabilities.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict the phenotypic ratio of offspring from the YyRr x YyRr cross and explain why.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States 9 yellow round : 3 yellow wrinkled : 3 green round : 1 green wrinkled; explains independent assortment.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Independent assortment of the two genes produces a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Calculate the probability of producing a plant that is homozygous dominant for both traits.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16; must show multiplication of individual probabilities.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The probability of YYRR is (1/4)(1/4) = 1/16, applying the product rule for independent events.

stem: Human ABO blood type is controlled by three alleles (I^A, I^B, i). I^A and I^B are codominant; i is recessive to both.

stem: A population of finches on a large island diverges into two populations that differ in beak size after a geographic barrier forms.
canonical_answer_1:
(a) A geographic barrier (e.g., a new mountain range, river, or physical separation) divides the ancestral finch population into two, preventing gene flow between them. Isolated from each other, the two populations independently accumulate different mutations and experience different selection pressures (adapting to their local environments) and genetic drift, causing them to diverge genetically and phenotypically (as reflected here in beak size) over time -- this is allopatric speciation.
(b) If the geographic barrier were removed, a reproductive isolating mechanism that evolved during the period of separation could still keep the two populations from interbreeding. For example, behavioral isolation: if the two populations diverged in mating calls, courtship displays, or other mate-recognition cues during their time apart, individuals from one population may fail to recognize individuals from the other as potential mates, so they would not interbreed even if brought into contact. (Other valid mechanisms include habitat isolation, temporal isolation, or postzygotic mechanisms such as hybrid inviability or sterility.)
canonical_answer_2: When the barrier is removed, reproductive isolation may have developed so the populations can no longer interbreed.

stem: A forest food web includes plants, caterpillars, birds, and a hawk. A student calculates that only 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels.
canonical_answer_1: The 10% rule reflects energy lost to heat, movement, and incomplete digestion at each trophic level.
canonical_answer_2: Biomass decreases at higher trophic levels because energy is dissipated; this explains why food chains are typically short. Using the 10% rule across the three trophic transfers from plants to hawk (plant → caterpillar → bird → hawk), each level requires 10× the energy of the level above it: the hawk needs 10 kJ, so birds must produce 100 kJ, caterpillars 1,000 kJ, and plants must produce 10,000 kJ of usable energy to ultimately support 10 kJ at the hawk's level.

stem: Scientists monitor nitrogen levels in a pond and find that excess agricultural runoff causes a bloom of algae followed by a dead zone.
canonical_answer_1: Nitrogen is a limiting nutrient; excess nitrogen from fertilizer causes eutrophication — explosive algal growth.
canonical_answer_2: When algae die, decomposers consume O2 in the process of breaking them down, creating hypoxic (low-oxygen) dead zones. Algae occupy the primary producer (first) trophic level in this pond ecosystem — as photosynthetic autotrophs, they convert sunlight into chemical energy that supports the rest of the food web. Under the runoff-driven nutrient surplus, this producer level grows unchecked (the algal bloom) before dying off and triggering the decomposer-driven oxygen crash described above.

stem: A field ecologist studies a predator-prey relationship between wolves and moose on an island, recording population cycles over 50 years.
canonical_answer_1: Predator-prey cycles are driven by time-delayed feedback: prey increase causes predator increase, which reduces prey.
canonical_answer_2: Classic Lotka-Volterra dynamics predict oscillating cycles where predator peaks follow prey peaks by a time lag. If all wolves were removed, the main top-down check on the moose population would be eliminated. Moose numbers would likely increase rapidly (predator release) until limited instead by bottom-up factors such as food availability (overgrazing) and density-dependent effects like starvation and disease, rather than by predation.

stem: A scientist studies stabilizing selection in human birth weight, finding that very low and very high birth weights have higher infant mortality.

stem: Researchers compare two populations of the same moth species separated by a river. They find the populations have diverged in wing pattern but can still interbreed.
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Under the biological species concept, populations that can interbreed and produce viable, fertile offspring are considered members of the same species, regardless of phenotypic differences such as wing pattern. Since these two moth populations can still interbreed, they represent ONE species, not two -- the divergence in wing pattern reflects population-level variation, not speciation, because reproductive isolation (the defining criterion under this concept) has not yet evolved.
(b) The river prevents individuals from migrating between the two populations, stopping gene flow between them. Without gene flow, each population accumulates different mutations and experiences different selection pressures (and genetic drift) independently, causing the two populations to diverge genetically and phenotypically (as seen in the different wing patterns) over time. If this divergence continues long enough that the populations evolve reproductive isolating mechanisms -- so that even if the river barrier were removed, they could no longer interbreed and produce viable, fertile offspring -- the biological species concept would then classify them as two separate species, but that point has not yet been reached here.
canonical_answer_2: If reproductive isolation has not evolved, the populations are still the same species despite phenotypic differences.

stem: Students studying animal behavior observe that male frogs produce species-specific calls, and females approach only males of their own species.
canonical_answer_1: Behavioral isolation is a prezygotic reproductive barrier where species-specific signals prevent mating between species.
canonical_answer_2: Prezygotic barriers prevent hybrid zygote formation; postzygotic barriers reduce hybrid fitness after fertilization.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Classify the frog mating call as a type of reproductive isolating mechanism and explain how it prevents hybridization.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States behavioral (prezygotic) isolation; female frogs recognize only conspecific calls and do not approach other species, preventing mating.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The species-specific call is a behavioral prezygotic barrier; females only approach males whose call matches, preventing cross-species mating.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Give one example of a postzygotic isolating mechanism and explain how it reduces hybrid fitness.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must name one: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, or hybrid breakdown; explains correctly.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Hybrid sterility is postzygotic: mules (horse x donkey) are born healthy but cannot reproduce, reducing hybrid fitness to zero.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a)(i) Define synapomorphy and explain why it is more informative for constructing phylogenies than symplesiomorphy (a shared ancestral character).
(a)(ii) Using the character matrix data, construct the most parsimonious cladogram for species A–E, identify the outgroup, and explain your reasoning.
(a)(iii) Explain what "most parsimonious" means in phylogenetic analysis.
(a)(iv) Explain why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.
stimulus:
Character matrix (1 = character present, 0 = absent):
               | Char 1 | Char 2 | Char 3 | Char 4
Species A      |   0    |   0    |   0    |   0    (outgroup)
Species B      |   1    |   0    |   0    |   0
Species C      |   1    |   1    |   0    |   0
Species D      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   0
Species E      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   1

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Defines synapomorphy as a shared derived character.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: A clear definition distinguishing a derived (newly evolved) character from an ancestral one.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that a synapomorphy is a shared character derived from a common ancestor, distinguishing it from an ancestral (underived) character.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains why synapomorphies, not symplesiomorphies, are informative for building phylogenies.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Explains that shared ancestral characters (symplesiomorphies) are present broadly across a group and do not distinguish sub-groups, while shared derived characters mark recent common ancestry.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that only shared derived characters indicate recent common ancestry; shared ancestral characters are uninformative because they are shared too broadly.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Constructs the most-parsimonious cladogram from the matrix, identifies species A as the outgroup, and explains the reasoning.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Correct nested topology (A,(B,(C,(D,E)))); identifies A as the outgroup because it lacks all four derived characters.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Give the correct topology and identify A as the outgroup because it has none of the derived characters shared by B-E.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains what "most parsimonious" means and why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that the most parsimonious tree requires the fewest evolutionary changes (character-state transitions), and that parsimony is preferred because it requires the fewest unsupported assumptions (independent convergent origins) of the character data.
frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that parsimony minimizes the number of required evolutionary changes, and that this is preferred because it assumes the fewest independent, unsupported evolutionary events.

parent_canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) A synapomorphy is a shared derived character — a trait that arose in a common ancestor of a group and is shared by its descendants — distinguishing that group (clade) from other lineages. A symplesiomorphy is a shared ancestral character present in the group's common ancestor and also in more distantly related outgroup taxa; it is not useful for resolving relationships within the group because its presence does not indicate which taxa share a more recent common ancestor — it is too broadly distributed to be informative.
(ii) Using the character matrix, Species A lacks all four characters and represents the ancestral condition, so it is the outgroup. Species B has only character 1; Species C has characters 1 and 2; Species D has characters 1, 2, and 3; Species E has characters 1, 2, 3, and 4. This nested pattern of shared derived characters produces the most parsimonious cladogram: (A,(B,(C,(D,E)))) — A branches off first as the outgroup, then B, then C, with D and E as the most closely related sister taxa (sharing character 3, with E uniquely possessing character 4).
(iii) "Most parsimonious" means the cladogram requiring the fewest total number of evolutionary character-state changes to explain the observed distribution of traits among the taxa. Parsimony is preferred in phylogenetic analysis because, all else being equal, the simplest explanation requiring the fewest independent (convergent) evolutionary events is the most probable and avoids unnecessary assumptions about homoplasy (the same trait evolving independently more than once).

(b)(i) Neutral mutations, by definition, do not affect an organism's fitness and so are not acted on by natural selection; their rate of fixation in a population is governed mainly by the underlying mutation rate, which tends to be relatively stable over time for a given gene and lineage. Because these mutations are not selected for or against, their accumulation approximates a constant, clock-like rate over time, forming the basis of the molecular clock.
(ii) Using the given calibration (1% cytochrome b sequence divergence corresponds to approximately 2 million years): Human-Gorilla divergence of 4.0% times 2 Mya per percent equals approximately 8.0 million years ago.
(iii) Two reasons the molecular clock is not perfectly constant: (1) mutation and generation rates differ among lineages — species with shorter generation times undergo more DNA replications per unit time and tend to accumulate mutations faster than species with longer generation times, so different lineages' clocks tick at different absolute rates; (2) selective pressures vary among genes, lineages, and over time — some genomic regions experience differing degrees of purifying or positive selection in different lineages, causing deviations from a strictly neutral, constant rate of accumulation (differences in DNA repair efficiency and uncertainty/inaccuracy in fossil calibration dates also contribute to clock imperfection).

(c)(i) Homoplasy (analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution) arises when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar traits in response to similar selective pressures or environments, rather than through shared ancestry. If a morphological phylogenetic analysis mistakenly treats these convergent similarities as synapomorphies (shared derived traits indicating common ancestry), it will incorrectly group these unrelated organisms together as if they were closely related, producing an inaccurate tree.
(ii) Molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable for resolving deep evolutionary relationships because DNA and protein sequences provide vastly more independent characters (thousands of nucleotide or amino acid positions) than morphology offers (a limited number of visible traits), which reduces the relative influence of any single misleading homoplasious character, and molecular changes are generally less subject to convergent selective pressures than gross external morphology. A well-known example is that molecular data revealed hippopotamuses to be the closest living relatives of whales (Cetacea), a relationship not evident from morphology alone, overturning earlier morphology-based classifications that had grouped whales more closely with other terrestrial mammal groups based on convergent similarities.

(d) Three lines of evidence: (1) Reproductive compatibility/hybridization testing — determining whether the two populations can successfully interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural or controlled conditions; full interbreeding with fertile offspring supports classification as the same species or subspecies, while reduced hybrid viability or sterility supports separate species status. (2) Genetic/DNA sequence divergence — comparing DNA sequence differences (such as mitochondrial DNA or whole-genome divergence) between the two populations; genetic distances comparable to those typically seen between recognized separate species would support species status, while smaller divergence comparable to normal within-species variation would support subspecies status. (3) Morphological and ecological differentiation — comparing consistent, diagnostic differences in physical traits (body size, coloration, skull shape) and ecological niche (habitat use, diet, behavior) between the populations; substantial and consistent diagnostic differences support species-level distinction, whereas overlapping or continuously varying traits support classification as subspecies.

parent_canonical_answer_1:
(a)(i) A synapomorphy is a shared derived character — a trait that arose in a common ancestor of a group and is shared by its descendants — distinguishing that group (clade) from other lineages. A symplesiomorphy is a shared ancestral character present in the group's common ancestor and also in more distantly related outgroup taxa; it is not useful for resolving relationships within the group because its presence does not indicate which taxa share a more recent common ancestor — it is too broadly distributed to be informative.
(ii) Using the character matrix, Species A lacks all four characters and represents the ancestral condition, so it is the outgroup. Species B has only character 1; Species C has characters 1 and 2; Species D has characters 1, 2, and 3; Species E has characters 1, 2, 3, and 4. This nested pattern of shared derived characters produces the most parsimonious cladogram: (A,(B,(C,(D,E)))) — A branches off first as the outgroup, then B, then C, with D and E as the most closely related sister taxa (sharing character 3, with E uniquely possessing character 4).
(iii) "Most parsimonious" means the cladogram requiring the fewest total number of evolutionary character-state changes to explain the observed distribution of traits among the taxa. Parsimony is preferred in phylogenetic analysis because, all else being equal, the simplest explanation requiring the fewest independent (convergent) evolutionary events is the most probable and avoids unnecessary assumptions about homoplasy (the same trait evolving independently more than once).

(b)(i) Neutral mutations, by definition, do not affect an organism's fitness and so are not acted on by natural selection; their rate of fixation in a population is governed mainly by the underlying mutation rate, which tends to be relatively stable over time for a given gene and lineage. Because these mutations are not selected for or against, their accumulation approximates a constant, clock-like rate over time, forming the basis of the molecular clock.
(ii) Using the given calibration (1% cytochrome b sequence divergence corresponds to approximately 2 million years): Human-Gorilla divergence of 4.0% times 2 Mya per percent equals approximately 8.0 million years ago.
(iii) Two reasons the molecular clock is not perfectly constant: (1) mutation and generation rates differ among lineages — species with shorter generation times undergo more DNA replications per unit time and tend to accumulate mutations faster than species with longer generation times, so different lineages' clocks tick at different absolute rates; (2) selective pressures vary among genes, lineages, and over time — some genomic regions experience differing degrees of purifying or positive selection in different lineages, causing deviations from a strictly neutral, constant rate of accumulation (differences in DNA repair efficiency and uncertainty/inaccuracy in fossil calibration dates also contribute to clock imperfection).

(c)(i) Homoplasy (analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution) arises when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar traits in response to similar selective pressures or environments, rather than through shared ancestry. If a morphological phylogenetic analysis mistakenly treats these convergent similarities as synapomorphies (shared derived traits indicating common ancestry), it will incorrectly group these unrelated organisms together as if they were closely related, producing an inaccurate tree.
(ii) Molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable for resolving deep evolutionary relationships because DNA and protein sequences provide vastly more independent characters (thousands of nucleotide or amino acid positions) than morphology offers (a limited number of visible traits), which reduces the relative influence of any single misleading homoplasious character, and molecular changes are generally less subject to convergent selective pressures than gross external morphology. A well-known example is that molecular data revealed hippopotamuses to be the closest living relatives of whales (Cetacea), a relationship not evident from morphology alone, overturning earlier morphology-based classifications that had grouped whales more closely with other terrestrial mammal groups based on convergent similarities.

(d) Three lines of evidence: (1) Reproductive compatibility/hybridization testing — determining whether the two populations can successfully interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural or controlled conditions; full interbreeding with fertile offspring supports classification as the same species or subspecies, while reduced hybrid viability or sterility supports separate species status. (2) Genetic/DNA sequence divergence — comparing DNA sequence differences (such as mitochondrial DNA or whole-genome divergence) between the two populations; genetic distances comparable to those typically seen between recognized separate species would support species status, while smaller divergence comparable to normal within-species variation would support subspecies status. (3) Morphological and ecological differentiation — comparing consistent, diagnostic differences in physical traits (body size, coloration, skull shape) and ecological niche (habitat use, diet, behavior) between the populations; substantial and consistent diagnostic differences support species-level distinction, whereas overlapping or continuously varying traits support classification as subspecies.

prior_prompt_json.subject: AP Biology

criteria.learner_facing_text: Plots all nine ordered pairs at recoverable locations.
Labels forage biomass and rabbit population size on the correct axes.
Sketches a reasonable increasing line through the point cloud.
Describes a strong, positive, roughly linear association in context.

prior_prompt_json.stimulus:
Ecologists recorded rabbit population size and available forage biomass across nine sample plots. Construct a scatterplot, sketch a reasonable trend line, and describe the direction, form, and strength of the association in context.

| Forage biomass (kg/hectare) | Rabbit population size |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 24 |
| 20 | 13 |
| 30 | 21 |
| 40 | 18 |
| 50 | 46 |
| 60 | 49 |
| 70 | 33 |
| 80 | 50 |
| 90 | 43 |
